passages.original: “There now,” she said. “I’ve talked broad Yorkshire again like Mrs. Medlock said I mustn’t. ‘Nowt o’ th’ soart’ means ‘nothin’-of-the-sort,’” slowly and carefully, “but it takes so long to say it. Yorkshire’s th’ sunniest place on earth when it is sunny. I told thee tha’d like th’ moor after a bit. Just you wait till you see th’ gold-colored gorse blossoms an’ th’ blossoms o’ th’ broom, an’ th’ heather flowerin’, all purple bells, an’ hundreds o’ butterflies flutterin’ an’ bees hummin’ an’ skylarks soarin’ up an’ singin’. You’ll want to get out on it at sunrise an’ live out on it all day like Dickon does.”
passages.vernacular: 「睇,」佢講。「我又講咗好濃嘅約克郡話,像梅德洛克太太講我唔能夠講嘅。『根本唔係嗰樣』嘅意思係『啲都唔係嗰樣』,」慢慢小心地講,「但講起嚟花咁長時間。約克郡有太陽時,係地球上最有陽光嘅地方。我告訴過你,你過一會兒會鍾意荒野。你只要等住睇金黃色嘅荊豆花同金雀花嘅花,同石楠開花,全係紫色嘅鈴鐺,同成百上千嘅蝴蝶飛舞、蜜蜂嗡嗡、雲雀升起歌唱。你會想喺日出時出去,像迪肯嗰樣整天生活喺嗰上面。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「看,」她說。「我又說了很濃的約克郡話,像梅德洛克太太說我不能說的。『根本不是那樣』的意思是『一點也不是那樣』,」慢慢小心地說,「但說起來花那麼長時間。約克郡有太陽時,是地球上最有陽光的地方。我告訴過你,你過一會兒會喜歡荒野。你只要等著看金黃色的荊豆花和金雀花的花,和石楠開花,全是紫色的鈴鐺,和成百上千的蝴蝶飛舞、蜜蜂嗡嗡、雲雀升起歌唱。你會想在日出時出去,像迪肯那樣整天生活在那上面。」

passages.original: “Could I ever get there?” asked Mary wistfully, looking through her window at the far-off blue. It was so new and big and wonderful and such a heavenly color.
passages.vernacular: 「我永遠能到嗰度去嗎?」瑪麗渴望地問,透過窗子睇遠處嘅藍色。佢咁新、咁大、咁奇妙,有咁天堂般嘅顏色。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我永遠能到那裡去嗎?」瑪麗渴望地問,透過窗子看遠處的藍色。它那麼新、那麼大、那麼奇妙,有那麼天堂般的顏色。

passages.original: “I don’t know,” answered Martha. “Tha’s never used tha’ legs since tha’ was born, it seems to me. Tha’ couldn’t walk five mile. It’s five mile to our cottage.”
passages.vernacular: 「我唔知道,」瑪莎回答。「喺我睇來,你自從出生就從冇用過你嘅腿。你走不咗五英里。到我哋小屋係五英里。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我不知道,」瑪莎回答。「在我看來,你自從出生就從沒用過你的腿。你走不了五英里。到我們小屋是五英里。」

passages.original: “I should like to see your cottage.”
passages.vernacular: 「我想睇睇你哋嘅小屋。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我想看看你們的小屋。」

passages.original: Martha stared at her a moment curiously before she took up her polishing brush and began to rub the grate again. She was thinking that the small plain face did not look quite as sour at this moment as it had done the first morning she saw it. It looked just a trifle like little Susan Ann’s when she wanted something very much.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎好奇地盯住佢一會兒,然後攞起佢嘅擦亮刷,又開始擦爐柵。佢喺想,呢張小小樸素嘅臉此刻睇起嚟不像佢第一天早晨睇到佢時咁酸喇。佢睇起嚟有點像小蘇珊·安好想要乜嘢時嘅樣子。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎好奇地盯著她一會兒,然後拿起她的擦亮刷,又開始擦爐柵。她在想,這張小小樸素的臉此刻看起來不像她第一天早晨看到它時那麼酸了。它看起來有點像小蘇珊·安非常想要什麼時的樣子。

passages.original: “I’ll ask my mother about it,” she said. “She’s one o’ them that nearly always sees a way to do things. It’s my day out today an’ I’m goin’ home. Eh! I am glad. Mrs. Medlock thinks a lot o’ mother. Perhaps she could talk to her.”
passages.vernacular: 「我去問我媽媽,」佢講。「佢係嗰種幾乎總能睇到辦法嘅人。今日係我休息日,我要回家。唉!我好高興。梅德洛克太太好睇重媽媽。或者佢可以同佢談。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我去問我媽媽,」她說。「她是那種幾乎總能看到辦法的人。今天是我休息日,我要回家。唉!我好高興。梅德洛克太太很看重媽媽。也許她可以同她談。」

passages.original: “I like your mother,” said Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「我鍾意你媽媽,」瑪麗講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我喜歡你媽媽,」瑪麗說。

passages.original: “I should think tha’ did,” agreed Martha, polishing away.
passages.vernacular: 「我想你會,」瑪莎同意,繼續擦住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我想你會,」瑪莎同意,繼續擦著。

passages.original: “I’ve never seen her,” said Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「我冇見過佢,」瑪麗講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我沒見過她,」瑪麗說。

passages.original: “No, tha’ hasn’t,” replied Martha.
passages.vernacular: 「係,你冇,」瑪莎回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是,你沒有,」瑪莎回答。

passages.original: She sat up on her heels again and rubbed the end of her nose with the back of her hand as if puzzled for a moment, but she ended quite positively.
passages.vernacular: 佢又坐直腳跟,用手背擦咗擦鼻尖,好像困惑咗一會兒,但佢相當肯定地結束喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她又坐直腳跟,用手背擦了擦鼻尖,好像困惑了一會兒,但她相當肯定地結束了。

passages.original: “Well, she’s that sensible an’ hard workin’ an’ good-natured an’ clean that no one could help likin’ her whether they’d seen her or not. When I’m goin’ home to her on my day out I just jump for joy when I’m crossin’ the moor.”
passages.vernacular: 「嗯,佢咁明理、辛勤工作、好心腸又乾淨,冇人不鍾意佢,不管佢哋見過佢同否。我休息日回家見佢時,穿過荒野時我高興得直跳。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗯,她那麼明理、辛勤工作、好心腸又乾淨,沒有人不喜歡她,不管他們見過她與否。我休息日回家見她時,穿過荒野時我高興得直跳。」

passages.original: “I like Dickon,” added Mary. “And I’ve never seen him.”
passages.vernacular: 「我鍾意迪肯,」瑪麗補充。「我從冇見過佢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我喜歡迪肯,」瑪麗補充。「我從沒見過他。」

passages.original: “Well,” said Martha stoutly, “I’ve told thee that th’ very birds likes him an’ th’ rabbits an’ wild sheep an’ ponies, an’ th’ foxes themselves. I wonder,” staring at her reflectively, “what Dickon would think of thee?”
passages.vernacular: 「嗯,」瑪莎堅定地講,「我告訴過你,連鳥都鍾意佢,仲有兔子、野羊同小馬,同狐狸本身。我喺想,」若有所思地盯住佢,「迪肯會點睇你?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗯,」瑪莎堅定地說,「我告訴過你,連鳥也喜歡他,還有兔子、野羊和小馬,和狐狸本身。我在想,」若有所思地盯著她,「迪肯會怎麼看你?」

passages.original: “He wouldn’t like me,” said Mary in her stiff, cold little way. “No one does.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢唔會鍾意我,」瑪麗用佢僵硬、冷淡嘅小方式講。「冇人鍾意。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他不會喜歡我,」瑪麗用她僵硬、冷淡的小方式說。「沒有人喜歡。」

passages.original: Martha looked reflective again.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎又若有所思。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎又若有所思。

passages.original: “How does tha’ like thysel’?” she inquired, really quite as if she were curious to know.
passages.vernacular: 「你點鍾意你自己?」佢問,真嘅好像好好奇想知道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你怎麼喜歡你自己?」她問,真的好像很好奇想知道。

passages.original: Mary hesitated a moment and thought it over.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗猶豫咗片刻,想咗想。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗猶豫了片刻,想了想。

passages.original: “Not at all—really,” she answered. “But I never thought of that before.”
passages.vernacular: 「啲都不——真嘅,」佢回答。「但我以前從冇想過呢個。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「一點也不——真的,」她回答。「但我以前從沒想過這個。」

passages.original: Martha grinned a little as if at some homely recollection.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎微微咧嘴笑,好像想起咗某個家常嘅回憶。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎微微咧嘴笑,好像想起了某個家常的回憶。

passages.original: “Mother said that to me once,” she said. “She was at her wash-tub an’ I was in a bad temper an’ talkin’ ill of folk, an’ she turns round on me an’ says: ‘Tha’ young vixen, tha’! There tha’ stands sayin’ tha’ doesn’t like this one an’ tha’ doesn’t like that one. How does tha’ like thysel’?’ It made me laugh an’ it brought me to my senses in a minute.”
passages.vernacular: 「媽媽有一次對我講呢個,」佢講。「佢喺洗衣盆邊,我脾氣不好,講人壞話,佢轉過身對我講:『你呢小潑婦!你站喺嗰度講你不鍾意呢個人,不鍾意嗰個人。你點鍾意你自己?』呢讓我笑喇,一下子使我清醒過嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「媽媽有一次對我說這個,」她說。「她在洗衣盆邊,我脾氣不好,說人壞話,她轉過身對我說:『你這小潑婦!你站在那裡說你不喜歡這個人,不喜歡那個人。你怎麼喜歡你自己?』這讓我笑了,一下子使我清醒過來。」

passages.original: She went away in high spirits as soon as she had given Mary her breakfast. She was going to walk five miles across the moor to the cottage, and she was going to help her mother with the washing and do the week’s baking and enjoy herself thoroughly.
passages.vernacular: 佢畀瑪麗送過早餐後就興高采烈地走喇。佢要走五英里穿過荒野到小屋,佢要幫媽媽洗衣服,做一週嘅烘焙,盡情享受。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她給瑪麗送過早餐後就興高采烈地走了。她要走五英里穿過荒野到小屋,她要幫媽媽洗衣服,做一週的烘焙,盡情享受。

passages.original: Mary felt lonelier than ever when she knew she was no longer in the house. She went out into the garden as quickly as possible, and the first thing she did was to run round and round the fountain flower garden ten times. She counted the times carefully and when she had finished she felt in better spirits. The sunshine made the whole place look different. The high, deep, blue sky arched over Misselthwaite as well as over the moor, and she kept lifting her face and looking up into it, trying to imagine what it would be like to lie down on one of the little snow-white clouds and float about. She went into the first kitchen-garden and found Ben Weatherstaff working there with two other gardeners. The change in the weather seemed to have done him good. He spoke to her of his own accord.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗知道佢唔再喺房子裡時,比以往更孤單。佢盡快走進花園,佢做嘅第一件事係繞住噴泉花園一圈又一圈跑咗十次。佢仔細數咗次數,跑完後,佢心情好些。陽光使整個地方睇起嚟不同。高高嘅、深藍色嘅天空既拱喺米瑟斯威特上空,都拱喺荒野上空,佢不斷抬起臉睇佢,試圖想像躺喺一朵雪白嘅小雲上漂浮係乜嘢樣。佢走進第一個菜園,發現班·韋瑟斯塔夫同另外兩個園丁喺嗰度工作。天氣嘅變化似乎對佢有好處。佢主動對佢講話。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗知道她不再在房子裡時,比以往更孤單。她盡快走進花園,她做的第一件事是繞著噴泉花園一圈又一圈跑了十次。她仔細數了次數,跑完後,她心情好些。陽光使整個地方看起來不同。高高的、深藍色的天空既拱在米瑟斯威特上空,也拱在荒野上空,她不斷抬起臉看它,試圖想像躺在一朵雪白的小雲上漂浮是什麼樣。她走進第一個菜園,發現班·韋瑟斯塔夫同另外兩個園丁在那裡工作。天氣的變化似乎對他有好處。他主動對她說話。

passages.original: “Springtime’s comin,’” he said. “Cannot tha’ smell it?”
passages.vernacular: 「春天嚟喇,」佢講。「你聞唔到嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「春天來了,」他說。「你聞不到嗎?」

passages.original: Mary sniffed and thought she could.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗嗅咗嗅,認為佢能。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗嗅了嗅,認為她能。

passages.original: “I smell something nice and fresh and damp,” she said.
passages.vernacular: 「我聞到一種好聞嘅、新鮮潮濕嘅嘢,」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我聞到一種好聞的、新鮮潮濕的東西,」她說。

passages.original: “That’s th’ good rich earth,” he answered, digging away. “It’s in a good humor makin’ ready to grow things. It’s glad when plantin’ time comes. It’s dull in th’ winter when it’s got nowt to do. In th’ flower gardens out there things will be stirrin’ down below in th’ dark. Th’ sun’s warmin’ ’em. You’ll see bits o’ green spikes stickin’ out o’ th’ black earth after a bit.”
passages.vernacular: 「嗰個係好嘅肥沃嘅土壤,」佢回答,繼續挖。「佢心情好,準備好長嘢。種植時間到時佢好高興。冬天佢無事可做時好沉悶。喺外面嘅花園裡,下面黑暗中嘅嘢會喺動。太陽喺溫暖佢哋。過一會兒你會睇到小小嘅綠尖從黑色嘅土裡伸出嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那是好的肥沃的土壤,」他回答,繼續挖。「它心情好,準備好長東西。種植時間到時它很高興。冬天它無事可做時很沉悶。在外面的花園裡,下面黑暗中的東西會在動。太陽在溫暖它們。過一會兒你會看到小小的綠尖從黑色的土裡伸出來。」

passages.original: “What will they be?” asked Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「佢哋係乜嘢?」瑪麗問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「它們是什麼?」瑪麗問。

passages.original: “Crocuses an’ snowdrops an’ daffydowndillys. Has tha’ never seen them?”
passages.vernacular: 「番紅花、雪花蓮同黃水仙。你從冇見過佢哋嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「番紅花、雪花蓮和黃水仙。你從沒見過它們嗎?」

passages.original: “No. Everything is hot, and wet, and green after the rains in India,” said Mary. “And I think things grow up in a night.”
passages.vernacular: 「冇。喺印度,雨後一切都係熱、濕、綠嘅,」瑪麗講。「我想嘢一夜之間就長起嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「沒有。在印度,雨後一切都是熱、濕、綠的,」瑪麗說。「我想東西一夜之間就長起來。」

passages.original: “These won’t grow up in a night,” said Weatherstaff. “Tha’ll have to wait for ’em. They’ll poke up a bit higher here, an’ push out a spike more there, an’ uncurl a leaf this day an’ another that. You watch ’em.”
passages.vernacular: 「呢啲唔會一夜長起嚟,」韋瑟斯塔夫講。「你得等佢哋。佢哋喺呢度長高啲,嗰度伸出一根尖,今日展開一片葉子,聽日又一片。你睇住佢哋。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這些不會一夜長起來,」韋瑟斯塔夫說。「你得等它們。它們在這裡長高一點,那裡伸出一根尖,今天展開一片葉子,明天又一片。你看著它們。」

passages.original: “I am going to,” answered Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「我會嘅,」瑪麗回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我會的,」瑪麗回答。

passages.original: Very soon she heard the soft rustling flight of wings again and she knew at once that the robin had come again. He was very pert and lively, and hopped about so close to her feet, and put his head on one side and looked at her so slyly that she asked Ben Weatherstaff a question.
passages.vernacular: 好快佢又聽到翅膀輕輕嘅沙沙飛行聲,佢即刻知道知更鳥又嚟喇。佢好活潑俏皮,喺佢腳邊蹦跳,把頭歪向一邊,咁狡黠地睇住佢,佢問咗班·韋瑟斯塔夫一個問題。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 很快她又聽到翅膀輕輕的沙沙飛行聲,她立刻知道知更鳥又來了。他非常活潑俏皮,在她腳邊蹦跳,把頭歪向一邊,那麼狡黠地看著她,她問了班·韋瑟斯塔夫一個問題。

passages.original: “Do you think he remembers me?” she said.
passages.vernacular: 「你認為佢記得我嗎?」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你認為他記得我嗎?」她說。

passages.original: “Remembers thee!” said Weatherstaff indignantly. “He knows every cabbage stump in th’ gardens, let alone th’ people. He’s never seen a little wench here before, an’ he’s bent on findin’ out all about thee. Tha’s no need to try to hide anything from him.”
passages.vernacular: 「記得你!」韋瑟斯塔夫憤慨地講。「佢知道花園裡每個白菜樁,更唔好講人喇。佢以前從冇喺呢度見過小丫頭,佢一心要查明你嘅一切。你唔使試圖對佢隱瞞任何事。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「記得你!」韋瑟斯塔夫憤慨地說。「他知道花園裡每個白菜樁,更別說人了。他以前從沒在這裡見過小丫頭,他一心要查明你的一切。你不必試圖對他隱瞞任何事。」

passages.original: “Are things stirring down below in the dark in that garden where he lives?” Mary inquired.
passages.vernacular: 「佢住嘅嗰個花園裡,下面黑暗中嘅嘢喺動嗎?」瑪麗問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他住的那個花園裡,下面黑暗中的東西在動嗎?」瑪麗問。

passages.original: “What garden?” grunted Weatherstaff, becoming surly again.
passages.vernacular: 「乜嘢花園?」韋瑟斯塔夫咕噥,又變得暴躁。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「什麼花園?」韋瑟斯塔夫咕噥,又變得暴躁。

passages.original: “The one where the old rose-trees are.” She could not help asking, because she wanted so much to know. “Are all the flowers dead, or do some of them come again in the summer? Are there ever any roses?”
passages.vernacular: 「有老玫瑰樹嘅嗰個。」佢忍不住問,因為佢太想知道。「花都死咗嗎,定係有些喺夏天會再嚟?有玫瑰嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「有老玫瑰樹的那個。」她忍不住問,因為她太想知道。「花都死了嗎,還是有些在夏天會再來?有玫瑰嗎?」

passages.original: “Ask him,” said Ben Weatherstaff, hunching his shoulders toward the robin. “He’s the only one as knows. No one else has seen inside it for ten year’.”
passages.vernacular: 「問佢,」班·韋瑟斯塔夫講,朝知更鳥聳咗聳肩。「佢係唯一知道嘅。十年嚟冇別人睇過裡面。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「問他,」班·韋瑟斯塔夫說,朝知更鳥聳了聳肩。「他是唯一知道的。十年來沒有別人看過裡面。」

passages.original: Ten years was a long time, Mary thought. She had been born ten years ago.
passages.vernacular: 十年係好長嘅時間,瑪麗想。佢就係十年前出生嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 十年是很長的時間,瑪麗想。她就是十年前出生的。

passages.original: She walked away, slowly thinking. She had begun to like the garden just as she had begun to like the robin and Dickon and Martha’s mother. She was beginning to like Martha, too. That seemed a good many people to like—when you were not used to liking. She thought of the robin as one of the people. She went to her walk outside the long, ivy-covered wall over which she could see the tree-tops; and the second time she walked up and down the most interesting and exciting thing happened to her, and it was all through Ben Weatherstaff’s robin.
passages.vernacular: 佢慢慢地走開,思考住。佢開始鍾意呢個花園,就像佢開始鍾意知更鳥、迪肯同瑪莎嘅母親一樣。佢都開始鍾意瑪莎。呢似乎係好多要鍾意嘅人——當你不習慣鍾意嘅時候。佢把知更鳥想成其中一個人。佢走到長長嘅、常春藤覆蓋嘅牆外佢嘅走道,喺嗰上面可以睇到樹梢;佢第二次嚟回走時,最有趣最令人興奮嘅事發生喺佢身上,呢全係通過班·韋瑟斯塔夫嘅知更鳥。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她慢慢地走開,思考著。她開始喜歡這個花園,就像她開始喜歡知更鳥、迪肯和瑪莎的母親一樣。她也開始喜歡瑪莎。這似乎是很多要喜歡的人——當你不習慣喜歡的時候。她把知更鳥想成其中一個人。她走到長長的、常春藤覆蓋的牆外她的走道,在那上面可以看到樹梢;她第二次來回走時,最有趣最令人興奮的事發生在她身上,這全是通過班·韋瑟斯塔夫的知更鳥。

passages.original: She heard a chirp and a twitter, and when she looked at the bare flower-bed at her left side there he was hopping about and pretending to peck things out of the earth to persuade her that he had not followed her. But she knew he had followed her and the surprise so filled her with delight that she almost trembled a little.
passages.vernacular: 佢聽到一聲啾啾同一聲鳴叫,睇佢左側光禿嘅花壇時,佢就喺嗰度蹦跳,假裝從地裡啄嘢,好講服佢佢冇跟住佢。但佢知道佢跟住佢,驚喜使佢咁高興,佢幾乎有點發抖。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她聽到一聲啾啾和一聲鳴叫,看她左側光禿的花壇時,他就在那裡蹦跳,假裝從地裡啄東西,好說服她他沒有跟著她。但她知道他跟著她,驚喜使她那麼高興,她幾乎有點發抖。

passages.original: “You do remember me!” she cried out. “You do! You are prettier than anything else in the world!”
passages.vernacular: 「你確實記得我!」佢喊道。「你確實!你比世上任何嘢都漂亮!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你確實記得我!」她喊道。「你確實!你比世上任何東西都漂亮!」

passages.original: She chirped, and talked, and coaxed and he hopped, and flirted his tail and twittered. It was as if he were talking. His red waistcoat was like satin and he puffed his tiny breast out and was so fine and so grand and so pretty that it was really as if he were showing her how important and like a human person a robin could be. Mistress Mary forgot that she had ever been contrary in her life when he allowed her to draw closer and closer to him, and bend down and talk and try to make something like robin sounds.
passages.vernacular: 佢啾啾叫,講話,哄佢,佢蹦跳,擺尾巴,啁啾。好像佢喺講話。佢嘅紅背心像緞子,佢挺起小小嘅胸脯,咁精緻、咁氣派、咁漂亮,真像係喺向佢展示一隻知更鳥可以幾咁重要、幾咁像人。瑪麗小姐忘咗佢呢輩子曾經任性,因為佢允許佢越嚟越靠近佢,彎下腰講話,試圖發出像知更鳥嘅聲音。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她啾啾叫,說話,哄他,他蹦跳,擺尾巴,啁啾。好像他在說話。他的紅背心像緞子,他挺起小小的胸脯,那麼精緻、那麼氣派、那麼漂亮,真像是在向她展示一隻知更鳥可以多麼重要、多麼像人。瑪麗小姐忘了她這輩子曾經任性,因為他允許她越來越靠近他,彎下腰說話,試圖發出像知更鳥的聲音。

passages.original: Oh! to think that he should actually let her come as near to him as that! He knew nothing in the world would make her put out her hand toward him or startle him in the least tiniest way. He knew it because he was a real person—only nicer than any other person in the world. She was so happy that she scarcely dared to breathe.
passages.vernacular: 哦!想想佢竟然真嘅讓佢靠得咁近!佢知道世上冇乜嘢會讓佢朝佢伸手,或以最小嘅方式驚嚇佢。佢知道,因為佢係個真正嘅人——只係比世上任何其他人更好。佢咁高興,幾乎唔敢呼吸。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 哦!想想他竟然真的讓她靠得那麼近!他知道世上沒有什麼會讓她朝他伸手,或以最小的方式驚嚇他。他知道,因為他是個真正的人——只是比世上任何其他人更好。她那麼高興,幾乎不敢呼吸。

passages.original: The flower-bed was not quite bare. It was bare of flowers because the perennial plants had been cut down for their winter rest, but there were tall shrubs and low ones which grew together at the back of the bed, and as the robin hopped about under them she saw him hop over a small pile of freshly turned up earth. He stopped on it to look for a worm. The earth had been turned up because a dog had been trying to dig up a mole and he had scratched quite a deep hole.
passages.vernacular: 花壇並不完全光禿。佢冇花,因為多年生植物已經被剪掉去過冬休息,但花壇後面有高嘅同矮嘅灌木長喺一起,知更鳥喺佢哋下面蹦跳時,佢睇到佢跳過一小堆新翻起嘅泥土。佢喺上面停下找蟲子。泥土被翻起嚟,係因為一隻狗曾試圖挖一隻鼴鼠,把洞抓得相當深。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 花壇並不完全光禿。它沒有花,因為多年生植物已經被剪掉去過冬休息,但花壇後面有高的和矮的灌木長在一起,知更鳥在它們下面蹦跳時,她看到他跳過一小堆新翻起的泥土。他在上面停下找蟲子。泥土被翻起來,是因為一隻狗曾試圖挖一隻鼴鼠,把洞抓得相當深。

passages.original: Mary looked at it, not really knowing why the hole was there, and as she looked she saw something almost buried in the newly-turned soil. It was something like a ring of rusty iron or brass and when the robin flew up into a tree nearby she put out her hand and picked the ring up. It was more than a ring, however; it was an old key which looked as if it had been buried a long time.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗睇住佢,真嘅唔知道洞點解喺嗰度,睇住時,佢睇到有乜嘢幾乎埋喺新翻嘅土裡。佢有點像一圈生鏽嘅鐵或黃銅,知更鳥飛到附近一棵樹上時,佢伸手撿起咗嗰圈嘢。然而,佢不只係個圈;佢係一把舊鑰匙,睇起嚟像被埋咗好長時間。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗看著它,真的不知道洞為什麼在那裡,看著時,她看到有什麼幾乎埋在新翻的土裡。它有點像一圈生鏽的鐵或黃銅,知更鳥飛到附近一棵樹上時,她伸手撿起了那圈東西。然而,它不只是個圈;它是一把舊鑰匙,看起來像被埋了很長時間。

passages.original: Mistress Mary stood up and looked at it with an almost frightened face as it hung from her finger.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗小姐站起嚟,臉上帶住幾乎驚恐嘅神情睇住佢,佢從佢手指上垂住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗小姐站起來,臉上帶著幾乎驚恐的神情看著它,它從她手指上垂著。

passages.original: “Perhaps it has been buried for ten years,” she said in a whisper. “Perhaps it is the key to the garden!”
passages.vernacular: 「或者佢已經被埋咗十年,」佢低聲講。「或者佢係花園嘅鑰匙!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「也許它已經被埋了十年,」她低聲說。「也許它是花園的鑰匙!」

chapters.title: Chapter VIII: The Robin Who Showed the Way 第八章:帶路的知更鳥

passages.original: She looked at the key quite a long time. She turned it over and over, and thought about it. As I have said before, she was not a child who had been trained to ask permission or consult her elders about things. All she thought about the key was that if it was the key to the closed garden, and she could find out where the door was, she could perhaps open it and see what was inside the walls, and what had happened to the old rose-trees. It was because it had been shut up so long that she wanted to see it. It seemed as if it must be different from other places and that something strange must have happened to it during ten years. Besides that, if she liked it she could go into it every day and shut the door behind her, and she could make up some play of her own and play it quite alone, because nobody would ever know where she was, but would think the door was still locked and the key buried in the earth. The thought of that pleased her very much.
passages.vernacular: 佢睇住嗰把鑰匙睇咗相當長嘅時間。佢把佢翻嚟覆去,思考佢。正如我以前講過嘅,佢唔係被訓練成要請求許可或就事情向長輩請教嘅細路。關於呢把鑰匙,佢所想嘅全部係:如果佢係關閉嘅花園嘅鑰匙,而佢能找出門喺邊度,佢或者可以打開佢,睇睇牆裡面有乜嘢,老玫瑰樹發生咗乜嘢事。正因為佢被關咗咁久,佢才想睇佢。似乎佢一定同其他地方不同,喺十年裡一定發生咗乜嘢奇怪嘅事。此外,如果佢鍾意,佢可以每天進去,把門喺身後關上,佢可以編造啲自己嘅遊戲,完全獨自玩,因為冇人會知道佢喺邊度,而會以為門仍然鎖住,鑰匙埋喺泥土裡。呢個念頭使佢好高興。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她看著那把鑰匙看了相當長的時間。她把它翻來覆去,思考它。正如我以前說過的,她不是被訓練成要請求許可或就事情向長輩請教的孩子。關於這把鑰匙,她所想的全部是:如果它是關閉的花園的鑰匙,而她能找出門在哪裡,她也許可以打開它,看看牆裡面有什麼,老玫瑰樹發生了什麼事。正因為它被關了那麼久,她才想看它。似乎它一定與其他地方不同,在十年裡一定發生了什麼奇怪的事。此外,如果她喜歡,她可以每天進去,把門在身後關上,她可以編造一些自己的遊戲,完全獨自玩,因為沒有人會知道她在哪裡,而會以為門仍然鎖著,鑰匙埋在泥土裡。這個念頭使她非常高興。

passages.original: Living as it were, all by herself in a house with a hundred mysteriously closed rooms and having nothing whatever to do to amuse herself, had set her inactive brain to working and was actually awakening her imagination. There is no doubt that the fresh, strong, pure air from the moor had a great deal to do with it. Just as it had given her an appetite, and fighting with the wind had stirred her blood, so the same things had stirred her mind. In India she had always been too hot and languid and weak to care much about anything, but in this place she was beginning to care and to want to do new things. Already she felt less “contrary,” though she did not know why.
passages.vernacular: 可以講獨自生活喺一座有一百個神祕關閉房間嘅房子裡,完全無事可做嚟消遣,已使佢不活動嘅大腦開始工作,並真嘅喚醒咗佢嘅想像力。毫無疑問,來自荒野嘅新鮮、強勁、純淨嘅空氣同此有好大關係。正如佢畀咗佢胃口,同風搏鬥激發咗佢嘅血液,同樣嘅嘢都激發咗佢嘅心智。喺印度佢總是太熱、太懶散、太虛弱,不太在乎任何事,但喺呢個地方,佢開始在乎並想做新嘅事。佢已經覺得不咁「任性」喇,雖然佢唔知道點解。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 可以說獨自生活在一座有一百個神祕關閉房間的房子裡,完全無事可做來消遣,已使她不活動的大腦開始工作,並真的喚醒了她的想像力。毫無疑問,來自荒野的新鮮、強勁、純淨的空氣與此有很大關係。正如它給了她胃口,同風搏鬥激發了她的血液,同樣的東西也激發了她的心智。在印度她總是太熱、太懶散、太虛弱,不太在乎任何事,但在這個地方,她開始在乎並想做新的事。她已經覺得不那麼「任性」了,雖然她不知道為什麼。

passages.original: She put the key in her pocket and walked up and down her walk. No one but herself ever seemed to come there, so she could walk slowly and look at the wall, or, rather, at the ivy growing on it. The ivy was the baffling thing. Howsoever carefully she looked she could see nothing but thickly growing, glossy, dark green leaves. She was very much disappointed. Something of her contrariness came back to her as she paced the walk and looked over it at the tree-tops inside. It seemed so silly, she said to herself, to be near it and not be able to get in. She took the key in her pocket when she went back to the house, and she made up her mind that she would always carry it with her when she went out, so that if she ever should find the hidden door she would be ready.
passages.vernacular: 佢把鑰匙放喺口袋裡,喺佢嘅走道上嚟回走。除咗佢自己似乎冇人嚟嗰度,所以佢可以慢慢走,睇嗰堵牆,或者更確切地講,睇牆上長嘅常春藤。常春藤係令人困惑嘅嘢。不管佢幾咁仔細地睇,佢乜嘢都睇唔到,只有濃密生長、發亮嘅深綠色葉子。佢好失望。佢喺走道上踱步,越過佢睇裡面嘅樹梢時,佢嘅啲任性回嚟喇。佢對自己講,靠近佢卻進不去似乎太愚蠢。佢回房子時把鑰匙放喺口袋裡,下定決心出去時總要帶住佢,咁樣如果佢找到隱藏嘅門,就準備好喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她把鑰匙放在口袋裡,在她的走道上來回走。除了她自己似乎沒有人來那裡,所以她可以慢慢走,看那堵牆,或者更確切地說,看牆上長的常春藤。常春藤是令人困惑的東西。不管她多麼仔細地看,她什麼也看不到,只有濃密生長、發亮的深綠色葉子。她非常失望。她在走道上踱步,越過它看裡面的樹梢時,她的一些任性回來了。她對自己說,靠近它卻進不去似乎太愚蠢。她回房子時把鑰匙放在口袋裡,下定決心出去時總要帶著它,這樣如果她找到隱藏的門,就準備好了。

passages.original: Mrs. Medlock had allowed Martha to sleep all night at the cottage, but she was back at her work in the morning with cheeks redder than ever and in the best of spirits.
passages.vernacular: 梅德洛克太太允許瑪莎整夜瞓喺小屋,但佢早晨回嚟工作,臉頰比以往更紅,精神極好。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 梅德洛克太太允許瑪莎整夜睡在小屋,但她早晨回來工作,臉頰比以往更紅,精神極好。

passages.original: “I got up at four o’clock,” she said. “Eh! it was pretty on th’ moor with th’ birds gettin’ up an’ th’ rabbits scamperin’ about an’ th’ sun risin’. I didn’t walk all th’ way. A man gave me a ride in his cart an’ I did enjoy myself.”
passages.vernacular: 「我四點起床,」佢講。「唉!荒野上好漂亮,鳥兒起嚟,兔子到處蹦跳,太陽升起。我冇一路走回嚟。一個人用佢嘅車載我一程,我真嘅好享受。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我四點起床,」她說。「唉!荒野上很漂亮,鳥兒起來,兔子到處蹦跳,太陽升起。我沒有一路走回來。一個人用他的車載我一程,我真的很享受。」

passages.original: She was full of stories of the delights of her day out. Her mother had been glad to see her and they had got the baking and washing all out of the way. She had even made each of the children a doughcake with a bit of brown sugar in it.
passages.vernacular: 佢滿係關於佢休息日歡樂嘅故事。佢母親好高興見到佢,佢哋把烘焙同洗衣都做完喇。佢甚至畀每個細路做咗一個加咗啲紅糖嘅麵團餅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她滿是關於她休息日歡樂的故事。她母親很高興見到她,她們把烘焙和洗衣都做完了。她甚至給每個孩子做了一個加了一點紅糖的麵團餅。

passages.original: “I had ’em all pipin’ hot when they came in from playin’ on th’ moor. An’ th’ cottage all smelt o’ nice, clean hot bakin’ an’ there was a good fire, an’ they just shouted for joy. Our Dickon he said our cottage was good enough for a king to live in.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢哋喺荒野上玩回嚟時,我讓佢哋都食到熱騰騰嘅。小屋聞起嚟全係好聞、乾淨、熱烘烘嘅烘焙味,有一堆好火,佢哋高興得叫喊。我哋嘅迪肯講我哋嘅小屋夠好,國王都可以住。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他們在荒野上玩回來時,我讓他們都吃到熱騰騰的。小屋聞起來全是好聞、乾淨、熱烘烘的烘焙味,有一堆好火,他們高興得叫喊。我們的迪肯說我們的小屋夠好,國王都可以住。」

passages.original: In the evening they had all sat round the fire, and Martha and her mother had sewed patches on torn clothes and mended stockings and Martha had told them about the little girl who had come from India and who had been waited on all her life by what Martha called “blacks” until she didn’t know how to put on her own stockings.
passages.vernacular: 傍晚佢哋都圍住火坐住,瑪莎同佢母親喺破衣服上縫補丁、補襪子,瑪莎告訴佢哋嗰個從印度嚟嘅小女孩,佢一生被瑪莎稱為「黑人」嘅人伺候,以致佢唔知道點穿自己嘅襪子。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 傍晚他們都圍著火坐著,瑪莎和她母親在破衣服上縫補丁、補襪子,瑪莎告訴他們那個從印度來的小女孩,她一生被瑪莎稱為「黑人」的人伺候,以致她不知道怎麼穿自己的襪子。

passages.original: “Eh! they did like to hear about you,” said Martha. “They wanted to know all about th’ blacks an’ about th’ ship you came in. I couldn’t tell ’em enough.”
passages.vernacular: 「唉!佢哋好愛聽關於你嘅事,」瑪莎講。「佢哋想知道關於黑人同你乘嘅船嘅一切。我點講都講唔夠。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「唉!他們很愛聽關於你的事,」瑪莎說。「他們想知道關於黑人和你乘的船的一切。我怎麼講也講不夠。」

passages.original: Mary reflected a little.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗想咗一會兒。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗想了一會兒。

passages.original: “I’ll tell you a great deal more before your next day out,” she said, “so that you will have more to talk about. I dare say they would like to hear about riding on elephants and camels, and about the officers going to hunt tigers.”
passages.vernacular: 「喺你下次休息日之前,我會告訴你更多,」佢講,「咁樣你就有更多話可講。我敢講佢哋會想聽騎大象同駱駝,同軍官去獵老虎。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「在你下次休息日之前,我會告訴你更多,」她說,「這樣你就有更多話可說。我敢說他們會想聽騎大象和駱駝,和軍官去獵老虎。」

passages.original: “My word!” cried delighted Martha. “It would set ’em clean off their heads. Would tha’ really do that, Miss? It would be same as a wild beast show like we heard they had in York once.”
passages.vernacular: 「天呀!」高興嘅瑪莎喊道。「嗰會讓佢哋完全發瘋。你真嘅會咁樣做嗎,小姐?嗰就像我哋聽講喺約克有過一次嘅野獸展覽。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「天哪!」高興的瑪莎喊道。「那會讓他們完全發瘋。你真的會這樣做嗎,小姐?那就像我們聽說在約克有過一次的野獸展覽。」

passages.original: “India is quite different from Yorkshire,” Mary said slowly, as she thought the matter over. “I never thought of that. Did Dickon and your mother like to hear you talk about me?”
passages.vernacular: 「印度和約克郡完全不同,」瑪麗慢慢講,思考住呢件事。「我以前從冇想過。迪肯同你媽媽鍾意聽你談我嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「印度和約克郡完全不同,」瑪麗慢慢說,思考著這件事。「我以前從沒想過。迪肯和你媽媽喜歡聽你談我嗎?」

passages.original: “Why, our Dickon’s eyes nearly started out o’ his head, they got that round,” answered Martha. “But mother, she was put out about your seemin’ to be all by yourself like. She said, ‘Hasn’t Mr. Craven got no governess for her, nor no nurse?’ and I said, ‘No, he hasn’t, though Mrs. Medlock says he will when he thinks of it, but she says he mayn’t think of it for two or three years.’”
passages.vernacular: 「哎呀,我哋嘅迪肯嘅眼睛幾乎凸出嚟,圓成嗰樣,」瑪莎回答。「但媽媽,佢對你似乎孤身一人感到不安。佢講:『克雷文先生冇畀佢請家庭教師,都冇請保姆嗎?』我講:『冇,雖然梅德洛克太太講佢想到時會嘅,但佢講佢或者兩三年都想唔到。』」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哎呀,我們的迪肯的眼睛幾乎凸出來,圓成那樣,」瑪莎回答。「但媽媽,她對你似乎孤身一人感到不安。她說:『克雷文先生沒給她請家庭教師,也沒請保姆嗎?』我說:『沒有,雖然梅德洛克太太說他想到時會的,但她說他也許兩三年也想不到。』」

passages.original: “I don’t want a governess,” said Mary sharply.
passages.vernacular: 「我唔好家庭教師,」瑪麗尖銳地講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我不要家庭教師,」瑪麗尖銳地說。

passages.original: “But mother says you ought to be learnin’ your book by this time an’ you ought to have a woman to look after you, an’ she says: ‘Now, Martha, you just think how you’d feel yourself, in a big place like that, wanderin’ about all alone, an’ no mother. You do your best to cheer her up,’ she says, an’ I said I would.”
passages.vernacular: 「但媽媽講你而家應該學書喇,你應該有個女人睇顧你,佢講:『而家,瑪莎,你想想你自己會有乜嘢感覺,喺嗰樣嘅大地方,獨自遊蕩,冇媽媽。你盡力讓佢高興起嚟,』佢講,我講我會。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「但媽媽說你現在應該學書了,你應該有個女人看顧你,她說:『現在,瑪莎,你想想你自己會有什麼感覺,在那樣的大地方,獨自遊蕩,沒有媽媽。你盡力讓她高興起來,』她說,我說我會。」

passages.original: Mary gave her a long, steady look.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗長時間穩定地睇住佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗長時間穩定地看著她。

passages.original: “You do cheer me up,” she said. “I like to hear you talk.”
passages.vernacular: 「你確實讓我高興起嚟,」佢講。「我鍾意聽你講話。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你確實讓我高興起來,」她說。「我喜歡聽你說話。」

passages.original: Presently Martha went out of the room and came back with something held in her hands under her apron.
passages.vernacular: 不久瑪莎走出房間,回嚟時手裡攞住乜嘢,藏喺圍裙下面。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 不久瑪莎走出房間,回來時手裡拿著什麼,藏在圍裙下面。

passages.original: “What does tha’ think,” she said, with a cheerful grin. “I’ve brought thee a present.”
passages.vernacular: 「你猜點住,」佢講,愉快地咧嘴笑。「我畀你帶咗一件禮物。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你猜怎麼著,」她說,愉快地咧嘴笑。「我給你帶了一件禮物。」

passages.original: “A present!” exclaimed Mistress Mary. How could a cottage full of fourteen hungry people give anyone a present!
passages.vernacular: 「禮物!」瑪麗小姐喊道。一個擠滿十四個飢餓嘅人嘅小屋點能畀任何人禮物!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「禮物!」瑪麗小姐喊道。一個擠滿十四個飢餓的人的小屋怎麼能給任何人禮物!

passages.original: “A man was drivin’ across the moor peddlin’,” Martha explained. “An’ he stopped his cart at our door. He had pots an’ pans an’ odds an’ ends, but mother had no money to buy anythin’. Just as he was goin’ away our ’Lizabeth Ellen called out, ‘Mother, he’s got skippin’-ropes with red an’ blue handles.’ An’ mother she calls out quite sudden, ‘Here, stop, mister! How much are they?’ An’ he says ‘Tuppence’, an’ mother she began fumblin’ in her pocket an’ she says to me, ‘Martha, tha’s brought me thy wages like a good lass, an’ I’ve got four places to put every penny, but I’m just goin’ to take tuppence out of it to buy that child a skippin’-rope,’ an’ she bought one an’ here it is.”
passages.vernacular: 「一個人趕車穿過荒野叫賣,」瑪莎解釋。「佢把車停喺我哋門口。佢有鍋碗瓢盆同雜七雜八嘅嘢,但媽媽冇錢買任何嘢。佢正要走時,我哋嘅伊麗莎白·艾倫喊道:『媽媽,佢有跳繩,紅色同藍色嘅手柄。』媽媽突然喊:『等一下,先生!多少錢?』佢講『兩便士』,媽媽開始喺口袋裡摸索,佢對我講:『瑪莎,你像好姑娘一樣把你嘅工資帶嚟畀我,我每一便士都有四個地方要放,但我要從中攞出兩便士,畀嗰細路買一根跳繩,』佢買咗一根,就係呢度呢根。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「一個人趕車穿過荒野叫賣,」瑪莎解釋。「他把車停在我們門口。他有鍋碗瓢盆和雜七雜八的東西,但媽媽沒有錢買任何東西。他正要走時,我們的伊麗莎白·艾倫喊道:『媽媽,他有跳繩,紅色和藍色的手柄。』媽媽突然喊:『等一下,先生!多少錢?』他說『兩便士』,媽媽開始在口袋裡摸索,她對我說:『瑪莎,你像好姑娘一樣把你的工資帶來給我,我每一便士都有四個地方要放,但我要從中拿出兩便士,給那孩子買一根跳繩,』她買了一根,就是這裡這根。」

passages.original: She brought it out from under her apron and exhibited it quite proudly. It was a strong, slender rope with a striped red and blue handle at each end, but Mary Lennox had never seen a skipping-rope before. She gazed at it with a mystified expression.
passages.vernacular: 佢從圍裙下攞出嚟,相當驕傲地展示。嗰個係一根結實、細長嘅繩子,兩端各有一個紅藍條紋嘅手柄,但瑪麗·倫諾克斯以前從冇見過跳繩。佢帶住困惑嘅表情凝視佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她從圍裙下拿出來,相當驕傲地展示。那是一根結實、細長的繩子,兩端各有一個紅藍條紋的手柄,但瑪麗·倫諾克斯以前從沒見過跳繩。她帶著困惑的表情凝視它。

passages.original: “What is it for?” she asked curiously.
passages.vernacular: 「呢個係做乜嘢用嘅?」佢好奇地問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這是做什麼用的?」她好奇地問。

passages.original: “For!” cried out Martha. “Does tha’ mean that they’ve not got skippin’-ropes in India, for all they’ve got elephants and tigers and camels! No wonder most of ’em’s black. This is what it’s for; just watch me.”
passages.vernacular: 「做乜嘢用!」瑪莎喊道。「你係講佢哋喺印度冇跳繩,雖然佢哋有大象、老虎同駱駝!難怪大多數人係黑嘅。呢個係咁樣用嘅;睇我。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「做什麼用!」瑪莎喊道。「你是說他們在印度沒有跳繩,雖然他們有大象、老虎和駱駝!難怪大多數人是黑的。這是這樣用的;看我。」

passages.original: And she ran into the middle of the room and, taking a handle in each hand, began to skip, and skip, and skip, while Mary turned in her chair to stare at her, and the queer faces in the old portraits seemed to stare at her, too, and wonder what on earth this common little cottager had the impudence to be doing under their very noses. But Martha did not even see them. The interest and curiosity in Mistress Mary’s face delighted her, and she went on skipping and counted as she skipped until she had reached a hundred.
passages.vernacular: 佢跑到房間中間,雙手各握一個手柄,開始跳,跳,跳,瑪麗喺椅子上轉身盯住佢,舊肖像裡嘅古怪面孔似乎都盯住佢,納悶呢個粗俗嘅小村婦到底有乜嘢膽量喺佢哋眼皮底下做呢個。但瑪莎甚至冇睇到佢哋。瑪麗小姐臉上嘅興趣同好奇使佢高興,佢繼續跳,邊跳邊數,直到數到一百。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她跑到房間中間,雙手各握一個手柄,開始跳,跳,跳,瑪麗在椅子上轉身盯著她,舊肖像裡的古怪面孔似乎也盯著她,納悶這個粗俗的小村婦到底有什麼膽量在他們眼皮底下做這個。但瑪莎甚至沒看到它們。瑪麗小姐臉上的興趣和好奇使她高興,她繼續跳,邊跳邊數,直到數到一百。

passages.original: “I could skip longer than that,” she said when she stopped. “I’ve skipped as much as five hundred when I was twelve, but I wasn’t as fat then as I am now, an’ I was in practice.”
passages.vernacular: 「我仲能跳得比嗰更久,」佢停下時講。「我十二歲時跳過多達五百下,但我嗰時不像而家咁胖,而且我喺練習。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我還能跳得比那更久,」她停下時說。「我十二歲時跳過多達五百下,但我那時不像現在這麼胖,而且我在練習。」

passages.original: Mary got up from her chair beginning to feel excited herself.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗從椅子上站起嚟,自己都開始興奮。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗從椅子上站起來,自己也開始興奮。

passages.original: “It looks nice,” she said. “Your mother is a kind woman. Do you think I could ever skip like that?”
passages.vernacular: 「睇起嚟好好,」佢講。「你媽媽係個好心嘅女人。你認為我能跳得像嗰樣嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「看起來很好,」她說。「你媽媽是個好心的女人。你認為我能跳得像那樣嗎?」

passages.original: “You just try it,” urged Martha, handing her the skipping-rope. “You can’t skip a hundred at first, but if you practice you’ll mount up. That’s what mother said. She says, ‘Nothin’ will do her more good than skippin’ rope. It’s th’ sensiblest toy a child can have. Let her play out in th’ fresh air skippin’ an’ it’ll stretch her legs an’ arms an’ give her some strength in ’em.’”
passages.vernacular: 「你試試,」瑪莎催促,把跳繩遞畀佢。「你一開始跳不咗一百下,但如果你練習,會一路增加。呢個係媽媽講嘅。佢講:『冇乜嘢比跳繩對佢更有好處。呢個係細路能有嘅最明智嘅玩具。讓佢喺新鮮空氣中出去跳繩,佢會伸展佢嘅腿同臂,畀佢哋啲力氣。』」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你試試,」瑪莎催促,把跳繩遞給她。「你一開始跳不了一百下,但如果你練習,會一路增加。這是媽媽說的。她說:『沒有什麼比跳繩對她更有好處。這是孩子能有的最明智的玩具。讓她在新鮮空氣中出去跳繩,它會伸展她的腿和臂,給它們一些力氣。』」

passages.original: It was plain that there was not a great deal of strength in Mistress Mary’s arms and legs when she first began to skip. She was not very clever at it, but she liked it so much that she did not want to stop.
passages.vernacular: 好明顯,瑪麗小姐剛開始跳時,佢嘅臂同腿冇多少力氣。佢跳得不太好,但佢咁鍾意,唔想停下嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 很明顯,瑪麗小姐剛開始跳時,她的臂和腿沒有多少力氣。她跳得不太好,但她那麼喜歡,不想停下來。

passages.original: “Put on tha’ things and run an’ skip out o’ doors,” said Martha. “Mother said I must tell you to keep out o’ doors as much as you could, even when it rains a bit, so as tha’ wrap up warm.”
passages.vernacular: 「穿上衣服,到外面跑跑跳跳,」瑪莎講。「媽媽講我要告訴你盡量待喺戶外,即使下啲雨,只要你穿暖同。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「穿上衣服,到外面跑跑跳跳,」瑪莎說。「媽媽說我要告訴你盡量待在戶外,即使下一點雨,只要你穿暖和。」

passages.original: Mary put on her coat and hat and took her skipping-rope over her arm. She opened the door to go out, and then suddenly thought of something and turned back rather slowly.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗穿上外套同帽子,把跳繩搭喺手臂上。佢打開門要出去,然後突然想到乜嘢,相當慢地轉身回嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗穿上外套和帽子,把跳繩搭在手臂上。她打開門要出去,然後突然想到什麼,相當慢地轉身回來。

passages.original: “Martha,” she said, “they were your wages. It was your two-pence really. Thank you.” She said it stiffly because she was not used to thanking people or noticing that they did things for her. “Thank you,” she said, and held out her hand because she did not know what else to do.
passages.vernacular: 「瑪莎,」佢講,「嗰個係你嘅工資。其實係你嘅兩便士。謝謝你。」佢講得好僵硬,因為佢不習慣謝謝人,或注意到別人為佢做事。「謝謝你,」佢講,伸出手,因為佢唔知道仲能做乜嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「瑪莎,」她說,「那是你的工資。其實是你的兩便士。謝謝你。」她說得很僵硬,因為她不習慣謝謝人,或注意到別人為她做事。「謝謝你,」她說,伸出手,因為她不知道還能做什麼。

passages.original: Martha gave her hand a clumsy little shake, as if she was not accustomed to this sort of thing either. Then she laughed.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎笨拙地輕輕握咗握佢嘅手,好像佢都不習慣呢類事。然後佢笑喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎笨拙地輕輕握了握她的手,好像她也不習慣這類事。然後她笑了。

passages.original: “Eh! th’ art a queer, old-womanish thing,” she said. “If tha’d been our ’Lizabeth Ellen tha’d have given me a kiss.”
passages.vernacular: 「唉!你呢個古怪嘅、像老太婆嘅嘢,」佢講。「如果你係我哋嘅伊麗莎白·艾倫,你會畀我一個吻。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「唉!你這個古怪的、像老太婆的東西,」她說。「如果你是我們的伊麗莎白·艾倫,你會給我一個吻。」

passages.original: Mary looked stiffer than ever.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗睇起嚟比以往更僵硬。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗看起來比以往更僵硬。

passages.original: “Do you want me to kiss you?”
passages.vernacular: 「你要我吻你嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你要我吻你嗎?」

passages.original: Martha laughed again.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎又笑喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎又笑了。

passages.original: “Nay, not me,” she answered. “If tha’ was different, p’raps tha’d want to thysel’. But tha’ isn’t. Run off outside an’ play with thy rope.”
passages.vernacular: 「不,唔係我,」佢回答。「如果你不同,或者你自己會想。但你唔係。跑到外面,玩你嘅繩。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「不,不是我,」她回答。「如果你不同,也許你自己會想。但你不是。跑到外面,玩你的繩。」

passages.original: Mistress Mary felt a little awkward as she went out of the room. Yorkshire people seemed strange, and Martha was always rather a puzzle to her. At first she had disliked her very much, but now she did not. The skipping-rope was a wonderful thing. She counted and skipped, and skipped and counted, until her cheeks were quite red, and she was more interested than she had ever been since she was born. The sun was shining and a little wind was blowing—not a rough wind, but one which came in delightful little gusts and brought a fresh scent of newly turned earth with it. She skipped round the fountain garden, and up one walk and down another. She skipped at last into the kitchen-garden and saw Ben Weatherstaff digging and talking to his robin, which was hopping about him. She skipped down the walk toward him and he lifted his head and looked at her with a curious expression. She had wondered if he would notice her. She wanted him to see her skip.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗小姐走出房間時,感到有點尷尬。約克郡人似乎奇怪,瑪莎對佢總是有點謎。起初佢好不鍾意佢,但而家佢不喇。跳繩係個奇妙嘅嘢。佢數啊跳、跳啊數,直到臉頰通紅,佢比佢出生以來任何時候都更有興趣。陽光燦爛,有啲風——唔係粗暴嘅風,而係以愉快嘅小陣吹嚟,帶住新翻泥土嘅清新氣味。佢繞住噴泉花園跳,上一條小路又下另一條。最後佢跳進菜園,睇到班·韋瑟斯塔夫喺挖地,同佢嘅知更鳥講話,知更鳥喺佢周圍蹦跳。佢沿住走道朝佢跳去,佢抬起頭,帶住好奇嘅表情睇住佢。佢曾納悶佢會唔會注意到佢。佢想讓佢睇佢跳繩。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗小姐走出房間時,感到有點尷尬。約克郡人似乎奇怪,瑪莎對她總是有點謎。起初她非常不喜歡她,但現在她不了。跳繩是個奇妙的東西。她數啊跳、跳啊數,直到臉頰通紅,她比她出生以來任何時候都更有興趣。陽光燦爛,有一點風——不是粗暴的風,而是以愉快的小陣吹來,帶著新翻泥土的清新氣味。她繞著噴泉花園跳,上一條小路又下另一條。最後她跳進菜園,看到班·韋瑟斯塔夫在挖地,同他的知更鳥說話,知更鳥在他周圍蹦跳。她沿著走道朝他跳去,他抬起頭,帶著好奇的表情看著她。她曾納悶他會不會注意到她。她想讓他看她跳繩。

passages.original: “Well!” he exclaimed. “Upon my word. P’raps tha’ art a young ’un, after all, an’ p’raps tha’s got child’s blood in thy veins instead of sour buttermilk. Tha’s skipped red into thy cheeks as sure as my name’s Ben Weatherstaff. I wouldn’t have believed tha’ could do it.”
passages.vernacular: 「嘿!」佢喊道。「講真嘅。或者你畢竟係個年輕人,或者你血管裡流嘅係細路嘅血,而唔係酸酪乳。你跳出咗臉頰嘅紅色,就像我叫班·韋瑟斯塔夫一樣肯定。我本不相信你能做到。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嘿!」他喊道。「說真的。也許你畢竟是個年輕人,也許你血管裡流的是孩子的血,而不是酸酪乳。你跳出了臉頰的紅色,就像我叫班·韋瑟斯塔夫一樣肯定。我本不相信你能做到。」

passages.original: “I never skipped before,” Mary said. “I’m just beginning. I can only go up to twenty.”
passages.vernacular: 「我以前從冇跳過,」瑪麗講。「我才剛開始。我只能跳到二十。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我以前從沒跳過,」瑪麗說。「我才剛開始。我只能跳到二十。」

passages.original: “Tha’ keep on,” said Ben. “Tha’ shapes well enough at it for a young ’un that’s lived with heathen. Just see how he’s watchin’ thee,” jerking his head toward the robin. “He followed after thee yesterday. He’ll be at it again today. He’ll be bound to find out what th’ skippin’-rope is. He’s never seen one. Eh!” shaking his head at the bird, “tha’ curiosity will be th’ death of thee sometime if tha’ doesn’t look sharp.”
passages.vernacular: 「你繼續,」班講。「對一個同異教徒生活過嘅年輕人,你跳得夠好喇。睇佢點睇住你,」朝知更鳥擺咗擺頭。「佢尋日跟住你。今日佢又會。佢一定要查明跳繩係乜嘢。佢從冇見過。唉!」朝鳥搖住頭,「你嘅好奇心有一天會害死你,如果你不當心。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你繼續,」班說。「對一個同異教徒生活過的年輕人,你跳得夠好了。看他怎麼看著你,」朝知更鳥擺了擺頭。「他昨天跟著你。今天他又會。他一定要查明跳繩是什麼。他從沒見過。唉!」朝鳥搖著頭,「你的好奇心有一天會害死你,如果你不當心。」

passages.original: Mary skipped round all the gardens and round the orchard, resting every few minutes. At length she went to her own special walk and made up her mind to try if she could skip the whole length of it. It was a good long skip and she began slowly, but before she had gone half-way down the path she was so hot and breathless that she was obliged to stop. She did not mind much, because she had already counted up to thirty. She stopped with a little laugh of pleasure, and there, lo and behold, was the robin swaying on a long branch of ivy. He had followed her and he greeted her with a chirp. As Mary had skipped toward him she felt something heavy in her pocket strike against her at each jump, and when she saw the robin she laughed again.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗繞住所有花園同果園跳,每隔幾分鐘休息一下。最後佢走到自己嘅專屬走道,下定決心試試能唔能夠跳完佢嘅全長。呢個係個相當長嘅跳,佢慢慢開始,但仲冇跳到小路一半,佢咁熱、咁喘不過氣,唔得不停下。佢不太介意,因為佢已經數到咗三十。佢帶住一聲愉快嘅小笑停下,睇邊,知更鳥正擺動喺一條長常春藤枝上。佢跟住佢,啾地向佢打招呼。瑪麗朝佢跳去時,佢感覺口袋裡有乜嘢重嘅嘢每跳一下就撞佢一下,睇到知更鳥時,佢又笑喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗繞著所有花園和果園跳,每隔幾分鐘休息一下。最後她走到自己的專屬走道,下定決心試試能不能跳完它的全長。這是個相當長的跳,她慢慢開始,但還沒跳到小路一半,她那麼熱、那麼喘不過氣,不得不停下。她不太介意,因為她已經數到了三十。她帶著一聲愉快的小笑停下,看哪,知更鳥正擺動在一條長常春藤枝上。他跟著她,啾地向她打招呼。瑪麗朝他跳去時,她感覺口袋裡有什麼重的東西每跳一下就撞她一下,看到知更鳥時,她又笑了。

passages.original: “You showed me where the key was yesterday,” she said. “You ought to show me the door today; but I don’t believe you know!”
passages.vernacular: 「尋日你畀我睇咗鑰匙喺邊度,」佢講。「今日你應該畀我睇門;但我不相信你知道!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「昨天你給我看了鑰匙在哪裡,」她說。「今天你應該給我看門;但我不相信你知道!」

passages.original: The robin flew from his swinging spray of ivy on to the top of the wall and he opened his beak and sang a loud, lovely trill, merely to show off. Nothing in the world is quite as adorably lovely as a robin when he shows off—and they are nearly always doing it.
passages.vernacular: 知更鳥從佢擺動嘅常春藤嫩枝飛到牆頂,張開喙,唱咗一段響亮可愛嘅顫音,純粹係為了炫耀。世上冇乜嘢像知更鳥炫耀時嗰樣可愛得令人崇拜——而佢哋幾乎總是喺炫耀。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 知更鳥從他擺動的常春藤嫩枝飛到牆頂,張開喙,唱了一段響亮可愛的顫音,純粹是為了炫耀。世上沒有什麼像知更鳥炫耀時那樣可愛得令人崇拜——而他們幾乎總是在炫耀。

passages.original: Mary Lennox had heard a great deal about Magic in her Ayah’s stories, and she always said that what happened almost at that moment was Magic.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗·倫諾克斯喺佢阿雅嘅故事裡聽過好多關於魔法嘅事,佢總是講幾乎就喺嗰一刻發生嘅事係魔法。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗·倫諾克斯在她阿雅的故事裡聽過很多關於魔法的事,她總是說幾乎就在那一刻發生的事是魔法。

passages.original: One of the nice little gusts of wind rushed down the walk, and it was a stronger one than the rest. It was strong enough to wave the branches of the trees, and it was more than strong enough to sway the trailing sprays of untrimmed ivy hanging from the wall. Mary had stepped close to the robin, and suddenly the gust of wind swung aside some loose ivy trails, and more suddenly still she jumped toward it and caught it in her hand. This she did because she had seen something under it—a round knob which had been covered by the leaves hanging over it. It was the knob of a door.
passages.vernacular: 一陣愉快嘅小風沖下走道,比其他嘅更強。佢強得足以搖動樹枝,而且比強得足以搖動從牆上垂下嘅未修剪嘅拖曳常春藤嫩枝仲強。瑪麗走近知更鳥,突然呢陣風把啲鬆散嘅常春藤藤蔓蕩向一邊,更突然地,佢跳向佢,一手抓住咗佢。佢咁樣做係因為佢喺佢下面睇到咗乜嘢——一個被垂喺上面嘅葉子遮住嘅圓門把。嗰個係一扇門嘅把手。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一陣愉快的小風沖下走道,比其他的更強。它強得足以搖動樹枝,而且比強得足以搖動從牆上垂下的未修剪的拖曳常春藤嫩枝還強。瑪麗走近知更鳥,突然這陣風把一些鬆散的常春藤藤蔓蕩向一邊,更突然地,她跳向它,一手抓住了它。她這樣做是因為她在它下面看到了什麼——一個被垂在上面的葉子遮住的圓門把。那是一扇門的把手。

passages.original: She put her hands under the leaves and began to pull and push them aside. Thick as the ivy hung, it nearly all was a loose and swinging curtain, though some had crept over wood and iron. Mary’s heart began to thump and her hands to shake a little in her delight and excitement. The robin kept singing and twittering away and tilting his head on one side, as if he were as excited as she was. What was this under her hands which was square and made of iron and which her fingers found a hole in?
passages.vernacular: 佢把手伸到葉子下面,開始拉開、推開佢哋。常春藤雖然垂得濃密,幾乎全係鬆散擺動嘅簾幕,雖然有些爬過咗木頭同鐵。瑪麗嘅心開始怦怦跳,佢嘅手喺喜悅同興奮中有點發抖。知更鳥不停地歌唱、啁啾,把頭歪向一邊,好像佢同佢一樣興奮。佢手下呢個方形、鐵做嘅、佢嘅手指喺上面發現一個洞嘅嘢係乜嘢?
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她把手伸到葉子下面,開始拉開、推開它們。常春藤雖然垂得濃密,幾乎全是鬆散擺動的簾幕,雖然有些爬過了木頭和鐵。瑪麗的心開始怦怦跳,她的手在喜悅和興奮中有點發抖。知更鳥不停地歌唱、啁啾,把頭歪向一邊,好像他和她一樣興奮。她手下這個方形、鐵做的、她的手指在上面發現一個洞的東西是什麼?

passages.original: It was the lock of the door which had been closed ten years and she put her hand in her pocket, drew out the key and found it fitted the keyhole. She put the key in and turned it. It took two hands to do it, but it did turn.
passages.vernacular: 嗰個係已關閉十年嘅門嘅鎖,佢把手伸進口袋,攞出鑰匙,發現佢正好適合鑰匙孔。佢把鑰匙插進去,轉動。要兩隻手才轉得動,但佢確實轉喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那是已關閉十年的門的鎖,她把手伸進口袋,拿出鑰匙,發現它正好適合鑰匙孔。她把鑰匙插進去,轉動。要兩隻手才轉得動,但它確實轉了。

passages.original: And then she took a long breath and looked behind her up the long walk to see if anyone was coming. No one was coming. No one ever did come, it seemed, and she took another long breath, because she could not help it, and she held back the swinging curtain of ivy and pushed back the door which opened slowly—slowly.
passages.vernacular: 然後佢深吸一口氣,回頭睇長長嘅走道,睇有冇人嚟。冇人嚟。似乎從來冇人嚟,佢又深吸咗一口氣,因為佢忍不住,佢扶住擺動嘅常春藤簾,推開門,門慢慢地——慢慢地打開喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後她深吸一口氣,回頭看長長的走道,看有沒有人來。沒有人來。似乎從來沒有人來,她又深吸了一口氣,因為她忍不住,她扶住擺動的常春藤簾,推開門,門慢慢地——慢慢地打開了。

passages.original: Then she slipped through it, and shut it behind her, and stood with her back against it, looking about her and breathing quite fast with excitement, and wonder, and delight.
passages.vernacular: 然後佢從中溜咗進去,喺身後關上佢,背靠住佢站住,環顧四周,因興奮、驚奇同喜悅而呼吸相當快。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後她從中溜了進去,在身後關上它,背靠著它站著,環顧四周,因興奮、驚奇和喜悅而呼吸相當快。

passages.original: She was standing inside the secret garden.
passages.vernacular: 佢站喺祕密花園裡面。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她站在祕密花園裡面。

chapters.title: Chapter IX: The Strangest House Anyone Ever Lived In 第九章:世上最奇怪的房子

passages.original: It was the sweetest, most mysterious-looking place anyone could imagine. The high walls which shut it in were covered with the leafless stems of climbing roses which were so thick that they were matted together. Mary Lennox knew they were roses because she had seen a great many roses in India. All the ground was covered with grass of a wintry brown and out of it grew clumps of bushes which were surely rosebushes if they were alive. There were numbers of standard roses which had so spread their branches that they were like little trees. There were other trees in the garden, and one of the things which made the place look strangest and loveliest was that climbing roses had run all over them and swung down long tendrils which made light swaying curtains, and here and there they had caught at each other or at a far-reaching branch and had crept from one tree to another and made lovely bridges of themselves. There were neither leaves nor roses on them now and Mary did not know whether they were dead or alive, but their thin gray or brown branches and sprays looked like a sort of hazy mantle spreading over everything, walls, and trees, and even brown grass, where they had fallen from their fastenings and run along the ground. It was this hazy tangle from tree to tree which made it all look so mysterious. Mary had thought it must be different from other gardens which had not been left all by themselves so long; and indeed it was different from any other place she had ever seen in her life.
passages.vernacular: 嗰個係任何人能想像到嘅最甜美、最神祕嘅地方。圍住佢嘅高牆上覆蓋住攀緣玫瑰冇葉子嘅枝幹,佢哋咁密,纏結喺一起。瑪麗·倫諾克斯知道佢哋係玫瑰,因為佢喺印度見過好多玫瑰。所有嘅地面都覆蓋住冬季褐色嘅草,草中長出一簇簇灌木,如果佢哋仲活住,肯定係玫瑰叢。有許多標準玫瑰,佢哋嘅枝條伸展開,像小樹一樣。花園裡仲有其他樹,使呢個地方顯得最奇怪最可愛嘅事物之一係,攀緣玫瑰爬滿咗佢哋,垂下長長嘅卷鬚,形成輕輕搖擺嘅簾幕,呢度嗰度佢哋互相纏住或勾住一根伸得遠嘅樹枝,從一棵樹爬到另一棵樹,把自己做成可愛嘅橋。佢哋上面而家既冇葉子都冇玫瑰,瑪麗唔知道佢哋係死係活,但佢哋纖細嘅灰色或褐色嘅枝條同嫩枝,睇起嚟像一種朦朧嘅披風,鋪喺一切上面,牆、樹,甚至褐色嘅草,佢哋從固定處掉落、沿地面蔓延之處。正是呢種從樹到樹嘅朦朧糾纏,使一切睇起嚟咁神祕。瑪麗認為佢一定同冇被獨自留下咁久嘅其他花園不同;確實佢同佢一生見過嘅任何其他地方都不同。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那是任何人能想像到的最甜美、最神祕的地方。圍住它的高牆上覆蓋著攀緣玫瑰沒有葉子的枝幹,它們那麼密,纏結在一起。瑪麗·倫諾克斯知道它們是玫瑰,因為她在印度見過很多玫瑰。所有的地面都覆蓋著冬季褐色的草,草中長出一簇簇灌木,如果它們還活著,肯定是玫瑰叢。有許多標準玫瑰,它們的枝條伸展開,像小樹一樣。花園裡還有其他樹,使這個地方顯得最奇怪最可愛的事物之一是,攀緣玫瑰爬滿了它們,垂下長長的卷鬚,形成輕輕搖擺的簾幕,這裡那裡它們互相纏住或勾住一根伸得遠的樹枝,從一棵樹爬到另一棵樹,把自己做成可愛的橋。它們上面現在既沒有葉子也沒有玫瑰,瑪麗不知道它們是死是活,但它們纖細的灰色或褐色的枝條和嫩枝,看起來像一種朦朧的披風,鋪在一切上面,牆、樹,甚至褐色的草,它們從固定處掉落、沿地面蔓延之處。正是這種從樹到樹的朦朧糾纏,使一切看起來那麼神祕。瑪麗認為它一定與沒有被獨自留下這麼久的其他花園不同;確實它與她一生見過的任何其他地方都不同。

passages.original: “How still it is!” she whispered. “How still!”
passages.vernacular: 「幾咁靜!」佢低聲講。「幾咁靜!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「多麼靜!」她低聲說。「多麼靜!」

passages.original: Then she waited a moment and listened at the stillness. The robin, who had flown to his treetop, was still as all the rest. He did not even flutter his wings; he sat without stirring, and looked at Mary.
passages.vernacular: 然後佢等咗片刻,聽住寂靜。飛到樹梢嘅知更鳥,同其餘嘅一切一樣靜。佢甚至冇拍動翅膀;佢坐住不動,睇住瑪麗。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後她等了片刻,聽著寂靜。飛到樹梢的知更鳥,和其餘的一切一樣靜。他甚至沒有拍動翅膀;他坐著不動,看著瑪麗。

passages.original: “No wonder it is still,” she whispered again. “I am the first person who has spoken in here for ten years.”
passages.vernacular: 「難怪咁靜,」佢又低聲講。「我係十年嚟第一個喺呢度面講話嘅人。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「難怪這麼靜,」她又低聲說。「我是十年來第一個在這裡面說話的人。」

passages.original: She moved away from the door, stepping as softly as if she were afraid of awakening someone. She was glad that there was grass under her feet and that her steps made no sounds. She walked under one of the fairy-like gray arches between the trees and looked up at the sprays and tendrils which formed them.
passages.vernacular: 佢從門邊移開,輕輕地走,好像怕吵醒邊個。佢好高興腳下有草,腳步冇聲音。佢走過樹木之間一個仙境般嘅灰色拱門,抬頭睇形成佢哋嘅嫩枝同卷鬚。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她從門邊移開,輕輕地走,好像怕吵醒誰。她很高興腳下有草,腳步沒有聲音。她走過樹木之間一個仙境般的灰色拱門,抬頭看形成它們的嫩枝和卷鬚。

passages.original: “I wonder if they are all quite dead,” she said. “Is it all a quite dead garden? I wish it wasn’t.”
passages.vernacular: 「我想知道佢哋係咪完全死喇,」佢講。「呢整個係一個完全死咗嘅花園嗎?我希望唔係。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我想知道它們是否完全死了,」她說。「這整個是一個完全死了的花園嗎?我希望不是。」

passages.original: If she had been Ben Weatherstaff she could have told whether the wood was alive by looking at it, but she could only see that there were only gray or brown sprays and branches and none showed any signs of even a tiny leaf-bud anywhere.
passages.vernacular: 如果佢係班·韋瑟斯塔夫,佢睇一眼就能知道木頭係咪活住,但佢只能睇到只有灰色或褐色嘅嫩枝同樹枝,冇一處顯出邊怕一個小葉芽嘅跡象。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 如果她是班·韋瑟斯塔夫,她看一眼就能知道木頭是否活著,但她只能看到只有灰色或褐色的嫩枝和樹枝,沒有一處顯出哪怕一個小葉芽的跡象。

passages.original: But she was inside the wonderful garden and she could come through the door under the ivy any time and she felt as if she had found a world all her own.
passages.vernacular: 但佢喺呢個奇妙嘅花園裡面,佢可以隨時穿過常春藤下嘅門進嚟,佢覺得好像找到咗一個完全屬於自己嘅世界。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 但她在這個奇妙的花園裡面,她可以隨時穿過常春藤下的門進來,她覺得好像找到了一個完全屬於自己的世界。

passages.original: The sun was shining inside the four walls and the high arch of blue sky over this particular piece of Misselthwaite seemed even more brilliant and soft than it was over the moor. The robin flew down from his tree-top and hopped about or flew after her from one bush to another. He chirped a good deal and had a very busy air, as if he were showing her things. Everything was strange and silent and she seemed to be hundreds of miles away from anyone, but somehow she did not feel lonely at all. All that troubled her was her wish that she knew whether all the roses were dead, or if perhaps some of them had lived and might put out leaves and buds as the weather got warmer. She did not want it to be a quite dead garden. If it were a quite alive garden, how wonderful it would be, and what thousands of roses would grow on every side!
passages.vernacular: 陽光照耀喺四堵牆裡面,米瑟斯威特呢個特定部分上方高高嘅藍色拱形天空,似乎比荒野上空更明亮柔和。知更鳥從佢嘅樹頂飛下嚟,蹦跳住或從一叢灌木到另一叢追住佢飛。佢啾啾叫咗好多,顯得好忙碌,好像喺畀佢睇嘢。一切都奇怪而沉默,佢似乎離任何人幾百英里遠,但唔知怎嘅佢啲都不覺得孤單。唯一困擾佢嘅係佢希望知道所有嘅玫瑰係咪都死喇,或者或者有些活咗下嚟,隨住天氣變暖可能長出葉子同花蕾。佢唔想佢係一個完全死咗嘅花園。如果佢係一個完全活住嘅花園,嗰會幾咁奇妙,四面八方會長出多少千朵玫瑰!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 陽光照耀在四堵牆裡面,米瑟斯威特這個特定部分上方高高的藍色拱形天空,似乎比荒野上空更明亮柔和。知更鳥從他的樹頂飛下來,蹦跳著或從一叢灌木到另一叢追著她飛。他啾啾叫了很多,顯得非常忙碌,好像在給她看東西。一切都奇怪而沉默,她似乎離任何人幾百英里遠,但不知怎的她一點也不覺得孤單。唯一困擾她的是她希望知道所有的玫瑰是否都死了,或者也許有些活了下來,隨著天氣變暖可能長出葉子和花蕾。她不想它是一個完全死了的花園。如果它是一個完全活著的花園,那會多麼奇妙,四面八方會長出多少千朵玫瑰!

passages.original: Her skipping-rope had hung over her arm when she came in and after she had walked about for a while she thought she would skip round the whole garden, stopping when she wanted to look at things. There seemed to have been grass paths here and there, and in one or two corners there were alcoves of evergreen with stone seats or tall moss-covered flower urns in them.
passages.vernacular: 佢進嚟時跳繩搭喺手臂上,走咗一會兒後,佢想佢要繞住整個花園跳,想睇嘢時停下。似乎呢度嗰度有草徑,喺一兩個角落有常青樹嘅凹室,裡面有石座或高高嘅長滿苔蘚嘅花瓶。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她進來時跳繩搭在手臂上,走了一會兒後,她想她要繞著整個花園跳,想看東西時停下。似乎這裡那裡有草徑,在一兩個角落有常青樹的凹室,裡面有石座或高高的長滿苔蘚的花瓶。

passages.original: As she came near the second of these alcoves she stopped skipping. There had once been a flowerbed in it, and she thought she saw something sticking out of the black earth—some sharp little pale green points. She remembered what Ben Weatherstaff had said and she knelt down to look at them.
passages.vernacular: 佢走近第二個咁樣嘅凹室時停止咗跳繩。佢裡面曾經有過花壇,佢以為佢睇到有乜嘢嘢從黑色嘅泥土裡冒出嚟——啲尖尖嘅淡綠色小尖。佢記起班·韋瑟斯塔夫講嘅,跪下去睇佢哋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她走近第二個這樣的凹室時停止了跳繩。它裡面曾經有過花壇,她以為她看到有什麼東西從黑色的泥土裡冒出來——一些尖尖的淡綠色小尖。她記起班·韋瑟斯塔夫說的,跪下去看它們。

passages.original: “Yes, they are tiny growing things and they might be crocuses or snowdrops or daffodils,” she whispered.
passages.vernacular: 「係嘅,佢哋係細小生長嘅嘢,可能係番紅花、雪花蓮或水仙,」佢低聲講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是的,它們是細小生長的東西,可能是番紅花、雪花蓮或水仙,」她低聲說。

passages.original: She bent very close to them and sniffed the fresh scent of the damp earth. She liked it very much.
passages.vernacular: 佢好靠近地彎下身,嗅濕泥土嘅清新氣味。佢好鍾意。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她非常靠近地彎下身,嗅濕泥土的清新氣味。她非常喜歡。

passages.original: “Perhaps there are some other ones coming up in other places,” she said. “I will go all over the garden and look.”
passages.vernacular: 「或者其他地方仲有別嘅長出嚟,」佢講。「我要走遍整個花園睇睇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「也許其他地方還有別的長出來,」她說。「我要走遍整個花園看看。」

passages.original: She did not skip, but walked. She went slowly and kept her eyes on the ground. She looked in the old border beds and among the grass, and after she had gone round, trying to miss nothing, she had found ever so many more sharp, pale green points, and she had become quite excited again.
passages.vernacular: 佢冇跳,而係走。佢走得慢,眼睛盯住地面。佢睇咗舊嘅花壇邊同草叢中,繞咗一圈,試圖不漏掉任何嘢後,佢發現咗更多更多尖尖嘅淡綠色小尖,佢又相當興奮。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她沒有跳,而是走。她走得慢,眼睛盯著地面。她看了舊的花壇邊和草叢中,繞了一圈,試圖不漏掉任何東西後,她發現了更多更多尖尖的淡綠色小尖,她又相當興奮。

passages.original: “It isn’t a quite dead garden,” she cried out softly to herself. “Even if the roses are dead, there are other things alive.”
passages.vernacular: 「呢唔係一個完全死咗嘅花園,」佢對自己輕輕喊道。「即使玫瑰死喇,仲有其他嘢活住。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這不是一個完全死了的花園,」她對自己輕輕喊道。「即使玫瑰死了,還有其他東西活著。」

passages.original: She did not know anything about gardening, but the grass seemed so thick in some of the places where the green points were pushing their way through that she thought they did not seem to have room enough to grow. She searched about until she found a rather sharp piece of wood and knelt down and dug and weeded out the weeds and grass until she made nice little clear places around them.
passages.vernacular: 佢對園藝一無所知,但喺啲綠尖正在鑽出嘅地方,草似乎咁密,佢以為佢哋似乎冇足夠嘅空間生長。佢四處搜尋,直到找到一塊相當尖嘅木頭,跪下去挖,把雜草同草拔掉,直到喺佢哋周圍做出漂亮嘅小空地。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她對園藝一無所知,但在一些綠尖正在鑽出的地方,草似乎那麼密,她以為它們似乎沒有足夠的空間生長。她四處搜尋,直到找到一塊相當尖的木頭,跪下去挖,把雜草和草拔掉,直到在它們周圍做出漂亮的小空地。

passages.original: “Now they look as if they could breathe,” she said, after she had finished with the first ones. “I am going to do ever so many more. I’ll do all I can see. If I haven’t time today I can come tomorrow.”
passages.vernacular: 「而家佢哋睇起嚟能呼吸喇,」佢處理完第一批後講。「我要做更多更多。我要做所有我睇到嘅。如果今日冇時間,聽日可以再嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「現在它們看起來能呼吸了,」她處理完第一批後說。「我要做更多更多。我要做所有我看到的。如果今天沒時間,明天可以再來。」

passages.original: She went from place to place, and dug and weeded, and enjoyed herself so immensely that she was led on from bed to bed and into the grass under the trees. The exercise made her so warm that she first threw her coat off, and then her hat, and without knowing it she was smiling down on to the grass and the pale green points all the time.
passages.vernacular: 佢從一處走到另一處,挖、除草,享受得咁極致,佢從一個花壇被引到另一個,又走進樹下嘅草地。運動使佢咁暖同,佢先脫掉外套,然後脫掉帽子,唔知不覺中佢一直微笑地低頭睇住草同淡綠色嘅小尖。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她從一處走到另一處,挖、除草,享受得那麼極致,她從一個花壇被引到另一個,又走進樹下的草地。運動使她那麼暖和,她先脫掉外套,然後脫掉帽子,不知不覺中她一直微笑地低頭看著草和淡綠色的小尖。

passages.original: The robin was tremendously busy. He was very much pleased to see gardening begun on his own estate. He had often wondered at Ben Weatherstaff. Where gardening is done all sorts of delightful things to eat are turned up with the soil. Now here was this new kind of creature who was not half Ben’s size and yet had had the sense to come into his garden and begin at once.
passages.vernacular: 知更鳥極其忙碌。佢好高興睇到自己領地上開始園藝。佢以前常常對班·韋瑟斯塔夫感到驚奇。有園藝嘅地方,各種好食嘅嘢隨住土壤被翻出嚟。而家呢度有呢種新嘅生物,大小仲唔到班嘅一半,卻有頭腦進入佢嘅花園並即刻開始。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 知更鳥極其忙碌。他非常高興看到自己領地上開始園藝。他以前常常對班·韋瑟斯塔夫感到驚奇。有園藝的地方,各種好吃的東西隨著土壤被翻出來。現在這裡有這種新的生物,大小還不到班的一半,卻有頭腦進入他的花園並馬上開始。

passages.original: Mistress Mary worked in her garden until it was time to go to her midday dinner. In fact, she was rather late in remembering, and when she put on her coat and hat, and picked up her skipping-rope, she could not believe that she had been working two or three hours. She had been actually happy all the time; and dozens and dozens of the tiny, pale green points were to be seen in cleared places, looking twice as cheerful as they had looked before when the grass and weeds had been smothering them.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗小姐喺佢嘅花園裡工作,直到食午飯嘅時間。其實,佢相當晚才想起,佢穿上外套同帽子,攞起跳繩時,唔敢相信佢工作咗兩三個小時。佢一直真嘅快樂;喺清理過嘅地方可以睇到幾十個、幾十個淡綠色嘅小尖,睇起嚟比之前草同雜草悶住佢哋時快樂兩倍。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗小姐在她的花園裡工作,直到吃午飯的時間。其實,她相當晚才想起,她穿上外套和帽子,拿起跳繩時,不敢相信她工作了兩三個小時。她一直真的快樂;在清理過的地方可以看到幾十個、幾十個淡綠色的小尖,看起來比之前草和雜草悶住它們時快樂兩倍。

passages.original: “I shall come back this afternoon,” she said, looking all round at her new kingdom, and speaking to the trees and the rose-bushes as if they heard her.
passages.vernacular: 「我今日下午會回嚟,」佢講,環顧佢嘅新王國,對樹同玫瑰叢講話,好像佢哋聽得到。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我今天下午會回來,」她說,環顧她的新王國,對樹和玫瑰叢說話,好像它們聽得到。

passages.original: Then she ran lightly across the grass, pushed open the slow old door and slipped through it under the ivy. She had such red cheeks and such bright eyes and ate such a dinner that Martha was delighted.
passages.vernacular: 然後佢輕快地跑過草地,推開緩慢嘅舊門,從常春藤下溜咗出去。佢有咁紅嘅臉頰、咁明亮嘅眼睛,食咗咁一頓飯,瑪莎高興極喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後她輕快地跑過草地,推開緩慢的舊門,從常春藤下溜了出去。她有那麼紅的臉頰、那麼明亮的眼睛,吃了那麼一頓飯,瑪莎高興極了。

passages.original: “Two pieces o’ meat an’ two helps o’ rice puddin’!” she said. “Eh! mother will be pleased when I tell her what th’ skippin’-rope’s done for thee.”
passages.vernacular: 「兩塊肉同兩份米布丁!」佢講。「唉!我告訴媽媽跳繩畀你做咗乜嘢,佢會高興嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「兩塊肉和兩份米布丁!」她說。「唉!我告訴媽媽跳繩給你做了什麼,她會高興的。」

passages.original: In the course of her digging with her pointed stick Mistress Mary had found herself digging up a sort of white root rather like an onion. She had put it back in its place and patted the earth carefully down on it and just now she wondered if Martha could tell her what it was.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗小姐用佢嘅尖棍挖掘嘅過程中,發現自己挖出一種白色嘅根,有點像洋蔥。佢把佢放回原位,小心地把土拍喺上面,而家佢納悶瑪莎能唔能夠告訴佢嗰個係乜嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗小姐用她的尖棍挖掘的過程中,發現自己挖出一種白色的根,有點像洋蔥。她把它放回原位,小心地把土拍在上面,現在她納悶瑪莎能不能告訴她那是什麼。

passages.original: “Martha,” she said, “what are those white roots that look like onions?”
passages.vernacular: 「瑪莎,」佢講,「嗰啲睇起嚟像洋蔥嘅白色根係乜嘢?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「瑪莎,」她說,「那些看起來像洋蔥的白色根是什麼?」

passages.original: “They’re bulbs,” answered Martha. “Lots o’ spring flowers grow from ’em. Th’ very little ones are snowdrops an’ crocuses an’ th’ big ones are narcissuses an’ jonquils and daffydowndillys. Th’ biggest of all is lilies an’ purple flags. Eh! they are nice. Dickon’s got a whole lot of ’em planted in our bit o’ garden.”
passages.vernacular: 「係球莖,」瑪莎回答。「好多春天嘅花從佢哋長出嚟。好小嘅係雪花蓮同番紅花,大嘅係水仙、長壽花同黃水仙。最大嘅係百合同紫鳶尾。唉!佢哋好好睇。迪肯喺我哋嗰小塊花園裡種咗一大堆。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是球莖,」瑪莎回答。「很多春天的花從它們長出來。很小的是雪花蓮和番紅花,大的是水仙、長壽花和黃水仙。最大的是百合和紫鳶尾。唉!它們很好看。迪肯在我們那小塊花園裡種了一大堆。」

passages.original: “Does Dickon know all about them?” asked Mary, a new idea taking possession of her.
passages.vernacular: 「迪肯知道所有關於佢哋嘅事嗎?」瑪麗問,一個新想法佔據咗佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「迪肯知道所有關於它們的事嗎?」瑪麗問,一個新想法佔據了她。

passages.original: “Our Dickon can make a flower grow out of a brick walk. Mother says he just whispers things out o’ th’ ground.”
passages.vernacular: 「我哋嘅迪肯能讓花從磚路上長出嚟。媽媽講佢只要低聲對地下講講,嘢就出嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我們的迪肯能讓花從磚路上長出來。媽媽說他只要低聲對地下說說,東西就出來。」

passages.original: “Do bulbs live a long time? Would they live years and years if no one helped them?” inquired Mary anxiously.
passages.vernacular: 「球莖能活好長時間嗎?如果冇人幫佢哋,佢哋會活好多好多年嗎?」瑪麗焦急地問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「球莖能活很長時間嗎?如果沒有人幫它們,它們會活很多很多年嗎?」瑪麗焦急地問。

passages.original: “They’re things as helps themselves,” said Martha. “That’s why poor folk can afford to have ’em. If you don’t trouble ’em, most of ’em’ll work away underground for a lifetime an’ spread out an’ have little ’uns. There’s a place in th’ park woods here where there’s snowdrops by thousands. They’re the prettiest sight in Yorkshire when th’ spring comes. No one knows when they was first planted.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢哋係能自己幫自己嘅嘢,」瑪莎講。「呢個就係窮人都養得起嘅原因。如果你不打擾佢哋,大多數會喺地下工作一輩子,擴散,生小嘅。呢度嘅公園樹林有一個地方有成千上萬嘅雪花蓮。春天嚟時,佢哋係約克郡最漂亮嘅景象。冇人知道佢哋最初係乜嘢時候種嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「它們是能自己幫自己的東西,」瑪莎說。「這就是窮人也養得起的原因。如果你不打擾它們,大多數會在地下工作一輩子,擴散,生小的。這裡的公園樹林有一個地方有成千上萬的雪花蓮。春天來時,它們是約克郡最漂亮的景象。沒人知道它們最初是什麼時候種的。」

passages.original: “I wish the spring was here now,” said Mary. “I want to see all the things that grow in England.”
passages.vernacular: 「我希望春天而家就嚟,」瑪麗講。「我想睇英國生長嘅所有嘢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我希望春天現在就來,」瑪麗說。「我想看英國生長的所有東西。」

passages.original: She had finished her dinner and gone to her favorite seat on the hearth-rug.
passages.vernacular: 佢食完咗午飯,去到佢最鍾意嘅爐前地毯座位上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她吃完了午飯,去到她最喜歡的爐前地毯座位上。

passages.original: “I wish—I wish I had a little spade,” she said.
passages.vernacular: 「我希望——我希望我有一把小鏟子,」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我希望——我希望我有一把小鏟子,」她說。

passages.original: “Whatever does tha’ want a spade for?” asked Martha, laughing. “Art tha’ goin’ to take to diggin’? I must tell mother that, too.”
passages.vernacular: 「你要鏟子幹乜嘢?」瑪莎笑住問。「你要開始挖地咗嗎?我都要告訴媽媽呢個。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你要鏟子幹什麼?」瑪莎笑著問。「你要開始挖地了嗎?我也要告訴媽媽這個。」

passages.original: Mary looked at the fire and pondered a little. She must be careful if she meant to keep her secret kingdom. She wasn’t doing any harm, but if Mr. Craven found out about the open door he would be fearfully angry and get a new key and lock it up forevermore. She really could not bear that.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗睇住火,想咗一會兒。如果佢想保住佢嘅祕密王國,佢必須小心。佢冇做任何壞事,但如果克雷文先生發現咗開住嘅門,佢會可怕地生氣,會弄一把新鑰匙把佢永遠鎖起嚟。佢真嘅受不了嗰樣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗看著火,想了一會兒。如果她想保住她的祕密王國,她必須小心。她沒有做任何壞事,但如果克雷文先生發現了開著的門,他會可怕地生氣,會弄一把新鑰匙把它永遠鎖起來。她真的受不了那樣。

passages.original: “This is such a big lonely place,” she said slowly, as if she were turning matters over in her mind. “The house is lonely, and the park is lonely, and the gardens are lonely. So many places seem shut up. I never did many things in India, but there were more people to look at—natives and soldiers marching by—and sometimes bands playing, and my Ayah told me stories. There is no one to talk to here except you and Ben Weatherstaff. And you have to do your work and Ben Weatherstaff won’t speak to me often. I thought if I had a little spade I could dig somewhere as he does, and I might make a little garden if he would give me some seeds.”
passages.vernacular: 「呢個係個咁大嘅孤獨嘅地方,」佢慢慢地講,好像喺腦子裡思考事情。「房子孤獨,公園孤獨,花園孤獨。咁多地方似乎都關住。喺印度我冇做好多事,但有更多人可睇——本地人同行軍嘅士兵——有時有樂隊演奏,我嘅阿雅畀我講故事。呢度除咗你同班·韋瑟斯塔夫,冇人可以講話。而你要做你嘅工作,班·韋瑟斯塔夫不常同我講話。我想如果我有一把小鏟子,我可以像佢一樣喺某處挖,如果佢畀我啲種子,我或者可以做一個小花園。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這是個這麼大的孤獨的地方,」她慢慢地說,好像在腦子裡思考事情。「房子孤獨,公園孤獨,花園孤獨。這麼多地方似乎都關著。在印度我沒做很多事,但有更多人可看——本地人和行軍的士兵——有時有樂隊演奏,我的阿雅給我講故事。這裡除了你和班·韋瑟斯塔夫,沒有人可以說話。而你要做你的工作,班·韋瑟斯塔夫不常同我說話。我想如果我有一把小鏟子,我可以像他一樣在某處挖,如果他給我一些種子,我也許可以做一個小花園。」

passages.original: Martha’s face quite lighted up.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎嘅臉完全亮喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎的臉完全亮了。

passages.original: “There now!” she exclaimed, “if that wasn’t one of th’ things mother said. She says, ‘There’s such a lot o’ room in that big place, why don’t they give her a bit for herself, even if she doesn’t plant nothin’ but parsley an’ radishes? She’d dig an’ rake away an’ be right down happy over it.’ Them was the very words she said.”
passages.vernacular: 「睇!」佢喊道,「呢不就係媽媽講嘅話之一嗎。佢講:『嗰座大地方有咁多空間,點解不畀佢一小塊,即使佢只種香芹同蘿蔔?佢會挖、會耙,會好快樂。』呢正是佢講嘅話。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「看!」她喊道,「這不就是媽媽說的話之一嗎。她說:『那座大地方有那麼多空間,為什麼不給她一小塊,即使她只種香芹和蘿蔔?她會挖、會耙,會非常快樂。』這正是她說的話。」

passages.original: “Were they?” said Mary. “How many things she knows, doesn’t she?”
passages.vernacular: 「係嗎?」瑪麗講。「佢知道多少事啊,唔係嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是嗎?」瑪麗說。「她知道多少事啊,不是嗎?」

passages.original: “Eh!” said Martha. “It’s like she says: ‘A woman as brings up twelve children learns something besides her A B C. Children’s as good as ’rithmetic to set you findin’ out things.’”
passages.vernacular: 「唉!」瑪莎講。「就像佢講嘅:『一個養大十二個細路嘅女人,學到嘅除咗ABC仲有別嘅。細路像算術一樣好,讓你去弄清事情。』」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「唉!」瑪莎說。「就像她說的:『一個養大十二個孩子的女人,學到的除了ABC還有別的。孩子像算術一樣好,讓你去弄清事情。』」

passages.original: “How much would a spade cost—a little one?” Mary asked.
passages.vernacular: 「一把鏟子要多少錢——小嘅?」瑪麗問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「一把鏟子要多少錢——小的?」瑪麗問。

passages.original: “Well,” was Martha’s reflective answer, “at Thwaite village there’s a shop or so an’ I saw little garden sets with a spade an’ a rake an’ a fork all tied together for two shillings. An’ they was stout enough to work with, too.”
passages.vernacular: 「嗯,」係瑪莎若有所思嘅回答,「特懷特村有一兩家店,我睇到小園藝套裝,一把鏟子、一把耙子同一把叉子綁喺一起,兩先令。而且佢哋都夠結實,可以工作。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗯,」是瑪莎若有所思的回答,「特懷特村有一兩家店,我看到小園藝套裝,一把鏟子、一把耙子和一把叉子綁在一起,兩先令。而且它們也夠結實,可以工作。」

passages.original: “I’ve got more than that in my purse,” said Mary. “Mrs. Morrison gave me five shillings and Mrs. Medlock gave me some money from Mr. Craven.”
passages.vernacular: 「我錢包裡比嗰更多,」瑪麗講。「莫里森太太畀咗我五先令,梅德洛克太太畀咗我啲克雷文先生嘅錢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我錢包裡比那更多,」瑪麗說。「莫里森太太給了我五先令,梅德洛克太太給了我一些克雷文先生的錢。」

passages.original: “Did he remember thee that much?” exclaimed Martha.
passages.vernacular: 「佢咁記得你?」瑪莎喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他那麼記得你?」瑪莎喊道。

passages.original: “Mrs. Medlock said I was to have a shilling a week to spend. She gives me one every Saturday. I didn’t know what to spend it on.”
passages.vernacular: 「梅德洛克太太講我每星期有一先令花。佢每星期六畀我一先令。我唔知道花喺乜嘢上。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「梅德洛克太太說我每星期有一先令花。她每星期六給我一先令。我不知道花在什麼上。」

passages.original: “My word! that’s riches,” said Martha. “Tha’ can buy anything in th’ world tha’ wants. Th’ rent of our cottage is only one an’ threepence an’ it’s like pullin’ eye-teeth to get it. Now I’ve just thought of somethin’,” putting her hands on her hips.
passages.vernacular: 「天呀!嗰個係財富,」瑪莎講。「你可以買世界上任何你想要嘅嘢。我哋小屋嘅租金只有一先令三便士,弄到佢像拔智齒一樣難。我剛想到一件事,」雙手叉腰。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「天哪!那是財富,」瑪莎說。「你可以買世界上任何你想要的東西。我們小屋的租金只有一先令三便士,弄到它像拔智齒一樣難。我剛想到一件事,」雙手叉腰。

passages.original: “What?” said Mary eagerly.
passages.vernacular: 「乜嘢?」瑪麗急切地講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「什麼?」瑪麗急切地說。

passages.original: “In the shop at Thwaite they sell packages o’ flower-seeds for a penny each, and our Dickon he knows which is th’ prettiest ones an’ how to make ’em grow. He walks over to Thwaite many a day just for th’ fun of it. Does tha’ know how to print letters?” suddenly.
passages.vernacular: 「特懷特嘅店賣花籽包,一便士一包,我哋嘅迪肯知道邊啲最漂亮,點讓佢哋長。佢常常走到特懷特去,只為好玩。你知道點寫印刷體字母嗎?」突然問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「特懷特的店賣花籽包,一便士一包,我們的迪肯知道哪些最漂亮,怎麼讓它們長。他常常走到特懷特去,只為好玩。你知道怎麼寫印刷體字母嗎?」突然問。

passages.original: “I know how to write,” Mary answered.
passages.vernacular: 「我知道點寫字,」瑪麗回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我知道怎麼寫字,」瑪麗回答。

passages.original: Martha shook her head.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎搖頭。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎搖頭。

passages.original: “Our Dickon can only read printin’. If tha’ could print we could write a letter to him an’ ask him to go an’ buy th’ garden tools an’ th’ seeds at th’ same time.”
passages.vernacular: 「我哋嘅迪肯只會讀印刷體。如果你會寫印刷體,我哋可以畀佢寫封信,請佢去買園藝工具同種子。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我們的迪肯只會讀印刷體。如果你會寫印刷體,我們可以給他寫封信,請他去買園藝工具和種子。」

passages.original: “Oh! you’re a good girl!” Mary cried. “You are, really! I didn’t know you were so nice. I know I can print letters if I try. Let’s ask Mrs. Medlock for a pen and ink and some paper.”
passages.vernacular: 「哦!你真係個好女孩!」瑪麗喊道。「真嘅!我唔知道你咁好。我知道如果我試,我可以寫印刷體字母。我哋向梅德洛克太太要一支筆、墨水同啲紙。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哦!你真是個好女孩!」瑪麗喊道。「真的!我不知道你這麼好。我知道如果我試,我可以寫印刷體字母。我們向梅德洛克太太要一支筆、墨水和一些紙。」

passages.original: “I’ve got some of my own,” said Martha. “I bought ’em so I could print a bit of a letter to mother of a Sunday. I’ll go and get it.”
passages.vernacular: 「我自己有啲,」瑪莎講。「我買佢哋係為了星期天畀媽媽寫一小封信。我去攞。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我自己有一些,」瑪莎說。「我買它們是為了星期天給媽媽寫一小封信。我去拿。」

passages.original: She ran out of the room, and Mary stood by the fire and twisted her thin little hands together with sheer pleasure.
passages.vernacular: 佢跑出房間,瑪麗站喺火邊,純粹出於喜悅扭住佢瘦小嘅手。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她跑出房間,瑪麗站在火邊,純粹出於喜悅扭著她瘦小的手。

passages.original: “If I have a spade,” she whispered, “I can make the earth nice and soft and dig up weeds. If I have seeds and can make flowers grow the garden won’t be dead at all—it will come alive.”
passages.vernacular: 「如果我有鏟子,」佢低聲講,「我可以把泥土弄得又好又軟,挖掉雜草。如果我有種子,能讓花生長,花園就啲都唔係死嘅喇——佢會活過嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「如果我有鏟子,」她低聲說,「我可以把泥土弄得又好又軟,挖掉雜草。如果我有種子,能讓花生長,花園就一點也不是死的了——它會活過來。」

passages.original: She did not go out again that afternoon because when Martha returned with her pen and ink and paper she was obliged to clear the table and carry the plates and dishes downstairs and when she got into the kitchen Mrs. Medlock was there and told her to do something, so Mary waited for what seemed to her a long time before she came back. Then it was a serious piece of work to write to Dickon. Mary had been taught very little because her governesses had disliked her too much to stay with her. She could not spell particularly well but she found that she could print letters when she tried. This was the letter Martha dictated to her:
passages.vernacular: 嗰天下午佢冇再出去,因為瑪莎帶住筆、墨水同紙回嚟時,佢唔得不收拾桌子,把盤子碗碟攞下樓,佢進廚房時梅德洛克太太喺嗰度,叫佢做乜嘢,所以瑪麗等咗似乎好長嘅時間佢才回嚟。然後畀迪肯寫信係件嚴肅嘅工作。瑪麗學得好少,因為佢嘅家庭教師哋太不鍾意佢,不留喺佢身邊。佢拼字唔係特別好,但發現佢試嘅話可以寫印刷體字母。呢個係瑪莎口述畀佢寫嘅信:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那天下午她沒有再出去,因為瑪莎帶著筆、墨水和紙回來時,她不得不收拾桌子,把盤子碗碟拿下樓,她進廚房時梅德洛克太太在那裡,叫她做什麼,所以瑪麗等了似乎很長的時間她才回來。然後給迪肯寫信是件嚴肅的工作。瑪麗學得很少,因為她的家庭教師們太不喜歡她,不留在她身邊。她拼字不是特別好,但發現她試的話可以寫印刷體字母。這是瑪莎口述給她寫的信:

passages.original: “My Dear Dickon:
passages.vernacular: 「親愛嘅迪肯:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「親愛的迪肯:

passages.original: This comes hoping to find you well as it leaves me at present. Miss Mary has plenty of money and will you go to Thwaite and buy her some flower seeds and a set of garden tools to make a flower-bed. Pick the prettiest ones and easy to grow because she has never done it before and lived in India which is different. Give my love to mother and everyone of you. Miss Mary is going to tell me a lot more so that on my next day out you can hear about elephants and camels and gentlemen going hunting lions and tigers.
passages.vernacular: 寫信希望你一切都好,我目前都好好。瑪麗小姐有好多錢,你能去特懷特畀佢買些花籽同一套園藝工具嚟做花壇嗎。挑最漂亮、最容易種嘅,因為佢從冇做過,而且住過不同嘅印度。向媽媽同你哋每個人問好。瑪麗小姐要告訴我更多,咁樣我下次休息日你可以聽到關於大象、駱駝同先生哋去獵獅子同老虎嘅事。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 寫信希望你一切都好,我目前也很好。瑪麗小姐有很多錢,你能去特懷特給她買些花籽和一套園藝工具來做花壇嗎。挑最漂亮、最容易種的,因為她從沒做過,而且住過不同的印度。向媽媽和你們每個人問好。瑪麗小姐要告訴我更多,這樣我下次休息日你可以聽到關於大象、駱駝和先生們去獵獅子和老虎的事。

passages.original: “Your loving sister,
passages.vernacular: 「你愛你嘅姐姐,
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你愛你的姐姐,

passages.original: “Martha Phœbe Sowerby.”
passages.vernacular: 「瑪莎·菲比·索爾比。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「瑪莎·菲比·索爾比。」

passages.original: “We’ll put the money in th’ envelope an’ I’ll get th’ butcher boy to take it in his cart. He’s a great friend o’ Dickon’s,” said Martha.
passages.vernacular: 「我哋把錢放進信封,我讓肉店男孩用佢嘅車帶去。佢係迪肯嘅好朋友,」瑪莎講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我們把錢放進信封,我讓肉店男孩用他的車帶去。他是迪肯的好朋友,」瑪莎說。

passages.original: “How shall I get the things when Dickon buys them?”
passages.vernacular: 「迪肯買咗嘢後,我點攞到?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「迪肯買了東西後,我怎麼拿到?」

passages.original: “He’ll bring ’em to you himself. He’ll like to walk over this way.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢會自己畀你帶嚟。佢會鍾意走呢邊。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他會自己給你帶來。他會喜歡走這邊。」

passages.original: “Oh!” exclaimed Mary, “then I shall see him! I never thought I should see Dickon.”
passages.vernacular: 「哦!」瑪麗喊道,「嗰我就會見到佢喇!我從冇想過我會見到迪肯。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哦!」瑪麗喊道,「那我就會見到他了!我從沒想過我會見到迪肯。」

passages.original: “Does tha’ want to see him?” asked Martha suddenly, for Mary had looked so pleased.
passages.vernacular: 「你想見佢嗎?」瑪莎突然問,因為瑪麗睇起嚟咁高興。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你想見他嗎?」瑪莎突然問,因為瑪麗看起來那麼高興。

passages.original: “Yes, I do. I never saw a boy foxes and crows loved. I want to see him very much.”
passages.vernacular: 「係嘅,我想。我從冇見過狐狸同烏鴉都愛嘅男孩。我好想見佢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是的,我想。我從沒見過狐狸和烏鴉都愛的男孩。我很想見他。」

passages.original: Martha gave a little start, as if she remembered something.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎輕輕一驚,好像想起咗乜嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎輕輕一驚,好像想起了什麼。

passages.original: “Now to think,” she broke out, “to think o’ me forgettin’ that there; an’ I thought I was goin’ to tell you first thing this mornin’. I asked mother—and she said she’d ask Mrs. Medlock her own self.”
passages.vernacular: 「而家想想,」佢脫口而出,「想想我竟忘咗嗰個;我以為我今早要第一件告訴你。我問咗媽媽——佢講佢親自去問梅德洛克太太。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「現在想想,」她脫口而出,「想想我竟忘了那個;我以為我今早要第一件告訴你。我問了媽媽——她說她親自去問梅德洛克太太。」

passages.original: “Do you mean—” Mary began.
passages.vernacular: 「你係講——」瑪麗開口。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你是說——」瑪麗開口。

passages.original: “What I said Tuesday. Ask her if you might be driven over to our cottage some day and have a bit o’ mother’s hot oat cake, an’ butter, an’ a glass o’ milk.”
passages.vernacular: 「我星期二講嘅。問佢你係咪可以邊天坐車到我哋小屋,食一塊媽媽嘅熱燕麥餅、奶油,同一杯牛奶。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我星期二說的。問她你是否可以哪天坐車到我們小屋,吃一塊媽媽的熱燕麥餅、奶油,和一杯牛奶。」

passages.original: It seemed as if all the interesting things were happening in one day. To think of going over the moor in the daylight and when the sky was blue! To think of going into the cottage which held twelve children!
passages.vernacular: 似乎所有有趣嘅事都喺一天裡發生喇。想想喺白天、天空藍色時穿過荒野!想想進入住十二個細路嘅小屋!
passages.vernacularMandarin: 似乎所有有趣的事都在一天裡發生了。想想在白天、天空藍色時穿過荒野!想想進入住著十二個孩子的小屋!

passages.original: “Does she think Mrs. Medlock would let me go?” she asked, quite anxiously.
passages.vernacular: 「佢認為梅德洛克太太會讓我去嗎?」佢問,相當焦急。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「她認為梅德洛克太太會讓我去嗎?」她問,相當焦急。

passages.original: “Aye, she thinks she would. She knows what a tidy woman mother is and how clean she keeps the cottage.”
passages.vernacular: 「係嘅,佢認為會。佢知道媽媽係個多整潔嘅女人,小屋保持得多乾淨。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是的,她認為會。她知道媽媽是個多整潔的女人,小屋保持得多乾淨。」

passages.original: “If I went I should see your mother as well as Dickon,” said Mary, thinking it over and liking the idea very much. “She doesn’t seem to be like the mothers in India.”
passages.vernacular: 「如果我去,我可以見到你母親都見到迪肯,」瑪麗講,思考住,好鍾意呢個主意。「佢似乎不像印度嘅母親哋。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「如果我去,我可以見到你母親也見到迪肯,」瑪麗說,思考著,非常喜歡這個主意。「她似乎不像印度的母親們。」

passages.original: Her work in the garden and the excitement of the afternoon ended by making her feel quiet and thoughtful. Martha stayed with her until tea-time, but they sat in comfortable quiet and talked very little. But just before Martha went downstairs for the tea-tray, Mary asked a question.
passages.vernacular: 佢喺花園嘅工作同下午嘅興奮,最終使佢感到安靜同若有所思。瑪莎陪佢到下午茶時間,但佢哋舒適安靜地坐住,講得好少。但就喺瑪莎下樓去攞茶盤前,瑪麗問咗一個問題。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她在花園的工作和下午的興奮,最終使她感到安靜和若有所思。瑪莎陪她到下午茶時間,但她們舒適安靜地坐著,說得很少。但就在瑪莎下樓去拿茶盤前,瑪麗問了一個問題。

passages.original: “Martha,” she said, “has the scullery-maid had the toothache again today?”
passages.vernacular: 「瑪莎,」佢講,「洗碗女工今日又牙疼咗嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「瑪莎,」她說,「洗碗女工今天又牙疼了嗎?」

passages.original: Martha certainly started slightly.
passages.vernacular: 瑪莎確實微微一驚。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪莎確實微微一驚。

passages.original: “What makes thee ask that?” she said.
passages.vernacular: 「你點解問呢個?」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你為什麼問這個?」她說。

passages.original: “Because when I waited so long for you to come back I opened the door and walked down the corridor to see if you were coming. And I heard that far-off crying again, just as we heard it the other night. There isn’t a wind today, so you see it couldn’t have been the wind.”
passages.vernacular: 「因為我等你回嚟等得咁久,我開咗門,沿走廊走,睇你係咪嚟喇。我又聽到嗰遠處嘅哭聲,就像我哋嗰天晚上聽到嘅一樣。今日冇風,所以你睇,唔可能係風。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「因為我等你回來等得那麼久,我開了門,沿走廊走,看你是否來了。我又聽到那遠處的哭聲,就像我們那天晚上聽到的一樣。今天沒有風,所以你看,不可能是風。」

passages.original: “Eh!” said Martha restlessly. “Tha’ mustn’t go walkin’ about in corridors an’ listenin’. Mr. Craven would be that there angry there’s no knowin’ what he’d do.”
passages.vernacular: 「唉!」瑪莎不安地講。「你不許喺走廊裡走嚟走去聽。克雷文先生會咁生氣,唔知佢會做乜嘢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「唉!」瑪莎不安地說。「你不許在走廊裡走來走去聽。克雷文先生會那麼生氣,不知他會做什麼。」

passages.original: “I wasn’t listening,” said Mary. “I was just waiting for you—and I heard it. That’s three times.”
passages.vernacular: 「我冇喺聽,」瑪麗講。「我只係喺等你——我聽到喇。嗰個係三次喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我沒有在聽,」瑪麗說。「我只是在等你——我聽到了。那是三次了。」

passages.original: “My word! There’s Mrs. Medlock’s bell,” said Martha, and she almost ran out of the room.
passages.vernacular: 「天呀!梅德洛克太太嘅鈴響喇,」瑪莎講,佢幾乎跑出咗房間。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「天哪!梅德洛克太太的鈴響了,」瑪莎說,她幾乎跑出了房間。

passages.original: “It’s the strangest house anyone ever lived in,” said Mary drowsily, as she dropped her head on the cushioned seat of the armchair near her. Fresh air, and digging, and skipping-rope had made her feel so comfortably tired that she fell asleep.
passages.vernacular: 「呢個係任何人住過嘅最奇怪嘅房子,」瑪麗昏昏欲瞓地講,把頭靠喺附近扶手椅嘅墊子座上。新鮮空氣、挖地同跳繩使佢感到咁舒服地累,佢瞓住喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這是任何人住過的最奇怪的房子,」瑪麗昏昏欲睡地說,把頭靠在附近扶手椅的墊子座上。新鮮空氣、挖地和跳繩使她感到那麼舒服地累,她睡著了。

chapters.title: Chapter X: Dickon 第十章:迪肯

passages.original: The sun shone down for nearly a week on the secret garden. The Secret Garden was what Mary called it when she was thinking of it. She liked the name, and she liked still more the feeling that when its beautiful old walls shut her in no one knew where she was. It seemed almost like being shut out of the world in some fairy place. The few books she had read and liked had been fairy-story books, and she had read of secret gardens in some of the stories. Sometimes people went to sleep in them for a hundred years, which she had thought must be rather stupid. She had no intention of going to sleep, and, in fact, she was becoming wider awake every day which passed at Misselthwaite. She was beginning to like to be out of doors; she no longer hated the wind, but enjoyed it. She could run faster, and longer, and she could skip up to a hundred. The bulbs in the secret garden must have been much astonished. Such nice clear places were made round them that they had all the breathing space they wanted, and really, if Mistress Mary had known it, they began to cheer up under the dark earth and work tremendously. The sun could get at them and warm them, and when the rain came down it could reach them at once, so they began to feel very much alive.
passages.vernacular: 陽光照喺祕密花園上將近一個星期。「祕密花園」係瑪麗想到佢時對佢嘅稱呼。佢鍾意呢個名字,更鍾意呢種感覺:當佢美麗嘅老牆把佢關喺裡面時,冇人知道佢喺邊度。呢幾乎像被關在世界之外,喺某個仙境。佢讀過並鍾意嘅少數幾本書係童話故事書,佢喺啲故事裡讀到過祕密花園。有時人哋喺裡面瞓一百年,佢曾認為呢一定相當愚蠢。佢冇打算去瞓覺,其實,喺米瑟斯威特過去嘅每一天,佢都變得更清醒。佢開始鍾意待喺戶外;佢唔再恨風,而係享受佢。佢可以跑得更快更久,佢可以跳繩跳到一百下。祕密花園裡嘅球莖一定好驚訝。佢哋周圍被弄出咗咁漂亮嘅乾淨空地,佢哋有咗想要嘅所有呼吸空間,講實在嘅,如果瑪麗小姐知道嘅話,佢哋喺黑暗嘅泥土下開始振作起嚟,拼命工作。太陽可以照到佢哋並溫暖佢哋,雨落下時可以即刻到達佢哋,所以佢哋開始感到好有生命力。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 陽光照在祕密花園上將近一個星期。「祕密花園」是瑪麗想到它時對它的稱呼。她喜歡這個名字,更喜歡這種感覺:當它美麗的老牆把她關在裡面時,沒有人知道她在哪裡。這幾乎像被關在世界之外,在某個仙境。她讀過並喜歡的少數幾本書是童話故事書,她在一些故事裡讀到過祕密花園。有時人們在裡面睡一百年,她曾認為這一定相當愚蠢。她沒有打算去睡覺,其實,在米瑟斯威特過去的每一天,她都變得更清醒。她開始喜歡待在戶外;她不再恨風,而是享受它。她可以跑得更快更久,她可以跳繩跳到一百下。祕密花園裡的球莖一定非常驚訝。它們周圍被弄出了那麼漂亮的乾淨空地,它們有了想要的所有呼吸空間,說實在的,如果瑪麗小姐知道的話,它們在黑暗的泥土下開始振作起來,拼命工作。太陽可以照到它們並溫暖它們,雨落下時可以馬上到達它們,所以它們開始感到非常有生命力。

passages.original: Mary was an odd, determined little person, and now she had something interesting to be determined about, she was very much absorbed, indeed. She worked and dug and pulled up weeds steadily, only becoming more pleased with her work every hour instead of tiring of it. It seemed to her like a fascinating sort of play. She found many more of the sprouting pale green points than she had ever hoped to find. They seemed to be starting up everywhere and each day she was sure she found tiny new ones, some so tiny that they barely peeped above the earth. There were so many that she remembered what Martha had said about the “snowdrops by the thousands,” and about bulbs spreading and making new ones. These had been left to themselves for ten years and perhaps they had spread, like the snowdrops, into thousands. She wondered how long it would be before they showed that they were flowers. Sometimes she stopped digging to look at the garden and try to imagine what it would be like when it was covered with thousands of lovely things in bloom.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗係個古怪、堅決嘅小人兒,而家佢有咗有趣嘅事去堅決,佢確實好專注。佢穩定地工作、挖、拔雜草,每小時只係對佢嘅工作更加滿意,而唔係厭倦。對佢來講,佢像一種迷人嘅遊戲。佢發現嘅萌芽嘅淡綠色小尖,比佢曾希望找到嘅多得多。佢哋似乎到處喺冒出嚟,每天佢肯定找到細小嘅新芽,有些小到幾乎剛露出泥土。有咁多,佢記起瑪莎講嘅關於「成千上萬嘅雪花蓮」,同球莖擴散並長出新嘅。呢啲被留喺自己嘅狀態十年喇,或者佢哋像雪花蓮一樣擴散成咗千上萬。佢納悶要多久佢哋才會顯示出係花。有時佢停止挖掘睇花園,試圖想像佢被成千上萬可愛嘅開花嘢覆蓋時係乜嘢樣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗是個古怪、堅決的小人兒,現在她有了有趣的事去堅決,她確實非常專注。她穩定地工作、挖、拔雜草,每小時只是對她的工作更加滿意,而不是厭倦。對她來說,它像一種迷人的遊戲。她發現的萌芽的淡綠色小尖,比她曾希望找到的多得多。它們似乎到處在冒出來,每天她肯定找到細小的新芽,有些小到幾乎剛露出泥土。有那麼多,她記起瑪莎說的關於「成千上萬的雪花蓮」,和球莖擴散並長出新的。這些被留在自己的狀態十年了,也許它們像雪花蓮一樣擴散成了千上萬。她納悶要多久它們才會顯示出是花。有時她停止挖掘看花園,試圖想像它被成千上萬可愛的開花東西覆蓋時是什麼樣。

passages.original: During that week of sunshine, she became more intimate with Ben Weatherstaff. She surprised him several times by seeming to start up beside him as if she sprang out of the earth. The truth was that she was afraid that he would pick up his tools and go away if he saw her coming, so she always walked toward him as silently as possible. But, in fact, he did not object to her as strongly as he had at first. Perhaps he was secretly rather flattered by her evident desire for his elderly company. Then, also, she was more civil than she had been.
