passages.original: “I’d almost lost him but for his song an’ I was wonderin’ how a chap could hear it when it seemed as if he’d get out o’ th’ world in a minute—an’ just then I heard somethin’ else far off among th’ gorse bushes. It was a weak bleatin’ an’ I knowed it was a new lamb as was hungry an’ I knowed it wouldn’t be hungry if it hadn’t lost its mother somehow, so I set off searchin’. Eh! I did have a look for it. I went in an’ out among th’ gorse bushes an’ round an’ round an’ I always seemed to take th’ wrong turnin’. But at last I seed a bit o’ white by a rock on top o’ th’ moor an’ I climbed up an’ found th’ little ’un half dead wi’ cold an’ clemmin’.”
passages.vernacular: 「若唔係牠嘅歌聲,我差點就睇唔見牠喇,我喺想,牠好像即刻要飛出世界,一個人點仲能聽見牠——就喺嗰時我聽到遠處金雀花叢中有別嘅聲音。係微弱嘅咩咩叫,我知道嗰個係一隻餓咗嘅新生小羊,我知道牠如果唔係以某種方式失去咗媽媽,唔會餓,所以我出發去找。唉!我找得可費勁喇。我喺金雀花叢中進進出出、轉咗一圈又一圈,好像老係轉錯咗彎。最後我睇見荒野頂上一塊岩石旁有一小片白,我爬上去,發現小傢伙冷得餓得半死。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「若不是牠的歌聲,我差點就看不見牠了,我在想,牠好像馬上要飛出世界,一個人怎麼還能聽見牠——就在那時我聽到遠處金雀花叢中有別的聲音。是微弱的咩咩叫,我知道那是一隻餓了的新生小羊,我知道牠如果不是以某種方式失去了媽媽,不會餓,所以我出發去找。唉!我找得可費勁了。我在金雀花叢中進進出出、轉了一圈又一圈,好像老是轉錯了彎。最後我看見荒野頂上一塊岩石旁有一小片白,我爬上去,發現小傢伙冷得餓得半死。」

passages.original: While he talked, Soot flew solemnly in and out of the open window and cawed remarks about the scenery while Nut and Shell made excursions into the big trees outside and ran up and down trunks and explored branches. Captain curled up near Dickon, who sat on the hearth-rug from preference.
passages.vernacular: 佢講話時,煤灰莊重地喺開住嘅窗子裡飛進飛出,呱呱地對風景發表意見,堅果同殼到外面嘅大樹上去遊玩,喺樹幹上跑上跑下,探索樹枝。上尉蜷喺迪肯旁邊,迪肯情願坐喺壁爐地毯上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他說話時,煤灰莊重地在開著的窗子裡飛進飛出,呱呱地對風景發表意見,堅果和殼到外面的大樹上去遊玩,在樹幹上跑上跑下,探索樹枝。上尉蜷在迪肯旁邊,迪肯情願坐在壁爐地毯上。

passages.original: They looked at the pictures in the gardening books and Dickon knew all the flowers by their country names and knew exactly which ones were already growing in the secret garden.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋睇園藝書裡嘅圖畫,迪肯用鄉下嘅名字認得所有嘅花,都確切知道邊啲已喺祕密花園裡生長。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們看園藝書裡的圖畫,迪肯用鄉下的名字認得所有的花,也確切知道哪些已在祕密花園裡生長。

passages.original: “I couldna’ say that there name,” he said, pointing to one under which was written “Aquilegia,” “but us calls that a columbine, an’ that there one it’s a snapdragon and they both grow wild in hedges, but these is garden ones an’ they’re bigger an’ grander. There’s some big clumps o’ columbine in th’ garden. They’ll look like a bed o’ blue an’ white butterflies flutterin’ when they’re out.”
passages.vernacular: 「我講不出嗰個名字,」佢指住一幅下面寫住「Aquilegia」嘅圖講,「不過我哋叫佢耬斗菜,嗰個係金魚草,兩樣都喺籬笆裡野生,不過呢啲係花園裡嘅,更大更氣派。花園裡有幾大叢耬斗菜。佢哋開花時,會像一床藍白色蝴蝶喺飛舞。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我說不出那個名字,」他指著一幅下面寫著「Aquilegia」的圖說,「不過我們叫它耬斗菜,那個是金魚草,兩樣都在籬笆裡野生,不過這些是花園裡的,更大更氣派。花園裡有幾大叢耬斗菜。它們開花時,會像一床藍白色蝴蝶在飛舞。」

passages.original: “I’m going to see them,” cried Colin. “I am going to see them!”
passages.vernacular: 「我要去睇佢哋,」柯林喊道。「我要去睇佢哋!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我要去看它們,」柯林喊道。「我要去看它們!」

passages.original: “Aye, that tha’ mun,” said Mary quite seriously. “An’ tha’ munnot lose no time about it.”
passages.vernacular: 「係啊,你得去,」瑪麗相當嚴肅地講。「而且唔能夠耽擱。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是啊,你得去,」瑪麗相當嚴肅地說。「而且不能耽擱。」

chapters.title: Chapter XX: "I Shall Live Forever—and Ever—and Ever!" 第二十章:「我要永遠活下去!」

passages.original: But they were obliged to wait more than a week because first there came some very windy days and then Colin was threatened with a cold, which two things happening one after the other would no doubt have thrown him into a rage but that there was so much careful and mysterious planning to do and almost every day Dickon came in, if only for a few minutes, to talk about what was happening on the moor and in the lanes and hedges and on the borders of streams. The things he had to tell about otters’ and badgers’ and water-rats’ houses, not to mention birds’ nests and field-mice and their burrows, were enough to make you almost tremble with excitement when you heard all the intimate details from an animal charmer and realized with what thrilling eagerness and anxiety the whole busy underworld was working.
passages.vernacular: 不過佢哋唔得不等咗一個多星期,因為先係嚟咗幾天大風,然後柯林有住涼嘅跡象,呢兩件事一件接一件,無疑會讓佢大發雷霆,只係有咁多謹慎而神祕嘅計劃要做,而且幾乎每天迪肯都進嚟,邊怕只幾分鐘,談談荒野、小路、籬笆同溪邊發生嘅事。佢要講嘅關於水獺、獾同水鼠嘅家,更別提鳥巢、田鼠同牠哋嘅洞穴,從一位動物迷惑者嗰度聽到所有呢啲親密細節,認識到整個忙碌嘅地下世界正以幾咁令人激動嘅熱切同焦慮喺工作,簡直讓你興奮得發抖。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 可是他們不得不等了一個多星期,因為先是來了幾天大風,然後柯林有著涼的跡象,這兩件事一件接一件,無疑會讓他大發雷霆,只是有那麼多謹慎而神祕的計劃要做,而且幾乎每天迪肯都進來,哪怕只幾分鐘,談談荒野、小路、籬笆和溪邊發生的事。他要講的關於水獺、獾和水鼠的家,更別提鳥巢、田鼠和牠們的洞穴,從一位動物迷惑者那裡聽到所有這些親密細節,認識到整個忙碌的地下世界正以多麼令人激動的熱切和焦慮在工作,簡直讓你興奮得發抖。

passages.original: “They’re same as us,” said Dickon, “only they have to build their homes every year. An’ it keeps ’em so busy they fair scuffle to get ’em done.”
passages.vernacular: 「牠哋跟我哋一樣,」迪肯講,「只係牠哋每年都得重建家園。呢讓牠哋忙得手忙腳亂地趕住完工。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「牠們跟我們一樣,」迪肯說,「只是牠們每年都得重建家園。這讓牠們忙得手忙腳亂地趕著完工。」

passages.original: The most absorbing thing, however, was the preparations to be made before Colin could be transported with sufficient secrecy to the garden. No one must see the chair-carriage and Dickon and Mary after they turned a certain corner of the shrubbery and entered upon the walk outside the ivied walls. As each day passed, Colin had become more and more fixed in his feeling that the mystery surrounding the garden was one of its greatest charms. Nothing must spoil that. No one must ever suspect that they had a secret. People must think that he was simply going out with Mary and Dickon because he liked them and did not object to their looking at him. They had long and quite delightful talks about their route. They would go up this path and down that one and cross the other and go round among the fountain flower-beds as if they were looking at the “bedding-out plants” the head gardener, Mr. Roach, had been having arranged. That would seem such a rational thing to do that no one would think it at all mysterious. They would turn into the shrubbery walks and lose themselves until they came to the long walls. It was almost as serious and elaborately thought out as the plans of march made by great generals in time of war.
passages.vernacular: 然而,最吸引人嘅係柯林能夠足夠隱祕地被送到花園之前必須做嘅準備。佢哋轉過灌木叢嘅某個拐角、進入常春藤牆外嘅小路後,任何人都唔能夠睇到嗰輛椅車同迪肯、瑪麗。隨住一天天過去,柯林越嚟越堅定地覺得,環繞花園嘅神祕係佢最大嘅魅力之一。唔能夠有任何事破壞佢。唔能夠有人懷疑佢哋有個祕密。人哋必須以為,佢只係鍾意瑪麗同迪肯、不介意佢哋睇佢,才跟佢哋出去。佢哋對路線進行咗長時間、相當愉快嘅商談。佢哋會走呢條路上去,嗰條路下嚟,穿過另一條,繞住噴泉花壇轉,好像喺睇總園丁羅奇先生一直喺佈置嘅「花壇植物」。呢個睇起嚟係咁合理嘅事,冇人會覺得佢有半點神祕。佢哋會轉進灌木叢小道,迷失其中,直到來到長牆邊。呢幾乎像戰時大將軍哋制定嘅進軍計劃一樣嚴肅而精心。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然而,最吸引人的是柯林能夠足夠隱祕地被送到花園之前必須做的準備。他們轉過灌木叢的某個拐角、進入常春藤牆外的小路後,任何人都不能看到那輛椅車和迪肯、瑪麗。隨著一天天過去,柯林越來越堅定地覺得,環繞花園的神祕是它最大的魅力之一。不能有任何事破壞它。不能有人懷疑他們有個祕密。人們必須以為,他只是喜歡瑪麗和迪肯、不介意他們看他,才跟他們出去。他們對路線進行了長時間、相當愉快的商談。他們會走這條路上去,那條路下來,穿過另一條,繞著噴泉花壇轉,好像在看總園丁羅奇先生一直在佈置的「花壇植物」。這看起來是那麼合理的事,沒有人會覺得它有半點神祕。他們會轉進灌木叢小道,迷失其中,直到來到長牆邊。這幾乎像戰時大將軍們制定的進軍計劃一樣嚴肅而精心。

passages.original: Rumors of the new and curious things which were occurring in the invalid’s apartments had of course filtered through the servants’ hall into the stable yards and out among the gardeners, but notwithstanding this, Mr. Roach was startled one day when he received orders from Master Colin’s room to the effect that he must report himself in the apartment no outsider had ever seen, as the invalid himself desired to speak to him.
passages.vernacular: 關於病人房間裡發生嘅新奇古怪嘅事,謠言當然已經從僕人廳滲到馬廄院子,又傳到園丁哋中間,但儘管如此,羅奇先生有一天定係食咗一驚,佢收到柯林少爺房間傳出嘅命令,講佢必須到嗰間從冇外人見過嘅房間報到,因為病人自己要同佢講話。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 關於病人房間裡發生的新奇古怪的事,謠言當然已經從僕人廳滲到馬廄院子,又傳到園丁們中間,但儘管如此,羅奇先生有一天還是吃了一驚,他收到柯林少爺房間傳出的命令,說他必須到那間從沒有外人見過的房間報到,因為病人自己要同他說話。

passages.original: “Well, well,” he said to himself as he hurriedly changed his coat, “what’s to do now? His Royal Highness that wasn’t to be looked at calling up a man he’s never set eyes on.”
passages.vernacular: 「好,好,」佢匆忙換外套時對自己講,「而家又係乜嘢事?嗰位不許睇嘅王室殿下,要召見一個佢從冇見過嘅人。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「好,好,」他匆忙換外套時對自己說,「現在又是什麼事?那位不許看的王室殿下,要召見一個他從沒見過的人。」

passages.original: Mr. Roach was not without curiosity. He had never caught even a glimpse of the boy and had heard a dozen exaggerated stories about his uncanny looks and ways and his insane tempers. The thing he had heard oftenest was that he might die at any moment and there had been numerous fanciful descriptions of a humped back and helpless limbs, given by people who had never seen him.
passages.vernacular: 羅奇先生唔係冇好奇心。佢連嗰細路嘅影子都冇瞥見過,卻聽過十幾個關於佢古怪嘅外貌同行為、佢瘋狂脾氣嘅誇張故事。佢聽得最多嘅係,佢隨時可能死去,而且有許多冇見過佢嘅人畀出咗幻想般嘅描述:駝背同無力嘅四肢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 羅奇先生不是沒有好奇心。他連那孩子的影子都沒瞥見過,卻聽過十幾個關於他古怪的外貌和行為、他瘋狂脾氣的誇張故事。他聽得最多的是,他隨時可能死去,而且有許多沒見過他的人給出了幻想般的描述:駝背和無力的四肢。

passages.original: “Things are changing in this house, Mr. Roach,” said Mrs. Medlock, as she led him up the back staircase to the corridor on to which opened the hitherto mysterious chamber.
passages.vernacular: 「呢座房子裡嘅事喺變,羅奇先生,」梅德洛克太太帶佢上後樓梯,走到嗰條通向迄今神祕嘅房間嘅走廊時講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這座房子裡的事在變,羅奇先生,」梅德洛克太太帶他上後樓梯,走到那條通向迄今神祕的房間的走廊時說。

passages.original: “Let’s hope they’re changing for the better, Mrs. Medlock,” he answered.
passages.vernacular: 「但願係喺往好嘅方向變,梅德洛克太太,」佢回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「但願是在往好的方向變,梅德洛克太太,」他回答。

passages.original: “They couldn’t well change for the worse,” she continued; “and queer as it all is there’s them as finds their duties made a lot easier to stand up under. Don’t you be surprised, Mr. Roach, if you find yourself in the middle of a menagerie and Martha Sowerby’s Dickon more at home than you or me could ever be.”
passages.vernacular: 「唔可能變得更壞喇,」佢繼續講;「雖然整件事古怪,但有人發現佢哋嘅職責變得容易承擔多喇。羅奇先生,如果您發現自己置身動物園中間,瑪莎·索爾比嘅迪肯比您我都更自在,您唔好食驚。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「不可能變得更壞了,」她繼續說;「雖然整件事古怪,但有人發現他們的職責變得容易承擔多了。羅奇先生,如果您發現自己置身動物園中間,瑪莎·索爾比的迪肯比您我都更自在,您不要吃驚。」

passages.original: There really was a sort of Magic about Dickon, as Mary always privately believed. When Mr. Roach heard his name he smiled quite leniently.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯身上確實有一種魔法,瑪麗總是私下咁樣相信。羅奇先生聽到佢嘅名字,相當寬容地笑喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯身上確實有一種魔法,瑪麗總是私下這樣相信。羅奇先生聽到他的名字,相當寬容地笑了。

passages.original: “He’d be at home in Buckingham Palace or at the bottom of a coal mine,” he said. “And yet it’s not impudence, either. He’s just fine, is that lad.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢喺白金漢宮或煤礦底下都會自在,」佢講。「而且嗰都唔係無禮。佢只係好,嗰小子。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他在白金漢宮或煤礦底下都會自在,」他說。「而且那也不是無禮。他只是好,那小子。」

passages.original: It was perhaps well he had been prepared or he might have been startled. When the bedroom door was opened a large crow, which seemed quite at home perched on the high back of a carven chair, announced the entrance of a visitor by saying “Caw—Caw” quite loudly. In spite of Mrs. Medlock’s warning, Mr. Roach only just escaped being sufficiently undignified to jump backward.
passages.vernacular: 或者幸好佢事先得到咗提醒,否則佢可能會食驚。臥室嘅門打開時,一隻大烏鴉似乎相當自在地棲喺一把雕花椅子高高嘅靠背上,相當大聲地講「呱——呱」,宣告有客人進嚟。儘管有梅德洛克太太嘅警告,羅奇先生都只係差啲冇唔夠莊重地向後跳開。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 也許幸好他事先得到了提醒,否則他可能會吃驚。臥室的門打開時,一隻大烏鴉似乎相當自在地棲在一把雕花椅子高高的靠背上,相當大聲地說「呱——呱」,宣告有客人進來。儘管有梅德洛克太太的警告,羅奇先生也只是差一點沒有不夠莊重地向後跳開。

passages.original: The young Rajah was neither in bed nor on his sofa. He was sitting in an armchair and a young lamb was standing by him shaking its tail in feeding-lamb fashion as Dickon knelt giving it milk from its bottle. A squirrel was perched on Dickon’s bent back attentively nibbling a nut. The little girl from India was sitting on a big footstool looking on.
passages.vernacular: 年輕嘅王公既不喺床上,都不喺沙發上。佢坐喺一張扶手椅裡,一隻小羊站喺佢身旁,以食奶小羊嘅方式搖住尾巴,迪肯跪住用奶瓶畀牠餵奶。一隻松鼠棲喺迪肯彎住嘅背上,專心地啃住一顆堅果。來自印度嘅小女孩坐喺一張大腳凳上睇住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 年輕的王公既不在床上,也不在沙發上。他坐在一張扶手椅裡,一隻小羊站在他身旁,以吃奶小羊的方式搖著尾巴,迪肯跪著用奶瓶給牠餵奶。一隻松鼠棲在迪肯彎著的背上,專心地啃著一顆堅果。來自印度的小女孩坐在一張大腳凳上看著。

passages.original: “Here is Mr. Roach, Master Colin,” said Mrs. Medlock.
passages.vernacular: 「羅奇先生來喇,柯林少爺,」梅德洛克太太講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「羅奇先生來了,柯林少爺,」梅德洛克太太說。

passages.original: The young Rajah turned and looked his servitor over—at least that was what the head gardener felt happened.
passages.vernacular: 年輕嘅王公轉過頭,把佢嘅僕人上下打量咗一番——至少總園丁覺得係咁樣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 年輕的王公轉過頭,把他的僕人上下打量了一番——至少總園丁覺得是這樣。

passages.original: “Oh, you are Roach, are you?” he said. “I sent for you to give you some very important orders.”
passages.vernacular: 「哦,你就係羅奇,係嗎?」佢講。「我叫你嚟,係要畀你啲好重要嘅命令。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哦,你就是羅奇,是嗎?」他說。「我叫你來,是要給你一些非常重要的命令。」

passages.original: “Very good, sir,” answered Roach, wondering if he was to receive instructions to fell all the oaks in the park or to transform the orchards into water-gardens.
passages.vernacular: 「好好,少爺,」羅奇回答,納悶佢係唔係要接到命令,把公園裡所有橡樹砍倒,或把果園改成水景園。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「很好,少爺,」羅奇回答,納悶他是不是要接到命令,把公園裡所有橡樹砍倒,或把果園改成水景園。

passages.original: “I am going out in my chair this afternoon,” said Colin. “If the fresh air agrees with me I may go out every day. When I go, none of the gardeners are to be anywhere near the Long Walk by the garden walls. No one is to be there. I shall go out about two o’clock and everyone must keep away until I send word that they may go back to their work.”
passages.vernacular: 「我今日下午要坐我嘅椅子出去,」柯林講。「如果新鮮空氣適合我,我或者每天都出去。我出去時,園丁哋邊個都不許喺靠近花園牆嘅長路附近。嗰度不許有任何人。我大約兩點出去,每個人都必須走開,直到我傳話講佢哋可以回去工作為止。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我今天下午要坐我的椅子出去,」柯林說。「如果新鮮空氣適合我,我也許每天都出去。我出去時,園丁們誰都不許在靠近花園牆的長路附近。那裡不許有任何人。我大約兩點出去,每個人都必須走開,直到我傳話說他們可以回去工作為止。」

passages.original: “Very good, sir,” replied Mr. Roach, much relieved to hear that the oaks might remain and that the orchards were safe.
passages.vernacular: 「好好,少爺,」羅奇先生回答,聽講橡樹可以留下、果園安全,大大鬆咗一口氣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「很好,少爺,」羅奇先生回答,聽說橡樹可以留下、果園安全,大大鬆了一口氣。

passages.original: “Mary,” said Colin, turning to her, “what is that thing you say in India when you have finished talking and want people to go?”
passages.vernacular: 「瑪麗,」柯林轉向佢講,「喺印度你講完話想讓人走時,講嘅嗰句話係乜嘢?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「瑪麗,」柯林轉向她說,「在印度你說完話想讓人走時,說的那句話是什麼?」

passages.original: “You say, ‘You have my permission to go,’” answered Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「你講:『你有我嘅許可離開』,」瑪麗回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你說:『你有我的許可離開』,」瑪麗回答。

passages.original: The Rajah waved his hand.
passages.vernacular: 王公揮揮手。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 王公揮揮手。

passages.original: “You have my permission to go, Roach,” he said. “But, remember, this is very important.”
passages.vernacular: 「你有我嘅許可離開,羅奇,」佢講。「不過,記住,呢個好重要。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你有我的許可離開,羅奇,」他說。「不過,記住,這非常重要。」

passages.original: “Caw—Caw!” remarked the crow hoarsely but not impolitely.
passages.vernacular: 「呱——呱!」烏鴉沙啞但並不無禮地評論。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「呱——呱!」烏鴉沙啞但並不無禮地評論。

passages.original: “Very good, sir. Thank you, sir,” said Mr. Roach, and Mrs. Medlock took him out of the room.
passages.vernacular: 「好好,少爺。謝謝您,少爺,」羅奇先生講,梅德洛克太太帶佢走出房間。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「很好,少爺。謝謝您,少爺,」羅奇先生說,梅德洛克太太帶他走出房間。

passages.original: Outside in the corridor, being a rather good-natured man, he smiled until he almost laughed.
passages.vernacular: 喺外面走廊裡,佢係個相當好脾氣嘅人,笑得幾乎要笑出聲嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在外面走廊裡,他是個相當好脾氣的人,笑得幾乎要笑出聲來。

passages.original: “My word!” he said, “he’s got a fine lordly way with him, hasn’t he? You’d think he was a whole Royal Family rolled into one—Prince Consort and all.”
passages.vernacular: 「天呀!」佢講,「佢嗰一套貴族派頭真係不錯,係唔係?你會以為佢係整個王室合喺一起——連親王都算上。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「天哪!」他說,「他那一套貴族派頭真是不錯,是不是?你會以為他是整個王室合在一起——連親王也算上。」

passages.original: “Eh!” protested Mrs. Medlock, “we’ve had to let him trample all over everyone of us ever since he had feet and he thinks that’s what folks was born for.”
passages.vernacular: 「唉!」梅德洛克太太抗議,「自從佢有腳以來,我哋每個人都唔得不讓佢踩喺頭上,佢以為人生下嚟就係為呢個。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「唉!」梅德洛克太太抗議,「自從他有腳以來,我們每個人都不得不讓他踩在頭上,他以為人生下來就是為這個。」

passages.original: “Perhaps he’ll grow out of it, if he lives,” suggested Mr. Roach.
passages.vernacular: 「或者佢會改掉,如果佢活下去,」羅奇先生提議。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「也許他會改掉,如果他活下去,」羅奇先生提議。

passages.original: “Well, there’s one thing pretty sure,” said Mrs. Medlock. “If he does live and that Indian child stays here I’ll warrant she teaches him that the whole orange does not belong to him, as Susan Sowerby says. And he’ll be likely to find out the size of his own quarter.”
passages.vernacular: 「嗯,有一件事相當肯定,」梅德洛克太太講。「如果佢活下去,嗰個印度小孩留喺呢度,我敢保證佢會教佢整個橘子不屬於佢,就像蘇珊·索爾比講嘅。佢好可能會發現佢自己嗰一瓣有多大。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「嗯,有一件事相當肯定,」梅德洛克太太說。「如果他活下去,那個印度小孩留在這裡,我敢保證她會教他整個橘子不屬於他,就像蘇珊·索爾比說的。他很可能會發現他自己那一瓣有多大。」

passages.original: Inside the room Colin was leaning back on his cushions.
passages.vernacular: 房間裡,柯林靠喺佢嘅墊子上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 房間裡,柯林靠在他的墊子上。

passages.original: “It’s all safe now,” he said. “And this afternoon I shall see it—this afternoon I shall be in it!”
passages.vernacular: 「而家一切都安全喇,」佢講。「今日下午我就會睇見佢喇——今日下午我就會喺裡面喇!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「現在一切都安全了,」他說。「今天下午我就會看見它了——今天下午我就會在裡面了!」

passages.original: Dickon went back to the garden with his creatures and Mary stayed with Colin. She did not think he looked tired but he was very quiet before their lunch came and he was quiet while they were eating it. She wondered why and asked him about it.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯帶住佢嘅動物哋回花園去喇,瑪麗留喺柯林身邊。佢不覺得佢睇起嚟累,不過午餐送嚟之前,佢好安靜,佢哋食午餐時都好安靜。佢納悶點解,就問佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯帶著他的動物們回花園去了,瑪麗留在柯林身邊。她不覺得他看起來累,不過午餐送來之前,他非常安靜,他們吃午餐時也很安靜。她納悶為什麼,就問他。

passages.original: “What big eyes you’ve got, Colin,” she said. “When you are thinking they get as big as saucers. What are you thinking about now?”
passages.vernacular: 「你嘅眼睛真大,柯林,」佢講。「你思考時佢哋大得像碟子。你而家喺想乜嘢?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你的眼睛真大,柯林,」她說。「你思考時它們大得像碟子。你現在在想什麼?」

passages.original: “I can’t help thinking about what it will look like,” he answered.
passages.vernacular: 「我忍不住想佢會係乜嘢樣子,」佢回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我忍不住想它會是什麼樣子,」他回答。

passages.original: “The garden?” asked Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「花園嗎?」瑪麗問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「花園嗎?」瑪麗問。

passages.original: “The springtime,” he said. “I was thinking that I’ve really never seen it before. I scarcely ever went out and when I did go I never looked at it. I didn’t even think about it.”
passages.vernacular: 「春天,」佢講。「我喺想我其實從冇見過佢。我幾乎從不出去,出去時都從不睇佢。我連想都冇想過佢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「春天,」他說。「我在想我其實從沒見過它。我幾乎從不出去,出去時也從不看它。我連想都沒想過它。」

passages.original: “I never saw it in India because there wasn’t any,” said Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「我喺印度都冇見過,因為嗰度冇,」瑪麗講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我在印度也沒見過,因為那裡沒有,」瑪麗說。

passages.original: Shut in and morbid as his life had been, Colin had more imagination than she had and at least he had spent a good deal of time looking at wonderful books and pictures.
passages.vernacular: 儘管佢嘅生活封閉而病態,柯林嘅想像力比佢強,至少佢花咗好多時間睇奇妙嘅書同圖畫。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 儘管他的生活封閉而病態,柯林的想像力比她強,至少他花了很多時間看奇妙的書和圖畫。

passages.original: “That morning when you ran in and said ‘It’s come! It’s come!’, you made me feel quite queer. It sounded as if things were coming with a great procession and big bursts and wafts of music. I’ve a picture like it in one of my books—crowds of lovely people and children with garlands and branches with blossoms on them, everyone laughing and dancing and crowding and playing on pipes. That was why I said, ‘Perhaps we shall hear golden trumpets’ and told you to throw open the window.”
passages.vernacular: 「嗰天早晨你跑進來講『佢嚟喇!佢嚟喇!』,你讓我覺得好奇怪。聽起嚟好像一切係帶住一個盛大嘅行列、大爆發同一陣陣音樂嚟嘅。我嘅一本書裡有一幅類似嘅畫——一大群可愛嘅人同細路,攞住花環同開花嘅樹枝,每個人都喺笑、跳舞、擁擠、吹笛。所以我才講:『或者我哋能聽到金喇叭聲』,叫你把窗子打開。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那天早晨你跑進來說『它來了!它來了!』,你讓我覺得很奇怪。聽起來好像一切是帶著一個盛大的行列、大爆發和一陣陣音樂來的。我的一本書裡有一幅類似的畫——一大群可愛的人和孩子,拿著花環和開花的樹枝,每個人都在笑、跳舞、擁擠、吹笛。所以我才說:『也許我們能聽到金喇叭聲』,叫你把窗子打開。」

passages.original: “How funny!” said Mary. “That’s really just what it feels like. And if all the flowers and leaves and green things and birds and wild creatures danced past at once, what a crowd it would be! I’m sure they’d dance and sing and flute and that would be the wafts of music.”
passages.vernacular: 「真有趣!」瑪麗講。「真嘅就係嗰種感覺。如果所有嘅花、葉子、綠色嘅嘢、鳥同野生動物同時跳住舞經過,嗰將係幾咁大嘅一群啊!我肯定牠哋會跳舞、歌唱、吹笛,嗰個就係一陣陣音樂。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「真有趣!」瑪麗說。「真的就是那種感覺。如果所有的花、葉子、綠色的東西、鳥和野生動物同時跳著舞經過,那將是多麼大的一群啊!我肯定牠們會跳舞、歌唱、吹笛,那就是一陣陣音樂。」

passages.original: They both laughed but it was not because the idea was laughable but because they both so liked it.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋兩個都笑喇,但並唔係因為呢個想法可笑,而係因為佢哋兩個都咁鍾意佢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們兩個都笑了,但並不是因為這個想法可笑,而是因為他們兩個都那麼喜歡它。

passages.original: A little later the nurse made Colin ready. She noticed that instead of lying like a log while his clothes were put on he sat up and made some efforts to help himself, and he talked and laughed with Mary all the time.
passages.vernacular: 稍後,護士畀柯林做準備。佢注意到,佢畀佢穿衣服時,唔再像一根木頭一樣躺住,而係坐起嚟,做些努力自己幫忙,仲一直同瑪麗講笑。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 稍後,護士給柯林做準備。她注意到,他給他穿衣服時,不再像一根木頭一樣躺著,而是坐起來,做些努力自己幫忙,還一直同瑪麗說笑。

passages.original: “This is one of his good days, sir,” she said to Dr. Craven, who dropped in to inspect him. “He’s in such good spirits that it makes him stronger.”
passages.vernacular: 「呢個係佢嘅好日子之一,先生,」佢對順路嚟檢查佢嘅克雷文醫生講。「佢心情咁好,讓佢更強壯喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這是他的好日子之一,先生,」她對順路來檢查他的克雷文醫生說。「他心情這麼好,讓他更強壯了。」

passages.original: “I’ll call in again later in the afternoon, after he has come in,” said Dr. Craven. “I must see how the going out agrees with him. I wish,” in a very low voice, “that he would let you go with him.”
passages.vernacular: 「我下午晚些時候,佢回嚟後再嚟,」克雷文醫生講。「我必須睇睇出門對佢係咪合適。我希望,」好低聲地,「佢會讓你跟佢一起去。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我下午晚些時候,他回來後再來,」克雷文醫生說。「我必須看看出門對他是否合適。我希望,」非常低聲地,「他會讓你跟他一起去。」

passages.original: “I’d rather give up the case this moment, sir, than even stay here while it’s suggested,” answered the nurse. With sudden firmness.
passages.vernacular: 「我寧可而家就放棄呢個病例,先生,都唔願喺有人建議呢個嘅時候仲留喺呢度,」護士回答。突然堅決起嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我寧可現在就放棄這個病例,先生,也不願在有人建議這個的時候還留在這裡,」護士回答。突然堅決起來。

passages.original: “I hadn’t really decided to suggest it,” said the doctor, with his slight nervousness. “We’ll try the experiment. Dickon’s a lad I’d trust with a new-born child.”
passages.vernacular: 「我並冇真嘅決定要建議,」醫生講,帶住佢輕微嘅緊張。「我哋嚟試試呢個實驗。迪肯係個我敢把新生嬰兒託付畀佢嘅細路。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我並沒有真的決定要建議,」醫生說,帶著他輕微的緊張。「我們來試試這個實驗。迪肯是個我敢把新生嬰兒託付給他的孩子。」

passages.original: The strongest footman in the house carried Colin downstairs and put him in his wheeled chair near which Dickon waited outside. After the manservant had arranged his rugs and cushions the Rajah waved his hand to him and to the nurse.
passages.vernacular: 房子裡最強壯嘅男僕把柯林抱下樓,放進佢嘅輪椅,迪肯喺外面等住。男僕整理好佢嘅毯子同墊子之後,王公向佢同護士揮咗揮手。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 房子裡最強壯的男僕把柯林抱下樓,放進他的輪椅,迪肯在外面等著。男僕整理好他的毯子和墊子之後,王公向他和護士揮了揮手。

passages.original: “You have my permission to go,” he said, and they both disappeared quickly and it must be confessed giggled when they were safely inside the house.
passages.vernacular: 「你哋有我嘅許可離開,」佢講,佢哋兩個好快消失喇,必須承認,佢哋到咗安全嘅屋裡面就咯咯笑喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你們有我的許可離開,」他說,他們兩個很快消失了,必須承認,他們到了安全的屋裡面就咯咯笑了。

passages.original: Dickon began to push the wheeled chair slowly and steadily. Mistress Mary walked beside it and Colin leaned back and lifted his face to the sky. The arch of it looked very high and the small snowy clouds seemed like white birds floating on outspread wings below its crystal blueness. The wind swept in soft big breaths down from the moor and was strange with a wild clear scented sweetness. Colin kept lifting his thin chest to draw it in, and his big eyes looked as if it were they which were listening—listening, instead of his ears.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯開始緩慢而穩定地推動輪椅。瑪麗小姐走喺旁邊,柯林靠後,把臉仰向天空。天空嘅拱頂睇上去好高,小小嘅雪白嘅雲像張開翅膀漂浮嘅白鳥,喺水晶般嘅藍色下面。風從荒野一大口一大口輕柔地吹下嚟,帶住奇異、野性、清澈、芬芳嘅甜味。柯林不斷抬起佢瘦削嘅胸脯去吸,佢嘅大眼睛睇起嚟像係佢哋喺聽——用眼睛聽,而唔係用耳朵。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯開始緩慢而穩定地推動輪椅。瑪麗小姐走在旁邊,柯林靠後,把臉仰向天空。天空的拱頂看上去很高,小小的雪白的雲像張開翅膀漂浮的白鳥,在水晶般的藍色下面。風從荒野一大口一大口輕柔地吹下來,帶著奇異、野性、清澈、芬芳的甜味。柯林不斷抬起他瘦削的胸脯去吸,他的大眼睛看起來像是它們在聽——用眼睛聽,而不是用耳朵。

passages.original: “There are so many sounds of singing and humming and calling out,” he said. “What is that scent the puffs of wind bring?”
passages.vernacular: 「有咁多歌唱、嗡嗡同呼喊嘅聲音,」佢講。「一陣陣風帶嚟嘅係乜嘢氣味?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「有那麼多歌唱、嗡嗡和呼喊的聲音,」他說。「一陣陣風帶來的是什麼氣味?」

passages.original: “It’s gorse on th’ moor that’s openin’ out,” answered Dickon. “Eh! th’ bees are at it wonderful today.”
passages.vernacular: 「係荒野上正開花嘅金雀花,」迪肯回答。「唉!今日蜜蜂喺嗰上面忙得真起勁。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是荒野上正開花的金雀花,」迪肯回答。「唉!今天蜜蜂在那上面忙得真起勁。」

passages.original: Not a human creature was to be caught sight of in the paths they took. In fact every gardener or gardener’s lad had been witched away. But they wound in and out among the shrubbery and out and round the fountain beds, following their carefully planned route for the mere mysterious pleasure of it. But when at last they turned into the Long Walk by the ivied walls the excited sense of an approaching thrill made them, for some curious reason they could not have explained, begin to speak in whispers.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋走嘅小路上,連一個人影都冇睇到。事實上,每個園丁或園丁嘅小夥計都被施魔法弄走喇。但係佢哋喺灌木叢中進進出出,繞住噴泉花壇走,沿住精心策劃嘅路線,純粹為了嗰神祕嘅樂趣。但當佢哋終於轉進常春藤牆邊嘅長路時,一種對即將到來嘅刺激嘅興奮感,出於某種佢哋解釋不咗嘅奇怪原因,使佢哋開始低聲講話。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們走的小路上,連一個人影也沒看到。事實上,每個園丁或園丁的小夥計都被施魔法弄走了。但是他們在灌木叢中進進出出,繞著噴泉花壇走,沿著精心策劃的路線,純粹為了那神祕的樂趣。但當他們終於轉進常春藤牆邊的長路時,一種對即將到來的刺激的興奮感,出於某種他們解釋不了的奇怪原因,使他們開始低聲說話。

passages.original: “This is it,” breathed Mary. “This is where I used to walk up and down and wonder and wonder.”
passages.vernacular: 「就係呢度,」瑪麗呼吸住講。「呢個就係我以前嚟回走、想咗又想嘅地方。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「就是這裡,」瑪麗呼吸著說。「這就是我以前來回走、想了又想的地方。」

passages.original: “Is it?” cried Colin, and his eyes began to search the ivy with eager curiousness. “But I can see nothing,” he whispered. “There is no door.”
passages.vernacular: 「係嗎?」柯林喊道,佢嘅眼睛開始熱切好奇地搜索常春藤。「不過我乜嘢都睇唔見,」佢低聲講。「冇門。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是嗎?」柯林喊道,他的眼睛開始熱切好奇地搜索常春藤。「可是我什麼也看不見,」他低聲說。「沒有門。」

passages.original: “That’s what I thought,” said Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「我都咁想過,」瑪麗講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我也這麼想過,」瑪麗說。

passages.original: Then there was a lovely breathless silence and the chair wheeled on.
passages.vernacular: 然後有一陣可愛嘅屏息嘅靜默,椅子繼續前行。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後有一陣可愛的屏息的靜默,椅子繼續前行。

passages.original: “That is the garden where Ben Weatherstaff works,” said Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「嗰個係班·韋瑟斯塔夫工作嘅花園,」瑪麗講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那是班·韋瑟斯塔夫工作的花園,」瑪麗說。

passages.original: “Is it?” said Colin.
passages.vernacular: 「係嗎?」柯林講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是嗎?」柯林說。

passages.original: A few yards more and Mary whispered again.
passages.vernacular: 再走幾碼,瑪麗又低聲講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 再走幾碼,瑪麗又低聲說。

passages.original: “This is where the robin flew over the wall,” she said.
passages.vernacular: 「知更鳥就係喺呢度飛過牆嘅,」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「知更鳥就是在這裡飛過牆的,」她說。

passages.original: “Is it?” cried Colin. “Oh! I wish he’d come again!”
passages.vernacular: 「係嗎?」柯林喊道。「哦!我希望牠再嚟!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是嗎?」柯林喊道。「哦!我希望牠再來!」

passages.original: “And that,” said Mary with solemn delight, pointing under a big lilac bush, “is where he perched on the little heap of earth and showed me the key.”
passages.vernacular: 「嗰度,」瑪麗講,帶住莊嚴嘅喜悅,指住一大叢丁香下面,「就係牠棲喺嗰堆小土堆上,畀我睇鑰匙嘅地方。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那裡,」瑪麗說,帶著莊嚴的喜悅,指著一大叢丁香下面,「就是牠棲在那堆小土堆上,給我看鑰匙的地方。」

passages.original: Then Colin sat up.
passages.vernacular: 然後柯林坐直喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後柯林坐直了。

passages.original: “Where? Where? There?” he cried, and his eyes were as big as the wolf’s in Red Riding-Hood, when Red Riding-Hood felt called upon to remark on them. Dickon stood still and the wheeled chair stopped.
passages.vernacular: 「邊度?邊度?嗰度?」佢喊道,佢嘅眼睛像《小紅帽》裡嘅狼嘅眼睛咁大,小紅帽覺得有必要評論佢哋嘅時候。迪肯站住不動,輪椅停喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哪裡?哪裡?那裡?」他喊道,他的眼睛像《小紅帽》裡的狼的眼睛那麼大,小紅帽覺得有必要評論它們的時候。迪肯站住不動,輪椅停了。

passages.original: “And this,” said Mary, stepping on to the bed close to the ivy, “is where I went to talk to him when he chirped at me from the top of the wall. And this is the ivy the wind blew back,” and she took hold of the hanging green curtain.
passages.vernacular: 「仲有呢度,」瑪麗講,踏上靠近常春藤嘅花壇,「係我去同牠講話嘅地方,當時牠喺牆頂上對我啁啾。呢個就係風吹開嘅常春藤,」佢抓住垂掛嘅綠簾。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「還有這裡,」瑪麗說,踏上靠近常春藤的花壇,「是我去同牠說話的地方,當時牠在牆頂上對我啁啾。這就是風吹開的常春藤,」她抓住垂掛的綠簾。

passages.original: “Oh! is it—is it!” gasped Colin.
passages.vernacular: 「哦!係嗎——係嗎!」柯林倒抽一口氣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「哦!是嗎——是嗎!」柯林倒抽一口氣。

passages.original: “And here is the handle, and here is the door. Dickon push him in—push him in quickly!”
passages.vernacular: 「呢度係把手,呢度係門。迪肯,推佢進去——快推佢進去!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「這裡是把手,這裡是門。迪肯,推他進去——快推他進去!」

passages.original: And Dickon did it with one strong, steady, splendid push.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯用一個有力、平穩、漂亮嘅推動做到喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯用一個有力、平穩、漂亮的推動做到了。

passages.original: But Colin had actually dropped back against his cushions, even though he gasped with delight, and he had covered his eyes with his hands and held them there shutting out everything until they were inside and the chair stopped as if by magic and the door was closed. Not till then did he take them away and look round and round and round as Dickon and Mary had done. And over walls and earth and trees and swinging sprays and tendrils the fair green veil of tender little leaves had crept, and in the grass under the trees and the gray urns in the alcoves and here and there everywhere were touches or splashes of gold and purple and white and the trees were showing pink and snow above his head and there were fluttering of wings and faint sweet pipes and humming and scents and scents. And the sun fell warm upon his face like a hand with a lovely touch. And in wonder Mary and Dickon stood and stared at him. He looked so strange and different because a pink glow of color had actually crept all over him—ivory face and neck and hands and all.
passages.vernacular: 不過柯林真嘅向後倒喺墊子上,雖然佢喜悅得喘不過氣,佢用手遮住眼睛,一直嗰樣擋住一切,直到佢哋到咗裡面,椅子像被魔法似嘅停住,門關上喇。直到嗰時佢才攞開手,像迪肯同瑪麗曾做嘅嗰樣,一圈又一圈地環顧。牆上、地上、樹上、擺動嘅枝條同卷鬚上,嫩小葉子織成嘅美麗綠紗已經爬滿喇,樹下嘅草地上、凹室裡嘅灰色花瓶上、到處都有點點或片片嘅金色、紫色同白色,頭頂上嘅樹顯出粉紅同雪白,有翅膀嘅拍動、微弱甜美嘅笛聲、嗡嗡聲、仲有一陣陣嘅香氣。陽光溫暖地落喺佢臉上,像一隻有可愛觸感嘅手。瑪麗同迪肯驚奇地站住,凝視住佢。佢睇起嚟咁奇怪、咁不同,因為一種粉紅色嘅光彩真嘅爬滿咗佢全身——象牙色嘅臉、脖子、手,全都係。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 可是柯林真的向後倒在墊子上,雖然他喜悅得喘不過氣,他用手遮住眼睛,一直那樣擋住一切,直到他們到了裡面,椅子像被魔法似的停住,門關上了。直到那時他才拿開手,像迪肯和瑪麗曾做的那樣,一圈又一圈地環顧。牆上、地上、樹上、擺動的枝條和卷鬚上,嫩小葉子織成的美麗綠紗已經爬滿了,樹下的草地上、凹室裡的灰色花瓶上、到處都有點點或片片的金色、紫色和白色,頭頂上的樹顯出粉紅和雪白,有翅膀的拍動、微弱甜美的笛聲、嗡嗡聲、還有一陣陣的香氣。陽光溫暖地落在他臉上,像一隻有可愛觸感的手。瑪麗和迪肯驚奇地站著,凝視著他。他看起來那麼奇怪、那麼不同,因為一種粉紅色的光彩真的爬滿了他全身——象牙色的臉、脖子、手,全都是。

passages.original: “I shall get well! I shall get well!” he cried out. “Mary! Dickon! I shall get well! And I shall live forever and ever and ever!”
passages.vernacular: 「我會好起嚟!我會好起嚟!」佢喊道。「瑪麗!迪肯!我會好起嚟!我會永遠永遠永遠活下去!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我會好起來!我會好起來!」他喊道。「瑪麗!迪肯!我會好起來!我會永遠永遠永遠活下去!」

chapters.title: Chapter XXI: Ben Weatherstaff 第二十一章:班·韋瑟斯塔夫

passages.original: One of the strange things about living in the world is that it is only now and then one is quite sure one is going to live forever and ever and ever. One knows it sometimes when one gets up at the tender solemn dawn-time and goes out and stands alone and throws one’s head far back and looks up and up and watches the pale sky slowly changing and flushing and marvelous unknown things happening until the East almost makes one cry out and one’s heart stands still at the strange unchanging majesty of the rising of the sun—which has been happening every morning for thousands and thousands and thousands of years. One knows it then for a moment or so. And one knows it sometimes when one stands by oneself in a wood at sunset and the mysterious deep gold stillness slanting through and under the branches seems to be saying slowly again and again something one cannot quite hear, however much one tries. Then sometimes the immense quiet of the dark blue at night with millions of stars waiting and watching makes one sure; and sometimes a sound of far-off music makes it true; and sometimes a look in someone’s eyes.
passages.vernacular: 活喺呢個世界上有一件奇怪嘅事:只係偶爾,人才會好肯定自己將永遠永遠永遠活下去。有時人喺溫柔肅穆嘅黎明時分起身,走出去獨自站住,把頭仰得好後,向上、向上睇,睇住蒼白嘅天空慢慢變化、泛紅,奇妙嘅未知事物發生住,直到東方幾乎讓人喊出聲嚟,心因日出嗰奇異不變嘅莊嚴而停止跳動——呢景象已喺每個早晨發生咗成千上萬年。嗰時人就知道喇,有咁一會兒。有時人獨自站喺日落時嘅樹林裡,神祕嘅深金色寂靜斜斜穿過樹枝同樹枝下面,似乎一遍又一遍緩緩地講住乜嘢,不管點努力都聽不清楚,人都知道。然後有時夜裡深藍色嘅無邊寂靜,千百萬星星喺等待、注視,使人確信;有時遠處音樂嘅聲音使佢成真;有時係某人眼睛裡嘅一個眼神。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 活在這個世界上有一件奇怪的事:只是偶爾,人才會十分肯定自己將永遠永遠永遠活下去。有時人在溫柔肅穆的黎明時分起身,走出去獨自站著,把頭仰得很後,向上、向上看,看著蒼白的天空慢慢變化、泛紅,奇妙的未知事物發生著,直到東方幾乎讓人喊出聲來,心因日出那奇異不變的莊嚴而停止跳動——這景象已在每個早晨發生了成千上萬年。那時人就知道了,有那麼一會兒。有時人獨自站在日落時的樹林裡,神祕的深金色寂靜斜斜穿過樹枝和樹枝下面,似乎一遍又一遍緩緩地說著什麼,不管怎麼努力都聽不清楚,人也知道。然後有時夜裡深藍色的無邊寂靜,千百萬星星在等待、注視,使人確信;有時遠處音樂的聲音使它成真;有時是某人眼睛裡的一個眼神。

passages.original: And it was like that with Colin when he first saw and heard and felt the Springtime inside the four high walls of a hidden garden. That afternoon the whole world seemed to devote itself to being perfect and radiantly beautiful and kind to one boy. Perhaps out of pure heavenly goodness the spring came and crowded everything it possibly could into that one place. More than once Dickon paused in what he was doing and stood still with a sort of growing wonder in his eyes, shaking his head softly.
passages.vernacular: 柯林第一次喺一座隱藏花園嘅四堵高牆裡睇見、聽見、感受到春天時,就係咁樣。嗰個下午,整個世界似乎都致力於為一個男孩變得完美、光輝燦爛、美麗而善良。或者出於純粹嘅天堂般嘅善意,春天嚟喇,把佢所能做到嘅一切都擠進咗嗰一個地方。不止一次,迪肯停下手中嘅事,靜靜站住,眼中帶住一種越嚟越深嘅驚奇,輕輕搖住頭。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 柯林第一次在一座隱藏花園的四堵高牆裡看見、聽見、感受到春天時,就是這樣。那個下午,整個世界似乎都致力於為一個男孩變得完美、光輝燦爛、美麗而善良。也許出於純粹的天堂般的善意,春天來了,把它所能做到的一切都擠進了那一個地方。不止一次,迪肯停下手中的事,靜靜站著,眼中帶著一種越來越深的驚奇,輕輕搖著頭。

passages.original: “Eh! it is graidely,” he said. “I’m twelve goin’ on thirteen an’ there’s a lot o’ afternoons in thirteen years, but seems to me like I never seed one as graidely as this ’ere.”
passages.vernacular: 「唉!真係太美喇,」佢講。「我十二歲快十三喇,十三年裡有好多個下午,不過我覺得我從冇見過像呢個咁樣美嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「唉!真是太美了,」他說。「我十二歲快十三了,十三年裡有很多個下午,可是我覺得我從沒見過像這個這樣美的。」

passages.original: “Aye, it is a graidely one,” said Mary, and she sighed for mere joy. “I’ll warrant it’s the graidelest one as ever was in this world.”
passages.vernacular: 「係啊,真係太美喇,」瑪麗講,佢純粹出於喜悅嘆咗口氣。「我敢講佢係呢個世界上有過嘅最美嘅一個。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是啊,真是太美了,」瑪麗說,她純粹出於喜悅嘆了口氣。「我敢說它是這個世界上有過的最美的一個。」

passages.original: “Does tha’ think,” said Colin with dreamy carefulness, “as happen it was made loike this ’ere all o’ purpose for me?”
passages.vernacular: 「你覺得,」柯林帶住夢幻般嘅小心講,「或者佢係為我專門咁樣做成嘅?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你覺得,」柯林帶著夢幻般的小心說,「也許它是為我專門這樣做成的?」

passages.original: “My word!” cried Mary admiringly, “that there is a bit o’ good Yorkshire. Tha’rt shapin’ first-rate—that tha’ art.”
passages.vernacular: 「天呀!」瑪麗讚嘆地喊道,「嗰個係一句標準嘅好約克郡話。你學得一流——真嘅係。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「天哪!」瑪麗讚嘆地喊道,「那是一句標準的好約克郡話。你學得一流——真的是。」

passages.original: And delight reigned.
passages.vernacular: 歡樂主宰咗一切。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 歡樂主宰了一切。

passages.original: They drew the chair under the plum-tree, which was snow-white with blossoms and musical with bees. It was like a king’s canopy, a fairy king’s. There were flowering cherry-trees near and apple-trees whose buds were pink and white, and here and there one had burst open wide. Between the blossoming branches of the canopy bits of blue sky looked down like wonderful eyes.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋把椅子拉到李樹下,樹上滿係雪白嘅花,蜜蜂嗡嗡作響像音樂。嗰像國王嘅華蓋,仙子國王嘅華蓋。附近有開花嘅櫻桃樹同蘋果樹,蘋果樹嘅花苞係粉紅色同白色嘅,呢度嗰度有嘅已經盛開。喺華蓋開花嘅枝條之間,片片藍天像奇妙嘅眼睛向下望住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們把椅子拉到李樹下,樹上滿是雪白的花,蜜蜂嗡嗡作響像音樂。那像國王的華蓋,仙子國王的華蓋。附近有開花的櫻桃樹和蘋果樹,蘋果樹的花苞是粉紅色和白色的,這裡那裡有的已經盛開。在華蓋開花的枝條之間,片片藍天像奇妙的眼睛向下望著。

passages.original: Mary and Dickon worked a little here and there and Colin watched them. They brought him things to look at—buds which were opening, buds which were tight closed, bits of twig whose leaves were just showing green, the feather of a woodpecker which had dropped on the grass, the empty shell of some bird early hatched. Dickon pushed the chair slowly round and round the garden, stopping every other moment to let him look at wonders springing out of the earth or trailing down from trees. It was like being taken in state round the country of a magic king and queen and shown all the mysterious riches it contained.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗同迪肯呢度嗰度做點活,柯林睇住佢哋。佢哋攞嘢畀佢睇——正在綻開嘅花苞、緊緊閉住嘅花苞、剛露出綠葉嘅小樹枝、掉喺草地上嘅一根啄木鳥嘅羽毛、某隻早孵出嘅鳥嘅空蛋殼。迪肯慢慢推住椅子繞花園一圈又一圈,每隔一會兒就停下,讓佢睇從土裡冒出嚟或從樹上垂下嚟嘅奇妙事物。嗰就像被人莊嚴地帶住遊覽一位魔法國王同王后嘅國土,畀佢睇佢所包含嘅所有神祕財富。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗和迪肯這裡那裡做點活,柯林看著他們。他們拿東西給他看——正在綻開的花苞、緊緊閉著的花苞、剛露出綠葉的小樹枝、掉在草地上的一根啄木鳥的羽毛、某隻早孵出的鳥的空蛋殼。迪肯慢慢推著椅子繞花園一圈又一圈,每隔一會兒就停下,讓他看從土裡冒出來或從樹上垂下來的奇妙事物。那就像被人莊嚴地帶著遊覽一位魔法國王和王后的國土,給他看它所包含的所有神祕財富。

passages.original: “I wonder if we shall see the robin?” said Colin.
passages.vernacular: 「我唔知道我哋能唔能夠睇到知更鳥?」柯林講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我不知道我們能不能看到知更鳥?」柯林說。

passages.original: “Tha’ll see him often enow after a bit,” answered Dickon. “When th’ eggs hatches out th’ little chap he’ll be kep’ so busy it’ll make his head swim. Tha’ll see him flyin’ backward an’ for’ard carryin’ worms nigh as big as himsel’ an’ that much noise goin’ on in th’ nest when he gets there as fair flusters him so as he scarce knows which big mouth to drop th’ first piece in. An’ gapin’ beaks an’ squawks on every side. Mother says as when she sees th’ work a robin has to keep them gapin’ beaks filled, she feels like she was a lady with nothin’ to do. She says she’s seen th’ little chaps when it seemed like th’ sweat must be droppin’ off ’em, though folk can’t see it.”
passages.vernacular: 「過一會兒你會常常睇到牠,」迪肯回答。「等蛋孵出嚟,嗰小子會忙得讓牠頭暈。你會睇到牠飛嚟飛去,叼住差不多跟牠自己一樣大嘅蟲子,牠到咗巢裡,吵得牠手忙腳亂,幾乎唔知道先把第一口食物塞進邊張大嘴裡。每一邊都係張住嘅喙同尖叫聲。媽媽講,佢睇到知更鳥為了填滿嗰啲張住嘅嘴所要做嘅活,覺得自己像個乜嘢事都冇嘅貴婦人。佢講佢見過嗰啲小傢伙,好像汗一定喺往下滴,雖然人睇唔見。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「過一會兒你會常常看到牠,」迪肯回答。「等蛋孵出來,那小子會忙得讓牠頭暈。你會看到牠飛來飛去,叼著差不多跟牠自己一樣大的蟲子,牠到了巢裡,吵得牠手忙腳亂,幾乎不知道先把第一口食物塞進哪張大嘴裡。每一邊都是張著的喙和尖叫聲。媽媽說,她看到知更鳥為了填滿那些張著的嘴所要做的活,覺得自己像個什麼事也沒有的貴婦人。她說她見過那些小傢伙,好像汗一定在往下滴,雖然人看不見。」

passages.original: This made them giggle so delightedly that they were obliged to cover their mouths with their hands, remembering that they must not be heard. Colin had been instructed as to the law of whispers and low voices several days before. He liked the mysteriousness of it and did his best, but in the midst of excited enjoyment it is rather difficult never to laugh above a whisper.
passages.vernacular: 呢讓佢哋高興得咯咯笑,唔得唔使手摀住嘴,記起佢哋唔能夠被聽見。幾天前,柯林就被教過低聲同耳語嘅規矩。佢鍾意呢其中嘅神祕感,盡咗自己嘅努力,但喺興奮嘅享受中,要始終不笑出超過耳語嘅聲音係相當困難嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這讓他們高興得咯咯笑,不得不用手摀住嘴,記起他們不能被聽見。幾天前,柯林就被教過低聲和耳語的規矩。他喜歡這其中的神祕感,盡了自己的努力,但在興奮的享受中,要始終不笑出超過耳語的聲音是相當困難的。

passages.original: Every moment of the afternoon was full of new things and every hour the sunshine grew more golden. The wheeled chair had been drawn back under the canopy and Dickon had sat down on the grass and had just drawn out his pipe when Colin saw something he had not had time to notice before.
passages.vernacular: 嗰個下午每一刻都充滿新鮮事,每過一小時,陽光就更金黃啲。輪椅已被拉回華蓋下,迪肯喺草地上坐下,剛攞出佢嘅笛子,柯林睇到咗一樣佢以前冇時間注意到嘅嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 那個下午每一刻都充滿新鮮事,每過一小時,陽光就更金黃一些。輪椅已被拉回華蓋下,迪肯在草地上坐下,剛拿出他的笛子,柯林看到了一樣他以前沒時間注意到的東西。

passages.original: “That’s a very old tree over there, isn’t it?” he said.
passages.vernacular: 「嗰邊嗰棵樹好老喇,係唔係?」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那邊那棵樹很老了,是不是?」他說。

passages.original: Dickon looked across the grass at the tree and Mary looked and there was a brief moment of stillness.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯隔住草地望嗰棵樹,瑪麗都望去,有一瞬間嘅靜止。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯隔著草地望那棵樹,瑪麗也望去,有一瞬間的靜止。

passages.original: “Yes,” answered Dickon, after it, and his low voice had a very gentle sound.
passages.vernacular: 「係嘅,」迪肯喺嗰之後回答,佢低低嘅聲音聽起嚟好溫柔。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是的,」迪肯在那之後回答,他低低的聲音聽起來很溫柔。

passages.original: Mary gazed at the tree and thought.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗凝視住嗰棵樹,思考住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗凝視著那棵樹,思考著。

passages.original: “The branches are quite gray and there’s not a single leaf anywhere,” Colin went on. “It’s quite dead, isn’t it?”
passages.vernacular: 「樹枝全係灰色嘅,到處冇一片葉子,」柯林接住講。「佢完全死喇,係唔係?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「樹枝全是灰色的,到處沒有一片葉子,」柯林接著說。「它完全死了,是不是?」

passages.original: “Aye,” admitted Dickon. “But them roses as has climbed all over it will near hide every bit o’ th’ dead wood when they’re full o’ leaves an’ flowers. It won’t look dead then. It’ll be th’ prettiest of all.”
passages.vernacular: 「係啊,」迪肯承認。「不過爬滿佢嘅嗰啲玫瑰,等佢哋長滿葉子開滿花時,會把死木頭幾乎全遮住。嗰時佢就不像死喇。佢會係最漂亮嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是啊,」迪肯承認。「不過爬滿它的那些玫瑰,等它們長滿葉子開滿花時,會把死木頭幾乎全遮住。那時它就不像死了。它會是最漂亮的。」

passages.original: Mary still gazed at the tree and thought.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗仍凝視住嗰棵樹,思考住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗仍凝視著那棵樹,思考著。

passages.original: “It looks as if a big branch had been broken off,” said Colin. “I wonder how it was done.”
passages.vernacular: 「睇起嚟好像有一根大樹枝折斷喇,」柯林講。「我唔知道係點斷嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「看起來好像有一根大樹枝折斷了,」柯林說。「我不知道是怎麼斷的。」

passages.original: “It’s been done many a year,” answered Dickon. “Eh!” with a sudden relieved start and laying his hand on Colin. “Look at that robin! There he is! He’s been foragin’ for his mate.”
passages.vernacular: 「斷咗好多年喇,」迪肯回答。「唉!」突然鬆咗口氣地一驚,把手放喺柯林身上。「睇嗰知更鳥!牠喺嗰兒!牠一直喺為牠嘅伴覓食。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「斷了好多年了,」迪肯回答。「唉!」突然鬆了口氣地一驚,把手放在柯林身上。「看那知更鳥!牠在那兒!牠一直在為牠的伴覓食。」

passages.original: Colin was almost too late but he just caught sight of him, the flash of red-breasted bird with something in his beak. He darted through the greenness and into the close-grown corner and was out of sight. Colin leaned back on his cushion again, laughing a little.
passages.vernacular: 柯林差點冇趕上,但剛好瞥見牠,嗰一閃紅胸脯嘅鳥,嘴裡叼住嘢。牠穿過綠葉,飛進緊密生長嘅角落,唔見喇。柯林又靠回墊子上,微微笑住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 柯林差點沒趕上,但剛好瞥見牠,那一閃紅胸脯的鳥,嘴裡叼著東西。牠穿過綠葉,飛進緊密生長的角落,不見了。柯林又靠回墊子上,微微笑著。

passages.original: “He’s taking her tea to her. Perhaps it’s five o’clock. I think I’d like some tea myself.”
passages.vernacular: 「牠畀佢送茶去喇。或者係五點鐘喇。我想我自己都想飲點茶。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「牠給她送茶去了。也許是五點鐘了。我想我自己也想喝點茶。」

passages.original: And so they were safe.
passages.vernacular: 就咁樣,佢哋安全喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 就這樣,他們安全了。

passages.original: “It was Magic which sent the robin,” said Mary secretly to Dickon afterward. “I know it was Magic.” For both she and Dickon had been afraid Colin might ask something about the tree whose branch had broken off ten years ago and they had talked it over together and Dickon had stood and rubbed his head in a troubled way.
passages.vernacular: 「係魔法派嚟咗知更鳥,」瑪麗後來私下對迪肯講。「我知道係魔法。」因為佢同迪肯都曾怕柯林會問起嗰棵十年前折斷咗一根枝嘅樹,佢哋一起商量過,迪肯站住不安地搓住頭。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是魔法派來了知更鳥,」瑪麗後來私下對迪肯說。「我知道是魔法。」因為她和迪肯都曾怕柯林會問起那棵十年前折斷了一根枝的樹,他們一起商量過,迪肯站著不安地搓著頭。

passages.original: “We mun look as if it wasn’t no different from th’ other trees,” he had said. “We couldn’t never tell him how it broke, poor lad. If he says anything about it we mun—we mun try to look cheerful.”
passages.vernacular: 「我哋得裝作佢同別嘅樹冇乜嘢不同,」佢講。「我哋可唔能夠告訴佢佢係點斷嘅,可憐嘅細路。如果佢講起佢,我哋得——我哋得試住睇起嚟高興。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我們得裝作它和別的樹沒什麼不同,」他說。「我們可不能告訴他它是怎麼斷的,可憐的孩子。如果他說起它,我們得——我們得試著看起來高興。」

passages.original: “Aye, that we mun,” had answered Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「係啊,我哋得咁樣,」瑪麗回答過。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是啊,我們得這樣,」瑪麗回答過。

passages.original: But she had not felt as if she looked cheerful when she gazed at the tree. She wondered and wondered in those few moments if there was any reality in that other thing Dickon had said. He had gone on rubbing his rust-red hair in a puzzled way, but a nice comforted look had begun to grow in his blue eyes.
passages.vernacular: 不過佢凝視嗰棵樹時,並冇覺得自己睇起嚟高興。喺嗰短短嘅片刻裡,佢一直納悶迪肯講嘅另一件事係唔係真嘅。佢當時一直困惑地搓住鐵鏽紅嘅頭髮,但佢嘅藍眼睛裡開始生出一種美好嘅、安慰嘅神色。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 可是她凝視那棵樹時,並沒覺得自己看起來高興。在那短短的片刻裡,她一直納悶迪肯說的另一件事是不是真的。他當時一直困惑地搓著鐵鏽紅的頭髮,但他的藍眼睛裡開始生出一種美好的、安慰的神色。

passages.original: “Mrs. Craven was a very lovely young lady,” he had gone on rather hesitatingly. “An’ mother she thinks maybe she’s about Misselthwaite many a time lookin’ after Mester Colin, same as all mothers do when they’re took out o’ th’ world. They have to come back, tha’ sees. Happen she’s been in the garden an’ happen it was her set us to work, an’ told us to bring him here.”
passages.vernacular: 「克雷文太太係個好可愛嘅年輕太太,」佢當時有點遲疑地接住講。「媽媽覺得,或者佢常常喺米瑟斯威特附近,照睇柯林少爺,就像所有被帶離世界嘅母親一樣。佢哋必須回嚟,你知道。或者佢一直喺花園裡,或者係佢讓我哋開始工作,叫我哋把佢帶到呢度。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「克雷文太太是個非常可愛的年輕太太,」他當時有點遲疑地接著說。「媽媽覺得,也許她常常在米瑟斯威特附近,照看柯林少爺,就像所有被帶離世界的母親一樣。她們必須回來,你知道。也許她一直在花園裡,也許是她讓我們開始工作,叫我們把他帶到這裡。」

passages.original: Mary had thought he meant something about Magic. She was a great believer in Magic. Secretly she quite believed that Dickon worked Magic, of course good Magic, on everything near him and that was why people liked him so much and wild creatures knew he was their friend. She wondered, indeed, if it were not possible that his gift had brought the robin just at the right moment when Colin asked that dangerous question. She felt that his Magic was working all the afternoon and making Colin look like an entirely different boy. It did not seem possible that he could be the crazy creature who had screamed and beaten and bitten his pillow. Even his ivory whiteness seemed to change. The faint glow of color which had shown on his face and neck and hands when he first got inside the garden really never quite died away. He looked as if he were made of flesh instead of ivory or wax.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗當時以為佢係指某種魔法。佢係個魔法嘅堅定信徒。佢私下完全相信,迪肯對佢附近嘅一切施行魔法,當然係好魔法,呢個就係點解人哋咁鍾意佢、野生動物知道佢係朋友。佢確實納悶,佢嘅天賦係咪喺柯林問嗰個危險問題時,恰到好處地帶嚟咗知更鳥。佢覺得佢嘅魔法整個下午都喺起作用,讓柯林睇起嚟像一個完全不同嘅男孩。佢似乎唔可能係嗰個尖叫、捶打、咬枕頭嘅瘋狂傢伙。連佢象牙般嘅蒼白都似乎喺改變。佢一進花園時臉、脖子同手上顯出嘅淡淡紅暈,其實從冇完全消失。佢睇起嚟好像係肉做嘅,而唔係象牙或蠟做嘅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗當時以為他是指某種魔法。她是個魔法的堅定信徒。她私下完全相信,迪肯對他附近的一切施行魔法,當然是好魔法,這就是為什麼人們那麼喜歡他、野生動物知道他是朋友。她確實納悶,他的天賦是否在柯林問那個危險問題時,恰到好處地帶來了知更鳥。她覺得他的魔法整個下午都在起作用,讓柯林看起來像一個完全不同的男孩。他似乎不可能是那個尖叫、捶打、咬枕頭的瘋狂傢伙。連他象牙般的蒼白也似乎在改變。他一進花園時臉、脖子和手上顯出的淡淡紅暈,其實從沒完全消失。他看起來好像是肉做的,而不是象牙或蠟做的。

passages.original: They saw the robin carry food to his mate two or three times, and it was so suggestive of afternoon tea that Colin felt they must have some.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋睇到知更鳥兩三次把食物叼畀牠嘅伴,呢太讓人聯想到下午茶,柯林覺得佢哋一定都得有些。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們看到知更鳥兩三次把食物叼給牠的伴,這太讓人聯想到下午茶,柯林覺得他們一定也得有些。

passages.original: “Go and make one of the men servants bring some in a basket to the rhododendron walk,” he said. “And then you and Dickon can bring it here.”
passages.vernacular: 「去叫一個男僕用籃子把茶送到杜鵑花小路嚟,」佢講。「然後你同迪肯可以把佢攞到呢度嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「去叫一個男僕用籃子把茶送到杜鵑花小路來,」他說。「然後你和迪肯可以把它拿到這裡來。」

passages.original: It was an agreeable idea, easily carried out, and when the white cloth was spread upon the grass, with hot tea and buttered toast and crumpets, a delightfully hungry meal was eaten, and several birds on domestic errands paused to inquire what was going on and were led into investigating crumbs with great activity. Nut and Shell whisked up trees with pieces of cake and Soot took the entire half of a buttered crumpet into a corner and pecked at and examined and turned it over and made hoarse remarks about it until he decided to swallow it all joyfully in one gulp.
passages.vernacular: 呢個係個愉快嘅主意,好容易辦到,白桌布鋪喺草地上,擺住熱茶、奶油吐司同烤鬆餅,佢哋愉快而饑餓地食咗一頓,幾隻為家務奔忙嘅鳥停下嚟打聽出咗乜嘢事,被引住極其起勁地研究起麵包屑嚟。堅果同殼叼住蛋糕片竄上樹,煤灰把整整半塊奶油烤鬆餅叼到一個角落,啄佢、檢查佢、翻佢,發表沙啞嘅評論,直到決定一口高興地全吞下去。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這是個愉快的主意,很容易辦到,白桌布鋪在草地上,擺著熱茶、奶油吐司和烤鬆餅,他們愉快而饑餓地吃了一頓,幾隻為家務奔忙的鳥停下來打聽出了什麼事,被引著極其起勁地研究起麵包屑來。堅果和殼叼著蛋糕片竄上樹,煤灰把整整半塊奶油烤鬆餅叼到一個角落,啄它、檢查它、翻它,發表沙啞的評論,直到決定一口高興地全吞下去。

passages.original: The afternoon was dragging towards its mellow hour. The sun was deepening the gold of its lances, the bees were going home and the birds were flying past less often. Dickon and Mary were sitting on the grass, the tea-basket was repacked ready to be taken back to the house, and Colin was lying against his cushions with his heavy locks pushed back from his forehead and his face looking quite a natural color.
passages.vernacular: 下午逐漸拖向佢柔和嘅時刻。太陽使佢嘅金色長矛更深,蜜蜂喺回家,鳥飛過嘅次數少喇。迪肯同瑪麗坐喺草地上,茶籃重新收拾好,準備帶回屋,柯林靠喺墊子上,濃密嘅頭髮從額頭撥開,臉色睇起嚟相當自然。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 下午逐漸拖向它柔和的時刻。太陽使它的金色長矛更深,蜜蜂在回家,鳥飛過的次數少了。迪肯和瑪麗坐在草地上,茶籃重新收拾好,準備帶回屋,柯林靠在墊子上,濃密的頭髮從額頭撥開,臉色看起來相當自然。

passages.original: “I don’t want this afternoon to go,” he said; “but I shall come back tomorrow, and the day after, and the day after, and the day after.”
passages.vernacular: 「我唔想呢個下午結束,」佢講;「但我聽日會回嚟,後天,大後天,再大後天。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我不想這個下午結束,」他說;「但我明天會回來,後天,大後天,再大後天。」

passages.original: “You’ll get plenty of fresh air, won’t you?” said Mary.
passages.vernacular: 「你會有好多新鮮空氣,係唔係?」瑪麗講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你會有很多新鮮空氣,是不是?」瑪麗說。

passages.original: “I’m going to get nothing else,” he answered. “I’ve seen the spring now and I’m going to see the summer. I’m going to see everything grow here. I’m going to grow here myself.”
passages.vernacular: 「我乜嘢都唔好,就要呢個,」佢回答。「我而家見到咗春天,我仲要見到夏天。我要睇呢度嘅一切生長。我自己都要喺呢度長大。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我什麼也不要,就要這個,」他回答。「我現在見到了春天,我還要見到夏天。我要看這裡的一切生長。我自己也要在這裡長大。」

passages.original: “That tha’ will,” said Dickon. “Us’ll have thee walkin’ about here an’ diggin’ same as other folk afore long.”
passages.vernacular: 「你肯定會,」迪肯講。「不久我哋就會讓你像別人一樣喺呢度走動、挖地。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你肯定會,」迪肯說。「不久我們就會讓你像別人一樣在這裡走動、挖地。」

passages.original: Colin flushed tremendously.
passages.vernacular: 柯林漲得通紅。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 柯林漲得通紅。

passages.original: “Walk!” he said. “Dig! Shall I?”
passages.vernacular: 「走路!」佢講。「挖地!我會嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「走路!」他說。「挖地!我會嗎?」

passages.original: Dickon’s glance at him was delicately cautious. Neither he nor Mary had ever asked if anything was the matter with his legs.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯睇佢嘅目光微妙而小心。佢同瑪麗都從冇問過佢嘅腿係咪有乜嘢毛病。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯看他的目光微妙而小心。他和瑪麗都從沒問過他的腿是否有什麼毛病。

passages.original: “For sure tha’ will,” he said stoutly. “Tha—tha’s got legs o’ thine own, same as other folks!”
passages.vernacular: 「肯定會,」佢堅定地講。「你——你有自己嘅腿,跟別人一樣!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「肯定會,」他堅定地說。「你——你有自己的腿,跟別人一樣!」

passages.original: Mary was rather frightened until she heard Colin’s answer.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗相當害怕,直到佢聽到柯林嘅回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗相當害怕,直到她聽到柯林的回答。

passages.original: “Nothing really ails them,” he said, “but they are so thin and weak. They shake so that I’m afraid to try to stand on them.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢哋其實冇乜嘢毛病,」佢講,「就係又瘦又弱。佢哋抖得厲害,我怕試住站喺上面。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「它們其實沒什麼毛病,」他說,「就是又瘦又弱。它們抖得厲害,我怕試著站在上面。」

passages.original: Both Mary and Dickon drew a relieved breath.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗同迪肯都鬆咗一口氣。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗和迪肯都鬆了一口氣。

passages.original: “When tha’ stops bein’ afraid tha’lt stand on ’em,” Dickon said with renewed cheer. “An’ tha’lt stop bein’ afraid in a bit.”
passages.vernacular: 「等你不害怕喇,你就能站喺上面,」迪肯重新振作地講。「而且過一會兒你就唔會怕喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「等你不害怕了,你就能站在上面,」迪肯重新振作地說。「而且過一會兒你就不會怕了。」

passages.original: “I shall?” said Colin, and he lay still as if he were wondering about things.
passages.vernacular: 「我會嗎?」柯林講,佢靜靜躺住,好像喺納悶各種事。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我會嗎?」柯林說,他靜靜躺著,好像在納悶各種事。

passages.original: They were really very quiet for a little while. The sun was dropping lower. It was that hour when everything stills itself, and they really had had a busy and exciting afternoon. Colin looked as if he were resting luxuriously. Even the creatures had ceased moving about and had drawn together and were resting near them. Soot had perched on a low branch and drawn up one leg and dropped the gray film drowsily over his eyes. Mary privately thought he looked as if he might snore in a minute.
passages.vernacular: 佢哋真嘅安靜咗好一會兒。太陽喺往下落。嗰個係一切都歸於平靜嘅時刻,佢哋呢個下午真嘅又忙碌又興奮。柯林睇起嚟像係喺舒適地休息。連動物哋都停止走動,聚喺一起,喺佢哋附近休息。煤灰棲喺一根低枝上,縮起一條腿,睏倦地把灰色嘅薄膜垂到眼睛上。瑪麗私下想,牠睇起嚟好像即刻就要打鼾喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他們真的安靜了好一會兒。太陽在往下落。那是一切都歸於平靜的時刻,他們這個下午真的又忙碌又興奮。柯林看起來像是在舒適地休息。連動物們也停止走動,聚在一起,在他們附近休息。煤灰棲在一根低枝上,縮起一條腿,睏倦地把灰色的薄膜垂到眼睛上。瑪麗私下想,牠看起來好像馬上就要打鼾了。

passages.original: In the midst of this stillness it was rather startling when Colin half lifted his head and exclaimed in a loud suddenly alarmed whisper:
passages.vernacular: 喺呢片寂靜之中,柯林半抬起頭,用突然驚慌嘅大聲耳語喊出嚟,真讓人食驚:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 在這片寂靜之中,柯林半抬起頭,用突然驚慌的大聲耳語喊出來,真讓人吃驚:

passages.original: “Who is that man?”
passages.vernacular: 「嗰個人係邊個?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「那個人是誰?」

passages.original: Dickon and Mary scrambled to their feet.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯同瑪麗連忙站起嚟。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯和瑪麗連忙站起來。

passages.original: “Man!” they both cried in low quick voices.
passages.vernacular: 「人!」佢哋兩個用低而急嘅聲音喊。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「人!」他們兩個用低而急的聲音喊。

passages.original: Colin pointed to the high wall.
passages.vernacular: 柯林指住高牆。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 柯林指著高牆。

passages.original: “Look!” he whispered excitedly. “Just look!”
passages.vernacular: 「睇!」佢興奮地低聲講。「你哋睇!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「看!」他興奮地低聲說。「你們看!」

passages.original: Mary and Dickon wheeled about and looked. There was Ben Weatherstaff’s indignant face glaring at them over the wall from the top of a ladder! He actually shook his fist at Mary.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗同迪肯轉過身去睇。班·韋瑟斯塔夫憤怒嘅臉,正從梯子頂上越過牆對佢哋怒目而視!佢真嘅朝瑪麗揮咗揮拳頭。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗和迪肯轉過身去看。班·韋瑟斯塔夫憤怒的臉,正從梯子頂上越過牆對他們怒目而視!他真的朝瑪麗揮了揮拳頭。

passages.original: “If I wasn’t a bachelder, an’ tha’ was a wench o’ mine,” he cried, “I’d give thee a hidin’!”
passages.vernacular: 「要唔係我係個單身漢,而你係我嘅丫頭,」佢喊道,「我要揍你一頓!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「要不是我是個單身漢,而你是我的丫頭,」他喊道,「我要揍你一頓!」

passages.original: He mounted another step threateningly as if it were his energetic intention to jump down and deal with her; but as she came toward him he evidently thought better of it and stood on the top step of his ladder shaking his fist down at her.
passages.vernacular: 佢威脅地又爬上一級,好像打算精力十足地跳下嚟收拾佢;但佢朝佢走嚟時,佢顯然想咗想改變咗主意,站喺梯子最頂一級,朝佢揮住拳頭。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他威脅地又爬上一級,好像打算精力十足地跳下來收拾她;但她朝他走來時,他顯然想了想改變了主意,站在梯子最頂一級,朝她揮著拳頭。

passages.original: “I never thowt much o’ thee!” he harangued. “I couldna’ abide thee th’ first time I set eyes on thee. A scrawny buttermilk-faced young besom, allus askin’ questions an’ pokin’ tha’ nose where it wasna, wanted. I never knowed how tha’ got so thick wi’ me. If it hadna’ been for th’ robin— Drat him—”
passages.vernacular: 「我從來冇點睇得起你!」佢訓斥道。「我第一次見你就受不了你。一個瘦巴巴、酸酪乳臉嘅年輕潑婦,老係問問題,把鼻子伸到不該伸嘅地方。我從不明白你點會同我咁親近。要唔係嗰知更鳥——該死嘅佢——」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我從來沒怎麼看得起你!」他訓斥道。「我第一次見你就受不了你。一個瘦巴巴、酸酪乳臉的年輕潑婦,老是問問題,把鼻子伸到不該伸的地方。我從不明白你怎麼會同我這麼親近。要不是那知更鳥——該死的它——」

passages.original: “Ben Weatherstaff,” called out Mary, finding her breath. She stood below him and called up to him with a sort of gasp. “Ben Weatherstaff, it was the robin who showed me the way!”
passages.vernacular: 「班·韋瑟斯塔夫,」瑪麗喊道,喘過氣嚟喇。佢站喺佢下面,抬頭帶住一種喘息向佢喊話。「班·韋瑟斯塔夫,係知更鳥畀我指嘅路!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「班·韋瑟斯塔夫,」瑪麗喊道,喘過氣來了。她站在他下面,抬頭帶著一種喘息向他喊話。「班·韋瑟斯塔夫,是知更鳥給我指的路!」

passages.original: Then it did seem as if Ben really would scramble down on her side of the wall, he was so outraged.
passages.vernacular: 呢陣班睇起嚟真嘅要從牆呢邊爬下嚟找佢喇,佢氣憤極喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這時班看起來真的要從牆這邊爬下來找她了,他氣憤極了。

passages.original: “Tha’ young bad ’un!” he called down at her. “Layin’ tha’ badness on a robin—not but what he’s impidint enow for anythin’. Him showin’ thee th’ way! Him! Eh! tha’ young nowt”—she could see his next words burst out because he was overpowered by curiosity—“however i’ this world did tha’ get in?”
passages.vernacular: 「你呢個壞丫頭!」佢朝佢喊。「把你嘅壞事賴喺知更鳥身上——不過牠確實夠放肆,乜嘢事都做得出嚟。牠畀你指路!牠!唉!你呢個小無賴」——佢能睇出佢接下嚟嘅話係因為好奇心壓倒咗佢才衝口而出——「你到底係點進嚟嘅?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你這個壞丫頭!」他朝她喊。「把你的壞事賴在知更鳥身上——不過牠確實夠放肆,什麼事都做得出來。牠給你指路!牠!唉!你這個小無賴」——她能看出他接下來的話是因為好奇心壓倒了他才衝口而出——「你到底是怎麼進來的?」

passages.original: “It was the robin who showed me the way,” she protested obstinately. “He didn’t know he was doing it but he did. And I can’t tell you from here while you’re shaking your fist at me.”
passages.vernacular: 「係知更鳥畀我指嘅路,」佢固執地抗議。「牠唔知道牠喺做,可牠做喇。你喺朝我揮拳頭,我喺呢下面冇法告訴你。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是知更鳥給我指的路,」她固執地抗議。「牠不知道牠在做,可牠做了。你在朝我揮拳頭,我在這下面沒法告訴你。」

passages.original: He stopped shaking his fist very suddenly at that very moment and his jaw actually dropped as he stared over her head at something he saw coming over the grass toward him.
passages.vernacular: 就喺嗰一刻,佢好突然地停止咗揮拳頭,下巴真嘅掉咗下嚟,佢越過佢嘅頭頂瞪住佢睇到嘅、正從草地上朝佢過嚟嘅乜嘢嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 就在那一刻,他很突然地停止了揮拳頭,下巴真的掉了下來,他越過她的頭頂瞪著他看到的、正從草地上朝他過來的什麼東西。

passages.original: At the first sound of his torrent of words Colin had been so surprised that he had only sat up and listened as if he were spellbound. But in the midst of it he had recovered himself and beckoned imperiously to Dickon.
passages.vernacular: 一聽到佢嗰一連串嘅話,柯林太食驚喇,只係坐起嚟聽住,像被施咗魔法。但講到一半時佢恢復咗過嚟,專橫地向迪肯招手。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一聽到他那一連串的話,柯林太吃驚了,只是坐起來聽著,像被施了魔法。但說到一半時他恢復了過來,專橫地向迪肯招手。

passages.original: “Wheel me over there!” he commanded. “Wheel me quite close and stop right in front of him!”
passages.vernacular: 「把我推到嗰邊去!」佢命令。「推近些,就停喺佢嘅正前面!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「把我推到那邊去!」他命令。「推近些,就停在他的正前面!」

passages.original: And this, if you please, this is what Ben Weatherstaff beheld and which made his jaw drop. A wheeled chair with luxurious cushions and robes which came toward him looking rather like some sort of State Coach because a young Rajah leaned back in it with royal command in his great black-rimmed eyes and a thin white hand extended haughtily toward him. And it stopped right under Ben Weatherstaff’s nose. It was really no wonder his mouth dropped open.
passages.vernacular: 呢,請注意,就係班·韋瑟斯塔夫所睇到、並使佢下巴掉下嚟嘅。一輛有豪華墊子同毯子嘅輪椅朝佢過嚟,睇起嚟有點像一輛國家御用馬車,因為一位年輕嘅王公靠坐喺裡面,佢黑邊嘅大眼睛裡有王者嘅命令,一隻瘦白嘅手傲慢地朝佢伸出。佢正好停喺班·韋瑟斯塔夫嘅鼻子底下。佢張大咗嘴,真嘅不足為奇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這,請注意,就是班·韋瑟斯塔夫所看到、並使他下巴掉下來的。一輛有豪華墊子和毯子的輪椅朝他過來,看起來有點像一輛國家御用馬車,因為一位年輕的王公靠坐在裡面,他黑邊的大眼睛裡有王者的命令,一隻瘦白的手傲慢地朝他伸出。它正好停在班·韋瑟斯塔夫的鼻子底下。他張大了嘴,真的不足為奇。

passages.original: “Do you know who I am?” demanded the Rajah.
passages.vernacular: 「你知道我係邊個嗎?」王公問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你知道我是誰嗎?」王公問。

passages.original: How Ben Weatherstaff stared! His red old eyes fixed themselves on what was before him as if he were seeing a ghost. He gazed and gazed and gulped a lump down his throat and did not say a word.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫瞪得多厲害啊!佢嘅紅紅嘅老眼睛盯住面前嘅嘢,好像睇見咗鬼。佢凝視咗又凝視,把一個硬塊嚥下喉嚨,一個字都冇講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫瞪得多厲害啊!他的紅紅的老眼睛盯著面前的東西,好像看見了鬼。他凝視了又凝視,把一個硬塊嚥下喉嚨,一個字也沒說。

passages.original: “Do you know who I am?” demanded Colin still more imperiously. “Answer!”
passages.vernacular: 「你知道我係邊個嗎?」柯林更加專橫地問。「回答!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你知道我是誰嗎?」柯林更加專橫地問。「回答!」

passages.original: Ben Weatherstaff put his gnarled hand up and passed it over his eyes and over his forehead and then he did answer in a queer shaky voice.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫抬起佢嘅粗糙嘅手,喺眼睛同額頭上抹咗一下,然後佢用古怪顫抖嘅聲音回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫抬起他的粗糙的手,在眼睛和額頭上抹了一下,然後他用古怪顫抖的聲音回答。

passages.original: “Who tha’ art?” he said. “Aye, that I do—wi’ tha’ mother’s eyes starin’ at me out o’ tha’ face. Lord knows how tha’ come here. But tha’rt th’ poor cripple.”
passages.vernacular: 「你係邊個?」佢講。「係啊,我知道——你母親嘅眼睛從你臉上盯住我。天曉得你點嚟到呢度。可你就係嗰個可憐嘅殘廢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你是誰?」他說。「是啊,我知道——你母親的眼睛從你臉上盯著我。天曉得你怎麼來到這裡。可你就是那個可憐的殘廢。」

passages.original: Colin forgot that he had ever had a back. His face flushed scarlet and he sat bolt upright.
passages.vernacular: 柯林忘咗佢曾有過背。佢嘅臉漲得通紅,佢挺直地坐住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 柯林忘了他曾有過背。他的臉漲得通紅,他挺直地坐著。

passages.original: “I’m not a cripple!” he cried out furiously. “I’m not!”
passages.vernacular: 「我唔係殘廢!」佢憤怒地喊道。「我唔係!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我不是殘廢!」他憤怒地喊道。「我不是!」

passages.original: “He’s not!” cried Mary, almost shouting up the wall in her fierce indignation. “He’s not got a lump as big as a pin! I looked and there was none there—not one!”
passages.vernacular: 「佢唔係!」瑪麗喊道,喺佢猛烈嘅憤慨中,幾乎係朝牆上喊。「佢連大頭針咁大嘅瘤都冇!我睇過,嗰度一個都冇——一個都冇!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他不是!」瑪麗喊道,在她猛烈的憤慨中,幾乎是朝牆上喊。「他連大頭針那麼大的瘤也沒有!我看過,那裡一個也沒有——一個也沒有!」

passages.original: Ben Weatherstaff passed his hand over his forehead again and gazed as if he could never gaze enough. His hand shook and his mouth shook and his voice shook. He was an ignorant old man and a tactless old man and he could only remember the things he had heard.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫又用手抹咗抹額頭,凝視住,好像永遠都睇唔夠。佢嘅手喺抖,佢嘅嘴喺抖,佢嘅聲音都喺抖。佢係個無知嘅老人,都係個唔會講話嘅老人,佢只記得佢聽到嘅嗰啲話。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫又用手抹了抹額頭,凝視著,好像永遠也看不夠。他的手在抖,他的嘴在抖,他的聲音也在抖。他是個無知的老人,也是個不會說話的老人,他只記得他聽到的那些話。

passages.original: “Tha’—tha’ hasn’t got a crooked back?” he said hoarsely.
passages.vernacular: 「你——你冇彎曲嘅背?」佢沙啞地講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你——你沒有彎曲的背?」他沙啞地說。

passages.original: “No!” shouted Colin.
passages.vernacular: 「冇!」柯林喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「沒有!」柯林喊道。

passages.original: “Tha’—tha’ hasn’t got crooked legs?” quavered Ben more hoarsely yet.
passages.vernacular: 「你——你冇彎曲嘅腿?」班更沙啞地顫聲講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你——你沒有彎曲的腿?」班更沙啞地顫聲說。

passages.original: It was too much. The strength which Colin usually threw into his tantrums rushed through him now in a new way. Never yet had he been accused of crooked legs—even in whispers—and the perfectly simple belief in their existence which was revealed by Ben Weatherstaff’s voice was more than Rajah flesh and blood could endure. His anger and insulted pride made him forget everything but this one moment and filled him with a power he had never known before, an almost unnatural strength.
passages.vernacular: 呢太過分喇。柯林平常用喺發脾氣上嘅力氣,而家以一種新嘅方式湧過佢全身。從來冇人講過佢有彎曲嘅腿——邊怕係低聲講——班·韋瑟斯塔夫嘅聲音所顯示嘅對佢哋存在嘅嗰種完全單純嘅信念,超出咗王公血肉之軀所能忍受嘅。佢嘅憤怒同受辱嘅驕傲讓佢忘記咗一切,只有呢一刻,並使佢充滿咗佢從未知道嘅力量,一種幾乎不自然嘅力量。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 這太過分了。柯林平常用在發脾氣上的力氣,現在以一種新的方式湧過他全身。從來沒有人說過他有彎曲的腿——哪怕是低聲說——班·韋瑟斯塔夫的聲音所顯示的對它們存在的那種完全單純的信念,超出了王公血肉之軀所能忍受的。他的憤怒和受辱的驕傲讓他忘記了一切,只有這一刻,並使他充滿了他從未知道的力量,一種幾乎不自然的力量。

passages.original: “Come here!” he shouted to Dickon, and he actually began to tear the coverings off his lower limbs and disentangle himself. “Come here! Come here! This minute!”
passages.vernacular: 「過嚟!」佢對迪肯喊道,佢真嘅開始扯掉蓋喺佢下肢上嘅嘢,把自己解脫出嚟。「過嚟!過嚟!即刻!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「過來!」他對迪肯喊道,他真的開始扯掉蓋在他下肢上的東西,把自己解脫出來。「過來!過來!馬上!」

passages.original: Dickon was by his side in a second. Mary caught her breath in a short gasp and felt herself turn pale.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯一秒鐘就到咗佢身邊。瑪麗短促地倒抽一口氣,覺得自己臉色變白。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯一秒鐘就到了他身邊。瑪麗短促地倒抽一口氣,覺得自己臉色變白。

passages.original: “He can do it! He can do it! He can do it! He can!” she gabbled over to herself under her breath as fast as ever she could.
passages.vernacular: 「佢能做到!佢能做到!佢能做到!佢能!」佢盡可能快地喺嘴裡對自己低聲急促地念叨。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他能做到!他能做到!他能做到!他能!」她盡可能快地在嘴裡對自己低聲急促地念叨。

passages.original: There was a brief fierce scramble, the rugs were tossed on the ground, Dickon held Colin’s arm, the thin legs were out, the thin feet were on the grass. Colin was standing upright—upright—as straight as an arrow and looking strangely tall—his head thrown back and his strange eyes flashing lightning.
passages.vernacular: 一陣短暫猛烈嘅忙亂,毯子被扔到地上,迪肯扶住柯林嘅手臂,瘦腿露咗出嚟,瘦腳踩喺草地上。柯林站住——站直喇——挺得像一支箭,睇起嚟奇異地高——頭向後仰,佢奇怪嘅眼睛閃住閃電。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 一陣短暫猛烈的忙亂,毯子被扔到地上,迪肯扶著柯林的手臂,瘦腿露了出來,瘦腳踩在草地上。柯林站著——站直了——挺得像一支箭,看起來奇異地高——頭向後仰,他奇怪的眼睛閃著閃電。

passages.original: “Look at me!” he flung up at Ben Weatherstaff. “Just look at me—you! Just look at me!”
passages.vernacular: 「睇住我!」佢向班·韋瑟斯塔夫甩出呢句話。「睇住我——你!睇住我!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「看著我!」他向班·韋瑟斯塔夫甩出這句話。「看著我——你!看著我!」

passages.original: “He’s as straight as I am!” cried Dickon. “He’s as straight as any lad i’ Yorkshire!”
passages.vernacular: 「佢同我一樣直!」迪肯喊道。「佢和約克郡任何一個小子一樣直!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他和我一樣直!」迪肯喊道。「他和約克郡任何一個小子一樣直!」

passages.original: What Ben Weatherstaff did Mary thought queer beyond measure. He choked and gulped and suddenly tears ran down his weather-wrinkled cheeks as he struck his old hands together.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫做嘅事,瑪麗覺得古怪得無法形容。佢哽咽、吞嚥,突然眼淚流下佢飽經風霜嘅皺紋臉頰,同時佢把粗老嘅雙手拍喺一起。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫做的事,瑪麗覺得古怪得無法形容。他哽咽、吞嚥,突然眼淚流下他飽經風霜的皺紋臉頰,同時他把粗老的雙手拍在一起。

passages.original: “Eh!” he burst forth, “th’ lies folk tells! Tha’rt as thin as a lath an’ as white as a wraith, but there’s not a knob on thee. Tha’lt make a mon yet. God bless thee!”
passages.vernacular: 「唉!」佢迸出,「人哋撒嘅謊啊!你瘦得像根木條,白得像個幽靈,不過你身上一個疙瘩都冇。你仲會成為一個男子漢。上帝保佑你!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「唉!」他迸出,「人們撒的謊啊!你瘦得像根木條,白得像個幽靈,可是你身上一個疙瘩也沒有。你還會成為一個男子漢。上帝保佑你!」

passages.original: Dickon held Colin’s arm strongly but the boy had not begun to falter. He stood straighter and straighter and looked Ben Weatherstaff in the face.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯有力地扶住柯林嘅手臂,但嗰男孩仲冇開始動搖。佢站得越嚟越直,直視班·韋瑟斯塔夫嘅臉。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯有力地扶著柯林的手臂,但那男孩還沒有開始動搖。他站得越來越直,直視班·韋瑟斯塔夫的臉。

passages.original: “I’m your master,” he said, “when my father is away. And you are to obey me. This is my garden. Don’t dare to say a word about it! You get down from that ladder and go out to the Long Walk and Miss Mary will meet you and bring you here. I want to talk to you. We did not want you, but now you will have to be in the secret. Be quick!”
passages.vernacular: 「我係你嘅主人,」佢講,「我父親不喺嘅時候。你必須服從我。呢個係我嘅花園。不許你敢講一個字!你從梯子上下嚟,到長路上去,瑪麗小姐會去接你,帶你到呢度嚟。我要同你講話。我哋本來唔好你,但而家你得進入祕密喇。快點!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我是你的主人,」他說,「我父親不在的時候。你必須服從我。這是我的花園。不許你敢說一個字!你從梯子上下來,到長路上去,瑪麗小姐會去接你,帶你到這裡來。我要同你說話。我們本來不要你,但現在你得進入祕密了。快點!」

passages.original: Ben Weatherstaff’s crabbed old face was still wet with that one queer rush of tears. It seemed as if he could not take his eyes from thin straight Colin standing on his feet with his head thrown back.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫暴躁嘅老臉仍被嗰一陣古怪嘅眼淚濕潤住。佢似乎無法把眼睛從瘦削、筆直、站喺自己腳上、頭向後仰嘅柯林身上移開。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫暴躁的老臉仍被那一陣古怪的眼淚濕潤著。他似乎無法把眼睛從瘦削、筆直、站在自己腳上、頭向後仰的柯林身上移開。

passages.original: “Eh! lad,” he almost whispered. “Eh! my lad!” And then remembering himself he suddenly touched his hat gardener fashion and said, “Yes, sir! Yes, sir!” and obediently disappeared as he descended the ladder.
passages.vernacular: 「唉!細路,」佢幾乎係低聲講。「唉!我嘅細路!」然後佢想起咗自己,突然像園丁嗰樣摸咗摸帽子,講:「係,少爺!係,少爺!」然後順從地順住梯子下去,消失喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「唉!孩子,」他幾乎是低聲說。「唉!我的孩子!」然後他想起了自己,突然像園丁那樣摸了摸帽子,說:「是,少爺!是,少爺!」然後順從地順著梯子下去,消失了。

chapters.title: Chapter XXII: When the Sun Went Down 第二十二章:日落時分

passages.original: When his head was out of sight Colin turned to Mary.
passages.vernacular: 班嘅頭消失喺視線之外後,柯林轉向瑪麗。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班的頭消失在視線之外後,柯林轉向瑪麗。

passages.original: “Go and meet him,” he said; and Mary flew across the grass to the door under the ivy.
passages.vernacular: 「去接佢,」佢講;瑪麗飛奔過草地,跑向常春藤下嘅門。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「去接他,」他說;瑪麗飛奔過草地,跑向常春藤下的門。

passages.original: Dickon was watching him with sharp eyes. There were scarlet spots on his cheeks and he looked amazing, but he showed no signs of falling.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯用銳利嘅眼睛睇住佢。佢臉頰上有鮮紅嘅斑點,佢睇上去令人驚奇,但佢冇顯出要倒下嘅跡象。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯用銳利的眼睛看著他。他臉頰上有鮮紅的斑點,他看上去令人驚奇,但他沒有顯出要倒下的跡象。

passages.original: “I can stand,” he said, and his head was still held up and he said it quite grandly.
passages.vernacular: 「我能站住,」佢講,頭仍然高高昂住,講得相當氣派。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我能站著,」他說,頭仍然高高昂著,說得相當氣派。

passages.original: “I told thee tha’ could as soon as tha’ stopped bein’ afraid,” answered Dickon. “An’ tha’s stopped.”
passages.vernacular: 「我跟你講過,你一不怕就能站,」迪肯回答。「而你不怕喇。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我跟你說過,你一不怕就能站,」迪肯回答。「而你不怕了。」

passages.original: “Yes, I’ve stopped,” said Colin.
passages.vernacular: 「對,我不怕喇,」柯林講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「對,我不怕了,」柯林說。

passages.original: Then suddenly he remembered something Mary had said.
passages.vernacular: 然後佢突然想起瑪麗講過嘅一件事。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 然後他突然想起瑪麗說過的一件事。

passages.original: “Are you making Magic?” he asked sharply.
passages.vernacular: 「你喺施魔法嗎?」佢尖銳地問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你在施魔法嗎?」他尖銳地問。

passages.original: Dickon’s curly mouth spread in a cheerful grin.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯捲曲嘅嘴咧開成一個愉快嘅笑。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯捲曲的嘴咧開成一個愉快的笑。

passages.original: “Tha’s doin’ Magic thysel’,” he said. “It’s same Magic as made these ’ere work out o’ th’ earth,” and he touched with his thick boot a clump of crocuses in the grass.
passages.vernacular: 「你自己喺施魔法,」佢講。「就係讓呢啲嘢從土裡長出嚟嘅同一種魔法,」佢用厚靴子碰咗碰草地裡嘅一叢番紅花。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你自己在施魔法,」他說。「就是讓這些東西從土裡長出來的同一種魔法,」他用厚靴子碰了碰草地裡的一叢番紅花。

passages.original: Colin looked down at them.
passages.vernacular: 柯林低頭睇佢哋。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 柯林低頭看它們。

passages.original: “Aye,” he said slowly, “there couldna’ be bigger Magic than that there—there couldna’ be.”
passages.vernacular: 「係啊,」佢慢慢地講,「唔可能有比嗰更大嘅魔法喇——唔可能。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是啊,」他慢慢地說,「不可能有比那更大的魔法了——不可能。」

passages.original: He drew himself up straighter than ever.
passages.vernacular: 佢把自己挺得比以往更直。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他把自己挺得比以往更直。

passages.original: “I’m going to walk to that tree,” he said, pointing to one a few feet away from him. “I’m going to be standing when Weatherstaff comes here. I can rest against the tree if I like. When I want to sit down I will sit down, but not before. Bring a rug from the chair.”
passages.vernacular: 「我要走到嗰棵樹嗰度,」佢講,指住離佢幾英尺遠嘅一棵。「韋瑟斯塔夫嚟嘅時候我要站住。我願意嘅話可以靠住樹休息。我想坐下時就坐下,但不喺嗰之前。從椅子上攞一條毯子嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我要走到那棵樹那裡,」他說,指著離他幾英尺遠的一棵。「韋瑟斯塔夫來的時候我要站著。我願意的話可以靠著樹休息。我想坐下時就坐下,但不在那之前。從椅子上拿一條毯子來。」

passages.original: He walked to the tree and though Dickon held his arm he was wonderfully steady. When he stood against the tree trunk it was not too plain that he supported himself against it, and he still held himself so straight that he looked tall.
passages.vernacular: 佢走向嗰棵樹,雖然迪肯扶住佢嘅手臂,佢卻穩得出奇。佢靠住樹幹站住時,不太睇得出佢係靠住佢支撐自己,佢仍把自己挺得咁直,睇起嚟好高。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他走向那棵樹,雖然迪肯扶著他的手臂,他卻穩得出奇。他靠著樹幹站著時,不太看得出他是靠著它支撐自己,他仍把自己挺得那麼直,看起來很高。

passages.original: When Ben Weatherstaff came through the door in the wall he saw him standing there and he heard Mary muttering something under her breath.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫從牆上嘅門進嚟時,睇見佢站喺嗰度,聽見瑪麗喺嘴裡嘀咕住乜嘢。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫從牆上的門進來時,看見他站在那裡,聽見瑪麗在嘴裡嘀咕著什麼。

passages.original: “What art sayin’?” he asked rather testily because he did not want his attention distracted from the long thin straight boy figure and proud face.
passages.vernacular: 「你喺講乜嘢?」佢相當暴躁地問,因為佢唔願意注意力被從嗰個又高又瘦又直嘅男孩身形同驕傲嘅臉上分散。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你在說什麼?」他相當暴躁地問,因為他不願意注意力被從那個又高又瘦又直的男孩身形和驕傲的臉上分散。

passages.original: But she did not tell him. What she was saying was this:
passages.vernacular: 但佢冇告訴佢。佢講嘅係:
passages.vernacularMandarin: 但她沒有告訴他。她說的是:

passages.original: “You can do it! You can do it! I told you you could! You can do it! You can do it! You can!”
passages.vernacular: 「你能做到!你能做到!我跟你講過你能!你能做到!你能做到!你能!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你能做到!你能做到!我跟你說過你能!你能做到!你能做到!你能!」

passages.original: She was saying it to Colin because she wanted to make Magic and keep him on his feet looking like that. She could not bear that he should give in before Ben Weatherstaff. He did not give in. She was uplifted by a sudden feeling that he looked quite beautiful in spite of his thinness. He fixed his eyes on Ben Weatherstaff in his funny imperious way.
passages.vernacular: 佢係對柯林講嘅,因為佢想施魔法,讓佢保持站住、睇起嚟嗰個樣子。佢受不了佢喺班·韋瑟斯塔夫面前認輸。佢冇認輸。佢被一種突然嘅感覺鼓舞,覺得佢儘管瘦,睇上去相當美。佢用佢嗰滑稽專橫嘅方式把眼睛盯喺班·韋瑟斯塔夫身上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 她是對柯林說的,因為她想施魔法,讓他保持站著、看起來那個樣子。她受不了他在班·韋瑟斯塔夫面前認輸。他沒有認輸。她被一種突然的感覺鼓舞,覺得他儘管瘦,看上去相當美。他用他那滑稽專橫的方式把眼睛盯在班·韋瑟斯塔夫身上。

passages.original: “Look at me!” he commanded. “Look at me all over! Am I a hunchback? Have I got crooked legs?”
passages.vernacular: 「睇住我!」佢命令。「全身都睇!我係駝背嗎?我有彎曲嘅腿嗎?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「看著我!」他命令。「全身都看!我是駝背嗎?我有彎曲的腿嗎?」

passages.original: Ben Weatherstaff had not quite got over his emotion, but he had recovered a little and answered almost in his usual way.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫仲冇完全從佢嘅情緒中恢復過嚟,但佢已恢復咗啲,幾乎用佢平常嘅方式回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫還沒完全從他的情緒中恢復過來,但他已恢復了一些,幾乎用他平常的方式回答。

passages.original: “Not tha’,” he said. “Nowt o’ th’ sort. What’s tha’ been doin’ with thysel’—hidin’ out o’ sight an’ lettin’ folk think tha’ was cripple an’ half-witted?”
passages.vernacular: 「你唔係,」佢講。「啲都唔係。你一直喺對你自己做乜嘢——躲住唔見人,讓人哋以為你係殘廢、半傻子?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你不是,」他說。「一點也不是。你一直在對你自己做什麼——躲著不見人,讓人們以為你是殘廢、半傻子?」

passages.original: “Half-witted!” said Colin angrily. “Who thought that?”
passages.vernacular: 「半傻子!」柯林憤怒地講。「邊個咁想?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「半傻子!」柯林憤怒地說。「誰這麼想?」

passages.original: “Lots o’ fools,” said Ben. “Th’ world’s full o’ jackasses brayin’ an’ they never bray nowt but lies. What did tha’ shut thysel’ up for?”
passages.vernacular: 「好多傻瓜,」班講。「世上全係驢子喺叫,牠哋叫嘅全係謊話。你把自己關起嚟幹乜嘢?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「很多傻瓜,」班說。「世上全是驢子在叫,牠們叫的全是謊話。你把自己關起來幹什麼?」

passages.original: “Everyone thought I was going to die,” said Colin shortly. “I’m not!”
passages.vernacular: 「每個人都以為我要死喇,」柯林簡短地講。「我唔會!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「每個人都以為我要死了,」柯林簡短地說。「我不會!」

passages.original: And he said it with such decision Ben Weatherstaff looked him over, up and down, down and up.
passages.vernacular: 佢講得咁堅決,班·韋瑟斯塔夫把佢上下、下上打量咗一遍。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他說得那麼堅決,班·韋瑟斯塔夫把他上下、下上打量了一遍。

passages.original: “Tha’ die!” he said with dry exultation. “Nowt o’ th’ sort! Tha’s got too much pluck in thee. When I seed thee put tha’ legs on th’ ground in such a hurry I knowed tha’ was all right. Sit thee down on th’ rug a bit young Mester an’ give me thy orders.”
passages.vernacular: 「你死!」佢帶住乾巴巴嘅得意講。「根本唔會!你身上嘅膽量太多喇。我睇到你咁急住把腿放喺地上,就知道你冇事喇。喺毯子上坐一會兒吧,小少爺,畀我下命令。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你死!」他帶著乾巴巴的得意說。「根本不會!你身上的膽量太多了。我看到你那麼急著把腿放在地上,就知道你沒事了。在毯子上坐一會兒吧,小少爺,給我下命令。」

passages.original: There was a queer mixture of crabbed tenderness and shrewd understanding in his manner. Mary had poured out speech as rapidly as she could as they had come down the Long Walk. The chief thing to be remembered, she had told him, was that Colin was getting well—getting well. The garden was doing it. No one must let him remember about having humps and dying.
passages.vernacular: 佢嘅態度中有一種奇特嘅、暴躁嘅溫柔同精明嘅了解嘅混合。佢哋沿住長路走下嚟時,瑪麗盡可能快地傾吐咗許多話。佢告訴佢,最重要要記住嘅係,柯林正在好起嚟——好起嚟。係花園喺咁做。唔能夠讓任何人使佢想起長駝背同死去。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 他的態度中有一種奇特的、暴躁的溫柔與精明的了解的混合。他們沿著長路走下來時,瑪麗盡可能快地傾吐了許多話。她告訴他,最重要要記住的是,柯林正在好起來——好起來。是花園在這麼做。不能讓任何人使他想起長駝背和死去。

passages.original: The Rajah condescended to seat himself on a rug under the tree.
passages.vernacular: 王公屈尊坐喺樹下嘅毯子上。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 王公屈尊坐在樹下的毯子上。

passages.original: “What work do you do in the gardens, Weatherstaff?” he inquired.
passages.vernacular: 「你喺花園裡做乜嘢工作,韋瑟斯塔夫?」佢問。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你在花園裡做什麼工作,韋瑟斯塔夫?」他問。

passages.original: “Anythin’ I’m told to do,” answered old Ben. “I’m kep’ on by favor—because she liked me.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢哋叫我做乜嘢我就做乜嘢,」老班回答。「我係靠恩惠被留下嘅——因為佢鍾意我。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「他們叫我做什麼我就做什麼,」老班回答。「我是靠恩惠被留下的——因為她喜歡我。」

passages.original: “She?” said Colin.
passages.vernacular: 「佢?」柯林講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「她?」柯林說。

passages.original: “Tha’ mother,” answered Ben Weatherstaff.
passages.vernacular: 「你母親,」班·韋瑟斯塔夫回答。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你母親,」班·韋瑟斯塔夫回答。

passages.original: “My mother?” said Colin, and he looked about him quietly. “This was her garden, wasn’t it?”
passages.vernacular: 「我母親?」柯林講,安靜地環顧四周。「呢個係佢嘅花園,係唔係?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我母親?」柯林說,安靜地環顧四周。「這是她的花園,是不是?」

passages.original: “Aye, it was that!” and Ben Weatherstaff looked about him too. “She were main fond of it.”
passages.vernacular: 「係啊,係嘅!」班·韋瑟斯塔夫都環顧四周。「佢好鍾意佢。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是啊,是的!」班·韋瑟斯塔夫也環顧四周。「她非常喜歡它。」

passages.original: “It is my garden now. I am fond of it. I shall come here every day,” announced Colin. “But it is to be a secret. My orders are that no one is to know that we come here. Dickon and my cousin have worked and made it come alive. I shall send for you sometimes to help—but you must come when no one can see you.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢而家係我嘅花園。我鍾意佢。我每天都要嚟,」柯林宣布。「但呢必須係個祕密。我嘅命令係,不許任何人知道我哋嚟呢度。迪肯同我表妹工作,讓佢活過嚟。我有時會叫你嚟幫忙——但你必須喺冇人睇得見你嘅時候嚟。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「它現在是我的花園。我喜歡它。我每天都要來,」柯林宣布。「但這必須是個祕密。我的命令是,不許任何人知道我們來這裡。迪肯和我表妹工作,讓它活過來。我有時會叫你來幫忙——但你必須在沒人看得見你的時候來。」

passages.original: Ben Weatherstaff’s face twisted itself in a dry old smile.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫嘅臉扭成一個乾巴巴嘅老笑。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫的臉扭成一個乾巴巴的老笑。

passages.original: “I’ve come here before when no one saw me,” he said.
passages.vernacular: 「我以前冇人睇見嘅時候嚟過呢度,」佢講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我以前沒人看見的時候來過這裡,」他說。

passages.original: “What!” exclaimed Colin. “When?”
passages.vernacular: 「乜嘢!」柯林喊道。「乜嘢時候?」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「什麼!」柯林喊道。「什麼時候?」

passages.original: “Th’ last time I was here,” rubbing his chin and looking round, “was about two year’ ago.”
passages.vernacular: 「我上次嚟呢度,」摸住下巴,環顧四周,「大約係兩年前。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我上次來這裡,」摸著下巴,環顧四周,「大約是兩年前。」

passages.original: “But no one has been in it for ten years!” cried Colin.
passages.vernacular: 「但十年嚟冇人進去過!」柯林喊道。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「但十年來沒有人進去過!」柯林喊道。

passages.original: “There was no door!”
passages.vernacular: 「冇門!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「沒有門!」

passages.original: “I’m no one,” said old Ben dryly. “An’ I didn’t come through th’ door. I come over th’ wall. Th’ rheumatics held me back th’ last two year’.”
passages.vernacular: 「我不算人,」老班乾巴巴地講。「我都唔係從門進嚟嘅。我係翻牆過嚟嘅。風濕病呢兩年攔住我。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我不算人,」老班乾巴巴地說。「我也不是從門進來的。我是翻牆過來的。風濕病這兩年攔著我。」

passages.original: “Tha’ come an’ did a bit o’ prunin’!” cried Dickon. “I couldn’t make out how it had been done.”
passages.vernacular: 「係你嚟修剪咗啲!」迪肯喊道。「我弄不明白佢係點被修剪嘅。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是你來修剪了一點!」迪肯喊道。「我弄不明白它是怎麼被修剪的。」

passages.original: “She was so fond of it—she was!” said Ben Weatherstaff slowly. “An’ she was such a pretty young thing. She says to me once, ‘Ben,’ says she laughin’, ‘if ever I’m ill or if I go away you must take care of my roses.’ When she did go away th’ orders was no one was ever to come nigh. But I come,” with grumpy obstinacy. “Over th’ wall I come—until th’ rheumatics stopped me—an’ I did a bit o’ work once a year. She’d gave her order first.”
passages.vernacular: 「佢咁鍾意佢——真嘅係!」班·韋瑟斯塔夫慢慢地講。「而佢又係咁漂亮嘅年輕人。佢有一次對我講:『班,』佢笑住講,『如果我病咗或走喇,你得照顧我嘅玫瑰。』佢真嘅走咗之後,命令係不許任何人靠近。不過我嚟喇,」帶住悶悶嘅固執。「我翻牆嚟——直到風濕病攔住我——我一年做一次活。佢先下過命令。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「她那麼喜歡它——真的是!」班·韋瑟斯塔夫慢慢地說。「而她又是那麼漂亮的年輕人。她有一次對我說:『班,』她笑著說,『如果我病了或走了,你得照顧我的玫瑰。』她真的走了之後,命令是不許任何人靠近。可是我來了,」帶著悶悶的固執。「我翻牆來——直到風濕病攔住我——我一年做一次活。她先下過命令。」

passages.original: “It wouldn’t have been as wick as it is if tha’ hadn’t done it,” said Dickon. “I did wonder.”
passages.vernacular: 「如果唔係你做喇,佢唔會像而家咁樣活住,」迪肯講。「我確實納悶過。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「如果不是你做了,它不會像現在這樣活著,」迪肯說。「我確實納悶過。」

passages.original: “I’m glad you did it, Weatherstaff,” said Colin. “You’ll know how to keep the secret.”
passages.vernacular: 「我好高興係你做嘅,韋瑟斯塔夫,」柯林講。「你會知道點保守祕密。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「我很高興是你做的,韋瑟斯塔夫,」柯林說。「你會知道怎麼保守祕密。」

passages.original: “Aye, I’ll know, sir,” answered Ben. “An’ it’ll be easier for a man wi’ rheumatics to come in at th’ door.”
passages.vernacular: 「係嘅,我會知道,少爺,」班回答。「對一個有風濕病嘅人來講,從門進嚟都容易些。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「是的,我會知道,少爺,」班回答。「對一個有風濕病的人來說,從門進來也容易些。」

passages.original: On the grass near the tree Mary had dropped her trowel. Colin stretched out his hand and took it up. An odd expression came into his face and he began to scratch at the earth. His thin hand was weak enough but presently as they watched him—Mary with quite breathless interest—he drove the end of the trowel into the soil and turned some over.
passages.vernacular: 瑪麗嘅小泥刀掉喺靠近樹嘅草地上。柯林伸出手把佢攞起嚟。一種古怪嘅表情出而家佢臉上,佢開始抓土。佢嘅瘦手好弱,但不久,當佢哋睇住佢——瑪麗興趣濃得屏住咗呼吸——佢把小泥刀尖插進土裡,翻起咗啲。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 瑪麗的小泥刀掉在靠近樹的草地上。柯林伸出手把它拿起來。一種古怪的表情出現在他臉上,他開始抓土。他的瘦手很弱,但不久,當他們看著他——瑪麗興趣濃得屏住了呼吸——他把小泥刀尖插進土裡,翻起了一些。

passages.original: “You can do it! You can do it!” said Mary to herself. “I tell you, you can!”
passages.vernacular: 「你能做到!你能做到!」瑪麗對自己講。「我告訴你,你能!」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你能做到!你能做到!」瑪麗對自己說。「我告訴你,你能!」

passages.original: Dickon’s round eyes were full of eager curiousness but he said not a word. Ben Weatherstaff looked on with interested face.
passages.vernacular: 迪肯圓圓嘅眼睛充滿咗熱切嘅好奇,但佢一個字都冇講。班·韋瑟斯塔夫帶住感興趣嘅臉睇住。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 迪肯圓圓的眼睛充滿了熱切的好奇,但他一個字也沒說。班·韋瑟斯塔夫帶著感興趣的臉看著。

passages.original: Colin persevered. After he had turned a few trowelfuls of soil he spoke exultantly to Dickon in his best Yorkshire.
passages.vernacular: 柯林堅持住。佢翻咗幾泥刀土之後,用佢最好嘅約克郡話得意地對迪肯講。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 柯林堅持著。他翻了幾泥刀土之後,用他最好的約克郡話得意地對迪肯說。

passages.original: “Tha’ said as tha’d have me walkin’ about here same as other folk—an’ tha’ said tha’d have me diggin’. I thowt tha’ was just leein’ to please me. This is only th’ first day an’ I’ve walked—an’ here I am diggin’.”
passages.vernacular: 「你講過你要我像別人一樣喺呢度走動——你講過你要我挖地。我以為你只係為了討我高興講謊。呢才第一天,我走喇——而家我喺挖地。」
passages.vernacularMandarin: 「你說過你要我像別人一樣在這裡走動——你說過你要我挖地。我以為你只是為了討我高興說謊。這才第一天,我走了——現在我在挖地。」

passages.original: Ben Weatherstaff’s mouth fell open again when he heard him, but he ended by chuckling.
passages.vernacular: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫聽到佢嘅話,嘴又張開喇,但最後佢咯咯笑喇。
passages.vernacularMandarin: 班·韋瑟斯塔夫聽到他的話,嘴又張開了,但最後他咯咯笑了。

passages.original: “Eh!” he said, “that sounds as if tha’d got wits enow. Tha’rt a Yorkshire lad for sure. An’ tha’rt diggin’, too. How’d tha’ like to plant a bit o’ somethin’? I can get thee a rose in a pot.”
